To address this challenge, we employ a decomposition approach, breaking the original problem into more manageable sub-problems with smoother diffusion processes. Solutions to these sub-problems are then combined to obtain an optimal control policy for the original problem. Through a technique called vanishing memory filtering, we establish a key estimate that enables us to converge to the desired solution by relaxing the memory effect as the time step decreases. As a result, we develop a viable numerical approach for approximating optimal control solutions, even when working with rough data sets. This method allows us to leverage established results for smooth systems while accommodating non-smooth state processes. Ultimately, we demonstrate numerically the effectiveness of this method in achieving high accuracy. The proposed approach holds broader relevance for modeling and numerical approximation in the presence of non-smooth processes. The model studied here can be seen as an extension of the Euler-Arvad model, a renowned stochastic integral system known for its rough dynamics. As such, this study provides a novel solution to the corresponding control problem, a long-standing challenge in the field. Ultimately, this study addresses an urgent need in the field, as many stochastic systems with non-degenerate diffusion components are inherently ill-posed, necessitating the incorporation of degenerate diffusion processes to maintain solvability. The success of cancer immunotherapy depends on several factors, including the ability to analyze digitized tissue sections for tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. To enhance this process, a comprehensive dataset of lymphocyte nuclei was created for the purpose of evaluating algorithms designed for their recognition. The dataset consists of 700 lymphocyte nuclei images, obtained from various tissue samples that were digitized at different resolutions, and contains diverse features such as morphology, orientation, and location. To evaluate the algorithms' performance, the dataset was divided into two parts: a training set of 300 images and a testing set of 400 images with different digitization levels. To determine the effectiveness of digitization-independent algorithms, the same algorithm was applied to the training set at multiple digitization levels. The results showed that the best accuracy achieved was 84.75%, which was obtained through a deep learning algorithm that was trained and tested without the use of transfer learning. The study demonstrates the potential for digitization-independent analysis of lymphocyte nuclei and suggests that future research can further improve the accuracy by incorporating additional features such as lymphocyte morphology and inter-nucleus relationships. Ultimately, this work has implications for the development of more effective cancer immunotherapy treatments. The dataset created for this study is available online for the purpose of advancing the research in this field.

Deepening convolutional networks like TCNs typically leads to significant efficiency gains but often results in increased model size and inference latency. We've developed an automated dilation optimizer that enhances TCNs while minimizing model growth and latency. Our optimizer gradually adjusts dilation rates across network layers to remove unnecessary dimensions and pack more computational power into smaller layers, promoting a balance between depth and width. It achieves this by solving a constrained layer optimization problem, seamlessly integrated into a unified TCN framework. Experimental results show our automatically optimized TCNs outperform baseline models with the same parameters in both real-world video classification and synthetic sequence prediction tasks, also demonstrating the approach leads to consistent improvements when comparing models of varying parameter counts. The optimized models exhibit compact models with improved accuracy and a remarkable 23.4% average reduction in latency while maintaining or surpassing the accuracy of significantly deeper networks. The recent data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) concerning the harmonic flow coefficients and elliptic flow fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions has been reanalyed with the aim of understanding the density and temperature properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). Initially, the initial state conditions were obtained by utilizing the Monte Carlo Glauber model and then the Lindhard approach was employed to link the QGP's macroscopic properties to the observed flow fluctuations. It was found that the observed v2 fluctuations stem primarily from the hydrodynamic response driven by the QGP's density-density interactions rather than the temperature fluctuations. Furthermore, the ratio of the QGP's density and temperature properties was determined to be approximately 0.15 $\pm$ 0.02 by leveraging the observed v2 coefficient and elliptic flow fluctuations at 5.02 TeV lead-lead collisions. This density to temperature ratio is consistent with existing theoretical predictions derived from the Functional Massive Gradient Expansion Method. It is also inferred that the QGP's density plays a more significant role than its temperature in driving the observed flow patterns. It is also demonstrated that the observed v2 coefficient is predominantly governed by the hydrodynamic response to initial anisotropic density distributions rather than the anisotropic temperature distributions. It is anticipated that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the QGP's thermodynamic properties, specifically its density and temperature relationships, which underpin the phenomenon of flow in heavy-ion collisions. It is also hoped that this analysis will pave the way for further exploration of the QGP's macroscopic properties through flow pattern analysis in future LHC experiments at higher energies. It is also proposed that this analysis be extended to include proton-proton collisions with the aim of uncovering the underlying mechanisms governing the observed flow patterns in these collisions. It is also suggested that this research be complemented by theoretical models that directly link the QGP's density and temperature properties to flow pattern observations. It is also hoped that this analysis, coupled with theoretical advancements, will provide a more coherent framework for interpreting flow pattern data across various heavy-ion collision experiments in the future. It is also proposed that this research be expanded to include observations beyond the v2 coefficient such as the cumulative flow and flow correlations which may offer further insight into the QGP's density and temperature properties. By incorporating TV-regression techniques and utilizing low-rank updates, we establish an efficient method for TV-PARX parameter estimation. To facilitate efficient learning of complex manipulation tasks from a limited number of demonstrations, we propose a framework that utilizes Neural Descriptor Fields. This approach leverages a neural network to define a symbolic representation of object relationships within a scene, and trains the network to predict task-related attributes from raw visual and tactile sensory data. By optimizing a loss function that minimizes the discrepancy between predicted attributes and task objectives, the network can learn to recognize the structural connectivity of objects within a graspable reach, even without demonstrations. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach by developing a series of reinforcement learning agents that master a range of manipulation tasks on the NJU-ITSO dataset with significant reductions in demonstration requirements. Our results show that our method significantly outperforms alternative comparison policies and efficiently learns to perform tasks with a small number of learning trials. Furthermore, we highlight the ability of our approach to support hierarchical task learning by successfully transferring knowledge from simpler to more complex tasks. This highlights the potential of Neural Descriptor Fields to tackle the fundamental challenge of learning to generalize across multiple, unrelated demonstrations in complex manipulation tasks. A newly analyzed population in the core of the high-metallicity Galactic globular cluster Tononzintla 2 has revealed a higher central density and a distinct distribution of stellar mass compared to other metal-rich cluster counterparts such as M22 and M55. Tononzintla 2's central region was studied through a spatially resolved spectroscopic analysis using the APOGEE-2 survey, which provided a comprehensive insight into the cluster's chemical composition. The data showed a significant metallicity and abundance spread within the cluster, with an overabundance of alpha-elements and a lower abundance of iron in its outer regions, which is an unusual pattern observed in Tononzintla 2. This unusual chemical composition, along with the presence of multiple stellar populations sharing the same Strömberg 7 radial abundance trend lines, supports the cluster's classification as a metal-rich globular cluster with multiple generations of stars. The presence of an extended horizontal branch and a relatively small compact central density typical of second-generation clusters in the Gaia survey is also a distinguishing feature of Tononzintla 2. This study analyzes the underlying structure of the dependency graph in the Formal Proof Archive of the Cauchy Candidate for Pi ($\pi$). The archive is a comprehensive collection of formally proven theorems from the Lean proof assistant, offering a unique opportunity to explore the complex relationships within its dependency graph. The distribution of nodes in the dependency graph reveals a notable deviation from random connectivity, instead exhibiting similarities to scale-free models. However, the magnitude of the pole does change with the number of color charges in the system. In particular, for $N=4$, the magnitude of the pole is roughly half of its value when $N=2$. This decrease in magnitude with increasing $N$ indicates a widening of the Mott smear and implies that the distance between adjacent Skyrme instantons grows with the number of color charges. Consequently, the density of instantons falls with rising $N$. Furthermore, the fall in instanton density with increasing $N$ is steeper than the rise in instanton density with decreasing quark mass. Additionally, we observed that the angular distribution of instantons is unaffected by the number of quark flavors but is modified by the quark mass. In contrast, the radial distribution of instantons is influenced both by the number of quark flavors and the quark mass. Lastly, we found that the deconfinement aspect of instantons is also impacted by the quark mass. In the presence of four quark flavors, the mass of the quark appears to counteract the effects of color charge on instanton sum confinement. It is possible that this is related to the phenomenon of vanishing quark mass at the conformal phase transition. It is also possible that this phenomenon may occur in the presence of only two quark flavors. It would be worthwhile to investigate this further, perhaps by studying the conformal phase transition in QCD in three dimensions with a range of quark flavors. It is also worth considering whether the relationship between antiperiodic instantons and the conformal phase transition, observed in lattice simulations at the conformal phase transition in QCD in four dimensions, extends to QCD in three dimensions. By integrating projection information from multiple sensors, a robot can accurately determine the pose of complex objects even in difficult environments. Unfortunately, conventional approaches that combine multiple projections typically assume a high image quality, which is not always feasible in real-world applications due to image noise and noxious conditions. As a result, the combined projections may be corrupted, making reliable object pose estimation impossible. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel algorithm that allows the inclusion of low-quality projections in object pose estimation. By linking similar projections together, our method (called projection grouping) identifies sets of similar features across images, effectively filtering out noisy information and incorporating only the valid projections. We demonstrate through extensive experiments that our technique outperforms industry-standard algorithms in both simulation and real-world scenarios, achieving a significant improvement in object pose accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, our method exhibits exceptional scalability, capable of processing thousands of projections simultaneously. Additionally, a user-friendly API and accompanying dataset and benchmarks are made publicly available to facilitate advancements in this area. By addressing the inclusion of low-quality projections, our algorithm paves the way for more reliable and robust object pose estimation in challenging, vision-based applications. This research is focused on analyzing the high-speed cavity formation and surface seal dynamics encountered in the failure of a thin metallic sheet with a pre-existing hole under drop impacts. A specially designed test setup enabled the capture of this cavity formation process at extremely high speeds (>10^6 fps) using intensified cameras and optical systems. The observed phenomena included the creation of a persistent thin film over the hole, the formation of a lip around the hole due to material accumulation, and the eventual rupture of this lip. The developed analytical models accurately predicted the pressure reduction inside the cavity, the film thickness, and the lip's formation and rupture behavior for various impact speeds. However, the models also indicated that the formation of a persistent film relies on the non-continuum effects and cannot be explained by standard fluid dynamics theories. The model's validity was further supported by experiments conducted with a surface that had already undergone initial failure and demonstrated its capability to anticipate the shift in pressure, film thickness, and lip formation/rupture behavior for different impact speeds. The models further suggested that the lip's formation and failure speed exhibit similar speeds to the film's failure speed due to the same underlying mechanism. The models were also capable of predicting the increase in failure speed with a harder sheet as it adheres to the square root relationship with the impact speed. The development of these models provides a deeper understanding of the high-speed cavity formation and surface seal dynamics involved in sheet metal failure with a hole and has the potential to expand its scope to different types of materials and geometries. Using the Wess-Zumino-Novikov-Alanis-Wightman model, we calculate the one-loop partition function for a bosonic string in a curved, two-dimensional spacetime with a U(1) symmetry. Our calculations confirm a generalized version of the Witten effect, which indicates that the ground state of the system, when coupled with gravity, has a charged state corresponding to the Witten effect. Furthermore, we find that the charged state is a fractional fermion state with a charge proportional to its mass, and that the zero-mode sector contributes a Cosmological Constant-like potential in a way that is consistent with the Witten effect. This suggests that the generalized version may be a manifestation of the Einstein gravity theory in two dimensions. Additionally, we observe that the charged state can be interpreted as a harvest of virtual fermions, and that their realisation requires a specific contribution from the fermionic sector that repacks the collective modes of the Wess-Zumino-Novikov-Alanis-Wightman field into gravitational and fractionally charged particles. This concept may have implications for understanding the relationship between the spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity and the harmonic term in the Wess-Zumino-Novikov-Alanis-Wightman action. We also find that the fractionally charged state can be linked to the harmonic term's Novikov algebras through the generalized Witten effect, providing these algebras are carefully selected to match the charged state's properties derived from the generalised Witten effect. This connection between the spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity and the harmonic term's algebras is an instance of what we term 'Witten's Harvest'. Finally, we propose that Witten's Harvest may be an intrinsic aspect of quantum gravity, enabling the harmonic term to predict the charged states of gravitational solitons through its algebras, foreshadowing a deeper comprehension of the relationship between the harmonic term and gravitational symmetries that emerge from its realization. This could potentially unlock the ability to derive the algebras of symmetry groups that emerge in quantum gravity, given the harmonic term's parameters, thereby offering a novel, physically motivated approach to classifying such algebras. This new approach to classifying algebras of symmetry groups emerging in quantum gravity is here referred to as 'Witten's Legacy'. Suggested further research includes using Witten's Legacy to classify the algebras of symmetry groups associated with higher spin gravitational solitons, and investigating its connections to conformal field theories

Our proposed system, OctopOS, is an innovative, multi-layer operating system adaptation for smartphones that provides a robust defense against sophisticated, high-risk threats like advanced mobile malware. By isolating critical functions and implementing a specially designed microkernel, OctopOS separates vulnerable application layers from essential services and securely manages privileged operations. To further enhance its security, OctopOS introduces a unique, multi-layer authentication mechanism, authenticating each layer separately to prevent malware from impersonating other layers and gaining unauthorized access. Additionally, OctopOS's microkernel is uniquely positioned to provide efficient, high-granularity access control, effectively limiting malware's ability to behave maliciously. We demonstrate the effectiveness of OctopOS by adapting it for Android and conducting a series of experiments using a modified version of the Dewey testing framework. Our results show that OctopOS can detect and prevent sophisticated malware attacks, such as those involving device authentication and data encryption, even when running concurrently with trusted applications. We also examine the practical implications and potential for adapting OctopOS to other mobile operating systems. Our analysis suggests that OctopOS's multi-layer design can serve as a secure foundation for developing a variety of mobile applications, including those involving critical infrastructure, while its scalable architecture makes it suitable for a range of platform configurations. To facilitate further research, we are making the Android version of OctopOS's source code freely available for download and modification. Through this work, we aim to inspire the development of secure, multi-layer operating systems for smartphones and contribute to creating a more reliable foundation for mobile applications. The results show that FPG outperforms the baseline algorithms, including the standard policy gradient method and the corrupted environment's optimal policy. We examine single-photon catalyzed coherent states produced via beam splitters and parametric amplifiers to gauge their quantum advantage in channel loss scenarios. Both types of states exhibit amplified amplitudes with minimal increased vacuum component, yet their structure and associated success probabilities vary notably. Notably, single-photon catalyzed coherent states generated via beam splitters possess substantially higher channel loss tolerance, indicating a potential application in robust, multi-use quantum communication. Furthermore, we find that the catalyzed states' quantum advantage in channel loss tolerance is a result of their structure, which distributes photons over multiple modes, thereby increasing the probability of successful transmission even in the presence of loss. This concept is exemplified through the realization of the quantum telepathy protocol using a beam splitter-based single-photon catalyzed coherent state, demonstrating the potential of multi-photon catalytic states for enhancing quantum communication over lossy channels.

To enhance the performance on this task, this paper proposes a novel architecture called Dilated Dense Attention Unet, which is a modification of the widely used Unet framework. The proposed DDAUnet model leverages a dense attention block to focus on specific image features and incorporate Dilated Conv2d to expand the attention mechanism's coverage while maintaining efficient computation. To evaluate the effectiveness of this model, it was applied to automatic segmentation of esophageal tumors from endoscopic video frames, yielding notable improvements in accuracy and real-time processing capability compared to established networks. Moreover, the method's practical utility was demonstrated through demanding scenario simulations and a proposed strategy for tumor segmentation from raw endoscopic video streams. Source code is available at https://github.com/zhengdf1123/DDAUnet. Experimental data has been uploaded to https://drive.google.

Real-time formation evaluation applications require both speed and accuracy, especially in complex hydraulic fracturing scenarios. To achieve this, the industry has been using general-purpose computers for hours or even days to calculate results. We've developed a method that uses a specialized algorithm to break down the problem into smaller, solvable parts, allowing for rapid "sketch" calculations to narrow down possibilities and subsequently refine the results. This approach was tested on actual well data and showed a significant reduction in computation time while maintaining accurate results. By leveraging the power of high-performance computers and the new algorithm, it's now possible to get accurate results in a matter of minutes, marking a major improvement in the efficiency of formation evaluation. Furthermore, this method has the potential to handle more complex scenarios and could also be applied to other inverse problems in the industry. To make this breakthrough accessible to the broader community, we're sharing the details of the algorithm under a permissive license. By openly discussing this method, we hope to spark further innovation and contribute to the advancement of the industry through collaborative problem-solving. To build upon this work, we're also providing the source code for this algorithm as a starting point for future development. We believe this open approach will not only speed up the adoption of this method but also facilitate ongoing improvement and refinement. This study confirms the existing hypothesis that named entity recognition (NER) can benefit from general knowledge. To further test this idea, we explore whether NER systems are strengthened by corpus-level information when both entity-level and corpus-level knowledge are available. To achieve this, we implement and evaluate both zero-shot and multi-task NER models utilizing BERT and employ six different entity types in Japanese NER. Our research employs the standard evaluation metric for NER, precision, and reveals that the models are equally effective regardless of whether entity-level knowledge alone is used or a combination of entity-level and corpus-level information is employed. Nonetheless, we find a notable increase in the model's ability to recognize entities in unseen texts when corpus-level information is incorporated. This added capability enables the model to excel in the zero-shot NER setting, allowing it to successfully identify entities in types that were not explicitly included in the entity-level data, thereby demonstrating a genuine advantage of using corpus-level information. Moreover, we find that the multi-task model performs comparably to the zero-shot model, and the benefit of corpus-level information is equally evident. Ultimately, we conclude that the benefit of corpus-level information extends beyond the particular models employed in this study, as the results mirror those reported in earlier studies conducted with English NER models. Consequently, this research offers additional evidence supporting the notion that named entity recognition is enhanced by corpus-level information. Furthermore, we also discover that the BERT-based NER model performs entity recognition with an F-score of approximately 80% when no entity-level information is employed, relying solely on corpus-level information. This finding is noteworthy because it implies that models utilizing corpus-level information have a built-in NER capability, potentially giving them a level of robustness. Nonetheless, it is also evident that entity-level information is still indispensable for developing high-performance NER models. Ultimately, our research suggests that the primary function of corpus-level information in NER models is to facilitate the transfer of entity information, rather than providing entity recognition functionality in its own right. As a complementary aspect, we also investigate the relationship between NER performance and corpus-level information density. Our research employs the density of named entities within the corpus as a reference point to measure the density of NER, thereby providing initial evidence that NER performance is linked to local NER density rather than overall corpus density. Nonetheless, the exact nature of the relationship between NER performance and corpus-level information density remains a topic for further research and analysis. The first part of this work builds upon a prior discovery by Gelfand, Kapranov, and Lakshmi, which links the variety of bitangents to a given curve and demonstrates that for certain curves with a high degree, this variety becomes rational. However, this reasoning only applies in the non-singular case. The second part of this research expands on the concepts of tropicalization and its relevance to algebraic geometry. It analyzes how the rationality of varieties like those of bitangents can be understood through the intersection of capacities in a simpler, numerical context. The third part explores a quartic curve in a plane and its associated varieties of bitangents. By examining the limitations imposed by its singular points and the "twisting" of its edges, the study reveals that certain rational components of these varieties are affected by the edge twisting, while others are not. The work also presents an alternative, geometric explanation for their rationality. The fourth part generalizes this finding to a broader class of curves. The fifth part applies this understanding to a related problem involving Schubert varieties and their association with linear subspaces. The research also offers numerical capacity theorems that can be used to determine the rationality of varieties in this context. The study also provides an example of a quartic curve in a plane whose associated varieties of bitangents have components that are non-rational in 2-dimensional spaces. The discovery is counter to the initial conjecture by Gelfand, Kapranov, and Lakshmi. The work also explores the connection between the rationality of these varieties and the concept of "filling" or completing these varieties to a higher-dimensional space. The study demonstrates that the rationality of these completed varieties can indicate whether the components of these varieties are rational in the lower-dimensional space. The research further reveals that the non-rational components of these varieties occur in a context where these completed varieties are also non-rational. The study also establishes a link between the twisting of these edge sets and the non-rational components of these varieties. The research also provides a definition of a new geometric concept called "T*4". The study demonstrates that this concept is a complete set of invariants for the classification of all possible varieties of bitangents associated with a given curve. The research also explores how this concept can be understood in a broader context of algebraic geometry. The work also presents an analysis of the properties of this concept, particularly its rationality, in relation to a wide variety of different types of curves

Researchers have successfully demonstrated the feasibility of using spatial audio and machine learning to accurately determine the position of users in virtual reality environments. However, the existing methods require sophisticated hardware and advanced computing devices. This paper presents a novel, low-cost system that uses two-dimensional spatial audio and deep learning to track users' positions. The system utilizes a simple, low-cost playback device and learns to identify the source based on bidirectional audio data from users. Our test results showed that the proposed algorithm is highly effective in pinpointing the source, with an average error of 7.5 cm when using a low-cost speaker and 4.5 cm when using a high-end one. Furthermore, we found that the algorithm performs well across various environments and can accurately determine the source even when the user moves significant distances. Additionally, we found that using bidirectional audio and a deep learning algorithm enhances the source-localization performance significantly. This suggests that the system has potential for tracking users in more complex, three-dimensional environments. We also found that the algorithm performs well when used with multiple simultaneous audio sources. The proposed system's simplicity and low cost make it an appealing solution for VR and AR applications that rely on audio feedback, such as video games and audio-based navigation tools. The system's track record of accurate source localization, coupled with its low cost, could also pave the way for new research applications, such as monitoring people's behavior in response to changing audio environments. This paper offers a comprehensive exploration of the proposed system, including its design, testing, and performance evaluation. Multilingual societies require a variety of services including information access, social media monitoring, and public opinion analysis that can be time-consuming and costly to establish across different languages. To facilitate the development of such cross-lingual applications, this study focuses on enhancing multilingual capabilities for pre-trained language models through a simple, efficient method called progressive zero-shot generalization. We fine-tune the model on non-target languages by replacing the output classifier and adapting the hidden representations, and evaluate this approach on six tasks and 13 language pairs using the PZ-ENGL benchmark. The results show that our method surpasses previous methods by achieving comparable performance to zero-shot generalization on average and outperforming it in some cases. Moreover, the model extends state-of-the-art performance to new language pairs such as English-Afrikaans and English-Swahili, and effectively utilizes resources from one language to improve performance in another, a phenomenon we call the "language resource boost". The code and model have been made available at https://github.com/THUNUSAI/pz-engl. To facilitate practical applications, we have launched an online demo at https://www.toutiao.com/c/6931458764258386175/. Future work will explore expanding this method to other tasks and models.

The growing popularity of computer vision technology like image description generation remains underexplored by automated evaluation methods. Current evaluation metrics such as accuracy and semantic similarity fall short of capturing the necessary aspects of high-quality image descriptions, especially considering the diverse needs of images descriptions, especially for visually impaired users. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for automated evaluation of image descriptions that prioritizes accessibility. This framework incorporates accessibility principles and incorporates user feedback from visually impaired individuals to assess image description quality. To support this, we also establish a dataset for automated evaluation of image descriptions in a visually impaired-centric context. The success of this framework relies on a combination of cutting-edge techniques including multi-modal models, attention mechanisms in deep learning, and style transfer networks. This paves the way for the development of more reliable and user-centric image description evaluation methods that align with the evolving requirements of computer vision technology. This framework's scope is expansive and its applications are broad, making it suitable for various multimedia evaluation tasks. This is exemplified through a case study involving automated video caption evaluation. The code and model for this research are available on GitHub at https://github.com/sonrojyanto/VAEIC. The dataset established through this research is accessible at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/0ADt1d9XTsQ1tdu. Accurate calculations of energy loss functions for Tantalum oxide molecules are challenging due to the large distance between the Ta+ core and the surrounding O atoms, which results in the influence of local field effects and spin-orbit coupling being significant. To address this issue, a method is developed by combining the restricted density functional theory with the one-photon exchange interaction, allowing for precise computation of dielectric functions. The proposed approach is verified by comparing with general gradientless RPA and TDLDA methods, and is found to yield improved results when spin-orbit coupling is considered. The method is applied to calculate the energy loss spectra of Ta+ @ O6 and Ta+ @ O8 clusters, showing that the vacuum gap in Ta+ can be reduced by approximately 1eV due to its interaction with nearby O atoms. Furthermore, the influence of spin-orbit coupling on the energy loss spectra is found to be substantial, resulting in shifts of up to 1eV in energy loss peaks. The proposed method offers a theoretical framework for understanding the electronic properties of single atom oxides in a vacuum and their interaction with surrounding molecules. The developed algorithm is also applicable to larger systems such as single atom salts where vacuum gaps of a few eV may be affected by single atom cores. The implementation of this method is feasible with current first principle codes. The computational tool developed in this study can potentially be expanded to consider other interactions like electron-photon, electron-phonon, and electron-magnetic field interactions. The proposed method is an advancement over current methods such as GGA+U, LDA+U, and SDA-RPA, as it takes into account local field effects and spin-orbit coupling more accurately. The study also highlights the significance of combining restricted density functional theory with one-photon exchange interaction in computing dielectric functions, especially for systems with large vacuum gaps. The proposed method is an evolution of current methods such as general RPA and TDLDA, as it considers j-dependent orbitals and spin-orbit coupling more accurately. The theory that voters are sorting themselves into like-minded communities has far-reaching implications for how information spreads online. This study examines the idea that the internet amplifies partisan biases, leading to limitless polarization. To investigate, we analyzed search queries, browsing history, online reading habits, social media use, news consumption, browsing patterns, political leanings, voting history, geographic location, internet usage frequency, device usage, online activities, news sources, political affiliation, and news reading frequency for over 1.6 million users in the United States. Our analysis reveals that users are indeed separated into geographical and online communities based on their partisan biases, but we found limited evidence to support the infinite polarization model. Instead, we discovered that users are actively seeking information that confirms their existing views, but this behavior appears to be a response to news sources that compromise their beliefs rather than a driver of polarization itself. To illustrate this, we used two scenarios: first, in which users encountered news that confirmed their views at a significantly lower rate than news that contradicted them; and second, in which users encountered news that threatened their beliefs almost as frequently as news that confirmed them. In the first scenario, we observed a significant increase in polarization, but in the second scenario, the effect was much less pronounced. Overall, our findings suggest that the internet may accelerate polarization, but the primary cause may be the ready availability of information that confirms users' existing views, making it necessary to reevaluate the concept of sorted communities. To this end, we propose an alternative explanation for the online spread of misinformation, one that is grounded in research, and suggest strategies for mitigating polarization, including promoting diverse online communities and news consumption. Ultimately, our analysis underscores the significance of online community structure in the dissemination of information, particularly in large, geographically segregated populations. To effectively combat the infinite polarization phenomenon, we must consider the online environment as a complementary component of society, one that is inextricably linked to offline community dynamics. Consequently, we should develop more comprehensive theories that account for the interplay between these online and offline communities. To this end, we outline a statistical framework for modeling this relationship and propose research into methods for identifying and estimating model parameters. By doing so, we can gain a deeper understanding of how online and offline communities influence one another and ultimately develop more impactful interventions to address the infinite polarization phenomenon. The potential of machine learning to enhance and accelerate various tasks has long been established but is often hindered due to high computational requirements or the need for extensive annotation. This challenge can be addressed by incorporating human decision-making into the learning process, allowing for fast and low-cost human-in-the-loop learning. This approach involves leveraging human judgment to refine the learning process, thus combining the benefits of artificial and human intelligence. This paper provides an overview of human-in-the-loop machine learning, covering its fundamental concepts, recent advances, and potential applications, and also highlights a key aspect - efficiency in human usage. Furthermore, it highlights several opportunities and outlines a future direction for this field, which holds significant promise due to its ability to offer cost-effective and fast solutions for complex problems. This direction is supported by the growing accessibility to large datasets, robust machine learning frameworks, and widespread adoption of machine learning. This paper aims to inspire further research in this area by providing an in-depth survey of human-in-the-loop learning, which is anticipated to open up numerous paths for exploration. This is particularly relevant in areas like data labeling, where current methods are predominantly focused on optimizing specific objectives rather than overall efficiency. This paper proposes a general framework for human-in-the-loop learning and suggests an initial assessment of its applicability to concurrent data labeling tasks. This is accompanied by a novel theoretical analysis that is supported by concurrent data labeling benchmark experiments, demonstrating that even basic variants of this approach can lead to significant performance improvements and models with reduced parameters. This is accompanied by a practical demonstration on a real-world concurrent data labeling task from the domain of special event detection, which is a critical application that requires extensive and expensive annotation. This event detection task is critical for applications such as community sensing, emergency response, and targeted advertising, among others. This paper also introduces a real-world concurrent data labeling platform called HIVE, which is designed for fast and low-cost annotation by unlabelled workers on modern annotation platforms. This is accompanied by a theoretical analysis that demonstrates the efficacy of this approach, which is supported by experiments on concurrent data labeling benchmarks and a real-world event detection dataset. We investigate the capacity of automatic speech recognition to capture semantic concepts in voices during learning tasks. Unlike previous studies which focused primarily on single variation factors such as variations in instructions or task types, our research aims to examine the speech recognition performance when confronted with multiple factors that influence speech, including variations in instructions, task types and error levels. Additionally, we seek to understand whether using audio instructions instead of text-based instructions affects this capability and provide a preliminary exploration of the underlying mental processes. To achieve this, we designed a crowd-sourced experiment in which participants were asked to complete tasks in response to either audio or text instructions, with or without errors, and with varying task types. The results showed that increasing error levels and task complexity led to a decline in the accuracy of speech recognition, while using audio instructions improved the accuracy to some extent. However, the overall accuracy remained lower than the accuracy achieved with text-based instructions. The findings also revealed that speech recognition performance was similar to the performance of humans in identifying semantic concepts, suggesting that the speech recognition model is influenced by the same underlying processes. The model is thought to encode input information through a limited short-term memory mechanism that is similar to the process proposed by the Minimalist Program in linguistics. The proposed model offers the potential for the integration of speech recognition and semantic concept recognition, and has implications for the hypothesis that the syntax of speech influences the sequence of speech. The study's results also raise questions about the nature of the errors made by speech recognition software and their potential impact on the model's performance. The study's design and the acknowledged limitations of the study are also discussed, including the use of a crowd-sourced approach that may limit the generalizability of the findings. The study's theory-driven design is contrasted with the prevailing practice of speech recognition research, and the study's results are seen as a step towards the development of a more theoretically grounded speech recognition model. The Generalized Staged Flow Algorithm (GSA) addresses the challenge of large-scale ordered tree generation by dividing the process into multiple stages and leveraging stage-wise dependencies. However, GSA's complexity restricts its flexibility, particularly when it comes to variable degree ordering. To enhance its generality, we modify the algorithm to allow for degree ordering adjustments and successfully extend it to generate ordered trees based on differential equations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the augmented algorithm to multiple problems and evaluate its performance using a set of highly complex test cases. The augmented GSA's increased computational efficiency and flexibility make it an improved version of the original algorithm. The code for this research is openly accessible on GitHub, featuring an intuitive mark-up language for tree specifications. Additionally, the project webpage includes example applications and detailed documentation. The augmented GSA is now freely available online.

In the evaluations section of the paper, we provide empirical analysis of the augmented GSA's performance on multiple challenging test sets. Conversational systems are increasingly integral to user interaction on mobile devices, prompting industry and academia to develop automated testing frameworks. However, creating and employing these frameworks poses difficulties, including designing suitable protocols for testing and comparing the performance of different models. Furthermore, the lack of a standardized approach for testing and evaluating conversational models persists. To address this issue, we present ConvTest, an open-source testing framework for API-based conversational models that can be configured to assess a range of performance indicators. ConvTest is adaptable across various model architectures and has been successfully applied to evaluate the performance of different pre-trained models, incorporating both single-turn and stateful models, within the Dialog-State Tracker task. Our research involving professional users revealed that ConvTest's testing protocols are time-efficient and comparable to industry standards. Ultimately, our framework facilitates the enhancement of conversational model quality through automated testing and facilitates collaboration among developers, researchers, and users in evaluating the performance of these models. ConvTest is available for download at https://github.com/shu3la/ConvTest.

Using pre-trained models to enhance memory-based methods has led to significant breakthroughs in neural machine translation. Our research focuses on developing a cross-lingual memory retriever to leverage multilingual data for improved performance. Unlike conventional bilingual translation memory approaches, our model utilizes a bilingual vector representation to allow for flexible memory retrieval. In particular, we employed a multi-layer BERT model to establish a rich contextual representation for both source and target language memories. The model's capability to maintain bilingual contextual representations enabled us to develop a retriever that can accurately identify relevant source language memories for target language sentences. Our results show that this cross-lingual retriever outperforms traditional bilingual translation memory models and significantly improves translation performance on low-resource and medium-resource settings, also demonstrating comparable performance to strong data augmentation methods on high-resource settings. Recent findings from Planck and WMAP on cosmic microwave background (CMB) anomalies have sparked new life in theories beyond the standard model. Certain scenarios, such as the Hawking point model and the dodecahedral model, could be confirmed through the presence of specific features in the CMB. However, these models might be undermined if the observed anomalies are artificial, resulting from the effects of the sky's observed edges on the model's parameters. This study employs fast spherical harmonic transforms and a realistic treatment of the sky's observed domain to address this issue. By analyzing the impact of the sky's edges on the detection of both the Hawking point model and the dodecahedral model, it is found that the effects of the sky's edges significantly alter the model's parameter estimates and that the models' signatures are altered in a way that could be misinterpreted as variance, thus rendering the proposed tests for the models' validity unreliable. Consequently, if the models are to be evaluated through cross-correlations with the CMB, the effects of the sky's edges must be accounted for through proper simulation and analysis techniques. Deep neural network models typically converge quickly to optimal solutions in the context of large training datasets. Nevertheless, few-shot learning remains a complex challenge due to deep networks' tendency to be influenced by outlier episodes in restricted datasets. We introduce a novel, flexible framework that allows for interpolating between decision boundaries to effectively reject outlier samples in the test stage. The proposed method is an episodic protocol where the framework learns from support samples to predict a set of function values on the surface of the support data's decision boundary in the parameter space. The algorithm then utilizes these predictions to determine a new boundary that minimizes the error of classifying the base dataset, thereby effectively discounting the influence of outlier samples. As a result, the algorithm is capable of learning from a reduced number of samples and exceling in tasks with high-fidelity outlier samples. The proposed framework is particularly effective in few-shot learning scenarios and demonstrates superior performance when evaluated on miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and few-shot charNum datasets. The algorithm's ability to reduce the impact of outlier samples is further highlighted by its success in the task of learning from a dataset that contains high-fidelity outlier samples. This comparison focuses on whether more complex formulations make problems easier to solve and whether this is reflected in the differences in LP and LP relaxation values. To explore this, we define a metric to assess the complexity of formulations and then examine whether this metric is linked to solution difficulty. Our research is applicable to any problem that can be represented using LP relaxation and also has an extended formulation. A single-task model is often expected to excel across multiple tasks but this isn't how human expertise works.  For example, radiologists don't learn to diagnose all possible conditions in an MRI scan by being exposed to the entire medical literature but rather by focusing on specific aspects and gradually expanding their knowledge.  This concept can be applied to the current benchmark for few-shot learning which assumes a model should be highly versatile and evaluate a wide range of tasks with minimal data.  We challenge this idea by developing a more realistic benchmark that tests whether a model can successfully apply its existing expertise to new but related tasks with limited data.  This is illustrated by evaluating the ability of a pre-trained medical imaging model to diagnose different conditions on MRI scans using datasets it hasn't been exposed to during training.  This leads to a significant improvement in performance as the model is now able to leverage its existing expertise to distinguish between similar conditions on unseen datasets.  This work is also complemented by an analysis of the composition of the training dataset and its impact on the model's evaluation on new MRI data.  This shows that the model's performance on unseen data relies heavily on the diversity of the conditions present within that dataset.  This is followed by an assessment of the model's ability to expand its own expertise by evaluating its performance on conditions it hasn't been exposed to during training but similar to those it has.  This demonstrates a notable improvement as the model is now able to diagnose new conditions that are somewhat different from those in the training dataset.  This indicates a step towards modeling the capability of human expertise that gradually expands over time. Despite offering significant performance benefits, these systems can result in unpredictable access patterns leading to slow core access delays. To mitigate this, the authors introduce NOVA-relaxed NVMM, a file system designed to optimize memory access efficiency. By classifying files into distinct categories, it separates their memory blocks into independent regions to minimize interference. The authors also analyze the implications of relaxing memory access rules on system reliability, addressing potential concerns with memory coherence and synchronization. In 2019, the Motivation Dynamics (MD) theory was proposed as a simple agent model to replicate complex social phenomena. The original single-agent model has been further developed to explore interagent interactions by modifying the dynamics in response to relative distances from other agents. This festival paper combines the two advancements, broadening the MD framework to a multiagent setup while preserving its basic dynamics. By doing so, it addresses critics' concerns and showcases a self-organization application – agents meeting at a designated point. The modified framework demonstrates comparable dynamics to its single-agent counterpart and can be applied to analyze various interagent scenarios. The associated code is openly accessible, enabling users to experiment with different festival setups beyond the presented results. The festival project is available online at https://md.festivals.dev/.

These high-energy processes correspond to four-dimensional glueballs that can be represented by purely imaginary scalar four-gauge-field configurations in the fundamental representation. Our model also demonstrates that these four-dimensional glueballs possess a direct connection to instantons of a lower dimensional nature. Furthermore, our findings indicate that instantons in d-dimensional space can be utilized to model the interactions of heavy quarks in (d+2)-dimensional QCD. We further derive a formula to compute the amplitude of these processes through the intersection coefficients of Wilson loops, thereby providing a new means of investigating heavy-quark interactions within QCD. Additionally, our study offers a framework for understanding the relationship between instantons in distinct dimensional settings. As an example, we derive the amplitude for bottom-antibottom combinations in four-dimensional QCD, which corresponds to a specific four-dimensional glueball that is connected to $SU(2)$ instantons in three-dimensional space. The vast halo regions of galaxies are critical to comprehend several cosmological phenomena, including the distribution of galaxies, the formation of galaxy clusters, and the diffuse cosmic radiation known as diffuse high-energy gamma-ray signal. Constraints on these halo volumes are typically based on assumptions about the behavior of particles within them. However, it is possible to determine the size and shape of the halo volumes by observing the effects of the gravitational interaction between the galaxy and its surrounding environment. The goal of this research is to use the gravitational influence of the Large Magellanic Cloud on the distribution of celestial objects in the Magellanic Bridge to estimate its halo volume. The study employs two independent methods to constrain the halo volume based on the observed rotation curve along the line of sight in the Magellanic Bridge. The results indicate a halo volume of approximately 1039 degrees cubic parsecs, with a density of approximately 1.4 times 10 to the power -3 times the mass density of the sun per kilogram per cubic parsec. The research also reveals that the mass distribution within one degree parsec of the LMC's center is consistent with that of a low-mass, stellar halo similar to that of the Milky Way. The discovery of a substantial, star-dominated halo volume in the LMC challenges previous models of the formation and evolution of this galaxy. The findings suggest that the LMC's halo was formed primarily through the merger of smaller galaxies, accompanied by the accretion of massive globular clusters, and that the LMC's core was shaped by the collision with the Milky Way, resulting in the expulsion of massive clusters and the formation of a dense, inner cluster population. The study also predicts that the detection of high-energy gamma-ray radiation in the LMC should occur within one degree parsec of its center within the next 10 to 15 years. The research uses an observational database of celestial objects and their velocities to model the LMC's gravitational influence and estimate its halo volume. The study of the LMC's halo provides a framework for studying the halo volumes of other galaxies and offers insights into the fundamental processes governing the evolution of galaxies and the cosmos. The discovery of a substantial, star-dominated halo volume in the LMC challenges previous models of this galaxy's formation and evolution and may influence our understanding of the growth of supermassive black holes at its center. The research also anticipates the detection of high-energy gamma-ray radiation in the LMC and may inform the development of strategies for detecting similar diffuse radiation in the Milky Way. The proposed method involves three key steps: 1) utilizing morphological operators to eliminate superfluous information and shape refinement; 2) applying region growth technique to tumor detection by creating a mask for the region of interest. The proposed method was evaluated using high-resolution CT scans of lungs before and after chemotherapy treatment. The accuracy of the proposed method was measured by comparing it with tumor detection results obtained from medical professionals through Visual Assessment and Semi-automated annotation tools. The study demonstrated that the proposed method achieves high precision and is relatively fast compared to other methods listed on CITE database. The developed algorithm is now available online for researchers to test and improve the method further. The research indicates that the proposed method is efficient in detecting tumors in follow-up imaging scans, which could be useful in reducing the time healthcare professionals spend on tumor detection. However, further studies are needed to assess the method's effectiveness in detecting tumors in various organs and in cases with significant changes post-treatment. The proposed algorithm has the potential to be adapted for other medical imaging modalities like MRI scans, but this would require additional research and testing. We investigate an unusual epidemic model where connections between individuals are randomly reconfigured after each epidemic outbreak. In this model, a fixed number of newly infected individuals are randomly linked to the current spreaders, except for a specific individual who is exempt from reconnection, which is designed to prevent further spread. Our analysis focuses on the most critical factors influencing the epidemic's behavior and provides exact results for achievable equilibrium and asymptotic stationary fractions infected, as well as asymptotic equilibrium and stationary distributions. Through extensive simulations, we verify the accuracy of our analytical findings. Interestingly, occasionally the model exhibits hysteresis, leading to distinct outcomes based on initial conditions, as well as unexpected peaks in infected individuals resulting from particular correlation structures. Furthermore, the model displays a robust phenomenon where an abrupt decrease in infected individuals can trigger another massive outbreak. Additionally, we identify the condition for the occurrence of hysteresis and explain its underlying mechanism. To further comprehend the model's behavior, particularly the appearance of peak states, we recommend exploring related models that involve multiple epidemic waves. The proposed model can also be applied to analyze the dynamics of other network models, particularly those featuring non-monotone relation structures. The model is particularly relevant to analyzing epidemic spreading on temporal, adaptive, and interdependent networks. The exact results we derived can be applied to a broader category of discrete-time, fixed-in-degree epidemic models. The model is available online at https://git.io/JcO6J. A mathematical framework used to dissect hadrons into their fundamental components, known as partons, particularly applies to the study of deep inelastic scattering. The development of the DGLAP equation, which governs the evolution of parton distribution functions (PDFs) with energy, is a significant aspect of this framework. To accurately understand the internal workings of a hadron, researchers employ phenomenological methods to reconstruct the PDFs within it. This process involves determining the probability functions for finding quarks and gluons of specific momentum within an hadron. The scale used in this analysis, denoted by Λ, is a critical parameter that essentially dictates the rate at which partons evolve from one scale to another. The precise value of Λ is not directly measurable and must be inferred through a process of elimination by comparing the fit parameters obtained from fitting PDFs at different scales, an approach that is both a hallmark and a challenge of this research. This study highlights the intricacies involved in determining the probability functions for finding quarks and gluons within hadrons and sheds light on the uncertainties associated with these functions, which are an inherent aspect of the hadron-disintegration approach. The research is a testament to the ongoing quest to understand the fundamental nature of hadrons and the evolution of hadronic phenomena. The principles developed in this research can be applied to a broader range of hadronic processes and may also provide insights into the behavior of quarks and gluons within hadrons. By allocating virtual experiences to minimize the unbiased risk estimator, the VRER method significantly improves the efficiency of sample coverage. Notably, the optimal virtual experience allocation is shown to be a multiple interval problem, allowing us to develop a precise algorithm and a simpler heuristic for optimal solution approximation. Theoretical performance bounds for the optimal algorithm and heuristic are provided. Empirical results across multiple scenarios demonstrate the method's effectiveness. This study reports the measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
reaching 12.3 fb^-1 in data with an integrated luminosity of 8.8 fb^-1. To 
achieve this, the production of top quarks in pairs is studied, selecting events 
characterized by a single lepton, missing energy, and exactly one b-quark in the 
detectors at the CERN LHC. Utilizing the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO generator for theoretical 
predictions, the spin asymmetry is found to be 0.310 ± 0.017, which differs notably 
from the standard model prediction of 0.000 ± 0.001, indicating a significant gap 
between the observed and predicted values of the spin asymmetry. Additionally, the 
likelihood ratio test confirms the existence of an excess at a 3.4 standard deviation 
level. To further explore the nature of this discrepancy, the probability density 
functions for various parameters related to the top quark are examined within the 
context of the Standard Model, leading to constraints on the effective weak mixing 
angle at a 10^-7 level of precision. These findings result in a more precise definition 
of the standard model's parameters and may provide a clue to understanding anomalies 
observed in other particle decays. Lastly, extensions to the standard model, such as 
an extra scalar singlet, are evaluated to determine if they could be discernible at 
the CERN LHC in future experiments. To accomplish this, the proposed research leverages 
existing searches and incorporates theoretical calculations that the extra scalar 
and its partner could operate outside the standard Higgs paradigm, making itself 
detectable through accurate measurements of top quark spin asymmetry and related 
quantities. To this end, a new analysis technique is developed to accurately 
reconstruct the polarization of the top quark, enabling the LHC to explore a wider 
range of new physics scenarios, thus potentially revealing itself in the process. 
This technique is anticipated to enhance the sensitivity of the LHC to a wide range of 
new physics scenarios, even beyond the standard model's parameter space that the LHC 
is currently capable of investigating. Consequently, this research has the potential to 
open up a new avenue for discovering new physics at the LHC. In addition, the technique 
developed can be applied to a broader range of new physics scenarios, leading to more 
accurate and sensitive searches for top quark-related new physics

To understand the electronic properties of LaNiO$_3$ and related materials, it's helpful to study bulk and layered versions of LaNiO$_3$. This study focuses on LaNiO$_3$ superlattices with varying thickness and temperature measurements of their relaxation constants. The results reveal that the relaxation constants are affected by the LaNiO$_3$ thickness and its alignment within the superlattice. When LaNiO$_3$ is thicker than two units, its relaxation constants exhibit distinct temperature-dependent behaviors. Notably, the average relaxation constant shows a notable increase with temperature across all superlattice constructions, which is attributed to LaNiO$_3$'s intrinsic characteristics. The findings also indicate that the mean relaxation ratio can differentiate between intrinsic and extrinsic relaxation mechanisms. The study utilized X-ray absorption spectroscopy to compare LaNiO$_3$ layers within superlattices and free-standing materials, showing that LaNiNiO$_5$ 4-d orbitals retain their structure regardless of LaNiO$_3$ thickness. The results suggest that LaNiO$_3$'s extrinsic relaxation is driven by its two-dimensional operation. The study discovered that LaNiO$_3$'s average relaxation ratio is temperature-independent when its thickness is two units or less. The findings also indicate that LaNiO$_3$'s average relaxation ratio is influenced by its boundary conditions within the superlattice, exhibiting a notable boost when LaNiO$_3$ layers are flanked by metallic CaNiO$_2$ layers. The research provides a deeper understanding of the intrinsic and extrinsic relaxation mechanisms in LaNiO$_3$ and its two-dimensional homologs. The study's findings are expected to inform the design of experiments aimed at uncovering the intrinsic versus extrinsic nature of relaxation in materials. Conversational AI systems have seen significant advancements in recent years, with various techniques developed for tasks like text classification and generation. Despite these improvements, it's unclear how these systems perceive others' intentions and mental states, which are fundamental components of human social interaction. We argue that conversational AI's ability to successfully engage with people requires the capacity for theory of mind. To investigate this, we created a knowledge graph that captures the cognitive connections between intentions, plans, and their outcomes, which can serve as a foundation for future conversational AI research. To test the efficacy of this approach, we used this graph to evaluate the ability of machine learning models to understand dialogues involving various levels of complexity. Our results show that models that have access to the intended meaning and underlying intentions perform better than those that do not. We also found that the best-performing models are capable of generating outcomes or plans that are connected to the initial intent, thus demonstrating a basic ability to think about others' mental states. However, there is still significant room for improvement, and numerous challenges persist in developing truly conversational AI systems that can grasp the intricacies of human social interaction. To overcome these challenges, we propose a framework that combines dialog-based theory of mind evaluation with more sophisticated methods of machine learning, such as reinforcement learning, which can provide a more comprehensive approach to this problem. This research lays the groundwork for advancing the dialog-based theory of mind capability in conversational AI systems and paves the way for related research in this area. We have developed MG-GLAM, a code that uses the Tree-PM method for large-scale simulations, and adapted it to utilize GPUs for computational acceleration. In order to maintain physical accuracy, MG-GLAM includes a variety of sophisticated physical models, such as gravity, dark matter particle interactions, dark energy, and gravitational waves. Furthermore, the code incorporates an advanced technique for correcting boundary values, which enhances its performance by an average of 10-fold while upholding precise numerical results when compared to its predecessor, Gadget-2. The significant boost in computational speed and the code's versatility make it an ideal platform for a wide range of sophisticated cosmological simulations. Additionally, MG-GLAM's modular design allows for ease of extension to include additional physical phenomena. We have successfully tested the GPU version of the code, achieving a speed increase of roughly 5 times over the CPU version for a given amount of processing power. We intend to contribute MG-GLAM to public access in the near future. In the meantime, we invite interested parties to contact us for access to the code.

We develop the concept of chordal Schramm–Loewener evolution (CSLE) within the context of single-point mapping currents in the complex Banach space $\mathbb{C}^+$. This extension allows us to view the evolution of such currents as continuous paths of single-point mapping currents in $\mathbb{C}^+$. We establish a connection between these CSLE paths and "imaginary surfaces" - a notion derived from the Riemann Mapping Theorem. Furthermore, we prove that any CSLE path can be represented as a combination of two independent processes: one preserving analytic domain maps and another associated with imaginary surfaces. Additionally, we demonstrate that the latter process comprises a natural metric space structure. We obtain a compactification of the space of CSLE paths by incorporating "boundary values" of such paths, which are defined through the associated imaginary surfaces. Within this context, we identify a natural parametrization for the space of CSLE paths and its compactification. Lastly, we identify an intrinsic metric that corresponds to a variant of the M\"obius metric on single-point mapping currents in $\mathbb{C}^+$. This underlying metric then gives rise to a compact metric space of the current types, which in turn gives us the space of CSLE paths and its compactification, leading to an intrinsic understanding of the Loewner kernel. We believe that this novel perspective may provide a useful framework for further analyzing the chordal Loewner equation and its associated processes. To support this, we present an initial problem related to the Loewner kernel's spectral structure. We anticipate that the introduced concepts of CSLE and its associated spaces, as well as the underlying ideas of map currents and imaginary surfaces, will also contribute to a broader appreciation of complex analysis in the Banach space $\mathbb{C}^+$. Recent research lies at the heart of a developing area within the study of complex systems, where the focus is on identifying the number of synchronized clusters through the use of reduced models. This effort is an extension of earlier work that described how to create a low-dimensional model that captures the collective behavior observed in a dynamic system. The present research expands upon this earlier finding by formulating it in a mathematical framework that can be applied to a broad range of nonlinear systems exhibiting synchronized cluster behavior. The method relies on the properties of the system's equation when the synchronization transition occurs and develops a simplified model that reflects the cluster structure. The proposed method is supported by numerical examples involving systems with spatial interactions and those without spatial interactions. Notably, it is demonstrated that the method can determine the number of synchronized clusters through an analytically tractable expression. The developed technique may have applications in interpreting the cluster structure observed in synchronized systems, often seen in biological and neurological contexts. Furthermore, the method suggests a direction for further exploration in the study of nonlinear systems near their bifurcation points. The algorithm introduced in this research is a direct method that does not involve the ongoing development and refinement of data analysis tools. The algorithm's simplicity is a key aspect, as it provides cluster solutions that can be used as initial conditions for further analysis in a full model. The paper also presents an application of the algorithm in conjunction with numerical tools to address cluster behavior in two acclaimed biological models. The acknowledged limitations of the direct algorithm highlight the value of its results and encourage its integration with numerical techniques and theoretical advancements in the field. Recent advancements in Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) have led to a diverse range of designs, catering to various application requirements and network scenarios. Nonetheless, replicating individual components of sophisticated CRDTs can result in impractical trial and error processes for developers. Furthermore, evaluating the correctness of these replicated data structures entails significant technical difficulties. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a design framework that can model abstract data types and ensure their correctness in a distributed setting, considering network latency and conflict scenarios. Such a framework should be capable of generating executable code and verifying the correctness of the designed data types through replication. To address this challenge, we present Raxor, a prototype tool that leverages the Z specification language to develop a design framework for Conflict-free Replicated Data Types. By combining formal verification techniques with a sophisticated syntax, Raxor enables developers to create refined data types that can be executed correctly in a distributed environment. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we recreated three existing CRDTs using the Raxor framework and successfully validated their correctness. To comprehend the impact of genetics on variation in the human body and face, our team has been contributing a comprehensive set of 3D phenotypic data linked to genomic information across multiple levels. In the current study, we enhance this collection by analyzing the physical differences brought about by thousands of protein-altering SNPs. By combining multiple approaches, our analysis uncovers the significant effect of protein sequence on the variation of phenotype-associated SNPs, with a notable discrepancy in how protein sequence and other types of genomic variations influence the variation of different traits. For instance, the immune system's response to pathogens is greatly affected by the sequence of proteins involved, whereas the influence of protein sequence on face shape is relatively minimal. Furthermore, our research reveals that certain SNPs with a profound impact on the face are often located near genes whose products participate in cellular processes that do not seem directly related to facial features, illustrating the complex mapping between the genetic code and physical appearance. By offering a more comprehensive understanding of the complex relationship between the genetic code and the human body and face, our expanded dataset provides valuable resources for researchers in the field of genomics and facial analysis. To enhance the reliability of driver assistance systems, it is crucial to create robust applications that can operate properly even with potentially inaccurate sensors like vision and lidar. Contemporary advanced computer vision techniques have significantly improved thanks to massive datasets and cutting-edge models, yet they often fail to handle critical aspects like data missing sections, noisiness, and label errors. A prominent example in this field is action recognition, which can benefit from a vast amount of annotated data, but its accuracy drops substantially when confronted with incomplete or corrupted visual data and inconsistent labels. This paper proposes an innovative action recognition approach that utilizes a minimal amount of clean data and extensive amounts of noisy and annotated data to learn a robust model. This method employs a combination of a simple model and a complex model: the former uses weak supervision on all data, creating a preliminary prediction, and the latter utilizes this prediction along with a limited amount of clean data to learn a robust model through a process of iterative refinement. This technique can be applied to various tasks, including action classification, segmentation, and multiple action recognition, making it a versatile high-impact solution that has significant potential to contribute to the development of robust and reliable driver assistance applications. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, experiments are conducted on multiple datasets annotated with class labels, action texts, and bounding boxes for action localization, demonstrating its superiority over multiple baseline models on accuracy, overall performance, and robustness on incomplete and noisy data. Additionally, this method is found to be energy-efficient in terms of required data and model complexity. This innovative technique is expected to have a significant impact on the development of driver assistance systems by providing a robust and reliable solution for action recognition in real-world driving scenarios. A public code repository is available at https://github.com/parthagg123/Robust-Action-Recognition for further reference.

We present a global jet model that accounts for the variable observed properties
of gamma-ray burst afterglows, resulting from a central engine generating high
energy emissions across the electromagnetic spectrum. This model bridges the ultra
-relativistic and non-relativistic afterglow phases, and is tested using 23
optical, X-ray, and radio data sets from well-studied GRBs. By minimizing the
global chi-squared, we obtain physically meaningful parameters, including the
initial jet half-opening angle, and latent and radiative times. These findings
reveal that the radiative time is significantly shorter than the latent time,
and that the latent time is comparable to the typical GRB duration. This model
successfully explains the variability in the circular polarization of GRBs, and
may also clarify the distinction between short and long GRBs. Furthermore, it
raises intriguing questions about the nature of GRBs, potentially linking them
to active galactic nuclei, and offering insights into the cosmic beaming effect.
