Quantum theory predicts that all superconductors will have vortex cores with some entropy, and this entropy should be comparable to that of a magnetic flux line moving through a superconductor. However, the exact difference in entropy between these two situations depends on the type of superconductor and its corresponding Ginzburg-Landau parameters. If a superconductor has an isolated coherence gap within its vortex core, then the entropy inside the core will actually be lower than the entropy associated with a moving magnetic flux line. On the other hand, if the coherence gap is not isolated, then the entropy inside the core will be higher than the entropy associated with a moving magnetic flux line. This higher entropy inside the non-isolated gap case leads to an entropy difference that can cause the vortex core to behave similarly to a magnetic flux line with an isolated coherence gap. This distinct entropy environment of the vortex core is proposed as an explanation for the existence of topological superconductors. Additionally, this theory is supported by numerical simulations of the entropy distribution within vortex cores in different materials. These simulations demonstrate that the entropy inside the core of an isolated gap indeed matches that of a moving magnetic flux line, whereas the entropy inside the core of a non-isolated gap is higher and follows the magnetic flux line entropy profile. This distinct entropy environment inside the vortex core could potentially be utilized in the detection of topological superconductors. Furthermore, this proposed mechanism may also provide a framework for understanding other phenomena related to vortex cores, such as their high frictional resistance and the formation of magnetic flux line lattice domains. Lastly, this concept is anticipated to contribute to a fresh perspective on the fundamental properties of superconducting materials and their corresponding vortex cores.

The vast majority of white dwarf mergers end in a conservative mass transfer, where the smaller WD orbits a more massive counterpart, aligning with the conditions needed for a merger to result in a supernova explosion. If such a conservative merger occurs, the outcome will be a stellar merger with enhanced elemental composition. In contrast, if the conservative merger fails and the system becomes a temporary non-conservative transfer, the outcome will depend on the ejected matter. In this study, we utilize a sophisticated computational approach to simulate conservative high-mass white dwarf mergers. By modeling these events with approximately 300 simulations, we found that only a small proportion, about 7%, of conservative high-mass white dwarf mergers lead to supernovae explosions. The remaining 93% result in stellar mergers with enhanced elemental composition, and only a minimal portion, about 0.1%, of these is visible in the observational spectrum. Furthermore, we discovered that stellar mergers with this enhanced composition can be identified by analyzing their spectral spectra, and that Big Dipper-like associations composed of stellar mergals are plausible and potentially detectable with the aid of advanced computational methods. Lastly, we found that the likelihood of detecting these associations is directly proportional to the density of the galactic bulge and that future observational surveys will be capable of identifying numerous stellar mergals and potentially several Big Dipper-like associations within the galactic bulge. Additionally, these findings imply that a significant portion, at least 30%, of supernovae with heavy element enrichment in their surroundings originate from white dwarf mergers. These predictions can be verified or disputed by comparing the theoretical models to future observational data on stellar mergals, and they highlight the significance of continuing to search for these objects. We investigate the double Higgs production process in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory and the Higgs Effective Field Theory using unitarity-based constraints at the LHC through its full energy spectrum. Our research focuses on the leading coefficient in each effective theory, which significantly influences the predicted signal at high energy levels. In the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, the leading coefficient is directly linked to the Standard Model itself, whereas in the Higgs Effective Field Theory, it corresponds to a dimension-5 operator. We find that the leading coefficient in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory has a similar magnitude to its counterpart in the Higgs Effective Field Theory, albeit with different underlying physics. As a result, both effective theories yield comparable predictions for double Higgs production at high energy levels, which could be as much as order-Eight times the Standard Model prediction by the time the LHC at its full energy. This enhanced signal may be distinguishable from the Standard Model scenario by the LHC at its full energy with an integrated luminance of at least 3 inverse femtobarns. Furthermore, we find that the unitarity-based constraint plays a crucial role in this prediction, particularly when considering the full energy spectrum rather than just the peak region. Additionally, we find that the unitarity-based constraint is more effective in enhancing the signal at high energy levels when using the Higgs Effective Field Theory rather than the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. This highlights the significance of employing both the Standard Model Effective Field Theory and the Higgs Effective Field Theory in the search for double Higgs production to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics. Our research highlights the value of incorporating a unitarity-based constraint in the effective field theories used for the analysis of new physics signatures at the LHC. Ultimately, our study underscores the significance of exploring both the peak and tail regions of a signal in the search for new physics at the LHC. The techniques developed in this research can be applied to other new physics processes at the LHC.

Hybrid consensus protocols are crucial for the functioning of blockchain-based systems, ensuring that consensus algorithms are efficient in finding a valid configuration. To address this issue, we present BoAnon, the first known protocol for hybrid consensus that runs both confidentially and in a timely manner. BoAnon uses a novel combination of random sampling and a priority-based selection algorithm to significantly accelerate the search process to an acceptable pace. Furthermore, BoAnon maintains complete confidentiality throughout the process. We examine BoAnon's performance under various conditions and demonstrate that it meets all key requirements for hybrid consensus protocols. BoAnon is the first step towards creating blockchain-based systems that can handle large-scale combinations and ensure confidentiality throughout the process. To achieve this, we propose modifying the BFT algorithm to a hybrid consensus protocol. BoAnon is now ready for use in cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and has the potential to accelerate the adoption of privacy-preserving cryptocurrencies. This study examines the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy. Identified particles such as pions, kaons, protons, deuterons, and $\Lambda$ and $\bar{\Lambda}$ hyperons are analyzed to determine their $v_3(p_T)/p_T$ values as a function of $p_T$. A distinct mass dependence is observed for the $v_3(p_T)/p_T$ values of these particles, exhibiting an increase in proportionality with mass from $p_T \approx 0.5$ to 10 GeV/c. Furthermore, when comparing $v_3(p_T)/p_T$ to $v_2(p_T)/p_T$, it is evident that $v_3(p_T)/p_T$ follows a similar trend with mass but at a shifted $p_T$ range. Additionally, the $K_T$-scaled $v_3$ and $v_2$ exhibit similar trends with mass for all centrality classes examined. The findings of this study can be interpreted utilizing existing models that incorporate coalescence and straining of flow dependencies. The observed $p_T$-scale shift suggests further investigation is required to thoroughly understand the underlying mechanisms governing the straining of $v_3$ and $v_2$. The discovered mass dependence of $v_3$ may also provide valuable insights into the properties of quark-gluon plasma at high temperatures, potentially shedding light on the initial conditions and viscosity of this system. The study of $v_3$ in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV, conducted by the ALICE collaboration, contributes significantly to the advancement of research in this area.

This study explores the properties of minimum density power divergence (MDPD) and maximum likelihood (ML) estimators when applied to independent increment and Markov processes. Our research focuses on obtaining independent and identically distributed observations, typically in the context of Poisson process modeling. We establish relationships between MDPD and ML estimators, demonstrating that the MDPD estimator is a special case of the self-consistent estimator, which generalizes the maximum likelihood estimator. These findings are relevant to modeling stochastic processes that include autoregressive and fractional processes. Our work also highlights the connection between MDPD/ML estimators and integral equations, enabling the direct solution of the associated operator equations. To evaluate the mean squared error of the MDPD/ML estimators, we investigate the properties of the associated operator. Our research shows that the MDPD estimator is a consistent estimator and that its mean squared error converges at a rate that is at least asymptotically equivalent to the inverse of the sample size. Our results are applicable to a broad range of models, including those with smooth and discontinuous parameters. Furthermore, our study finds that the asymptotic relative efficiency of the MDPD estimator to the ML estimator is always greater than the inverse of the convergence rate. Due to the general nature of the MDPD estimator, its properties can be extended to other types of processes, such as multivariate processes and empirical processes. Our research is complemented by numerical studies that demonstrate the efficiency of the MDPD estimator in relation to the ML estimator through simulated and real-world data analyses. Our findings indicate that the MDPD estimator generally outperforms the ML estimator, obtaining smaller mean squared errors in a consistent manner. This is observed across a range of models, including autoregressive models of order 1 and 2, and fractional models with smooth and discontinuous parameters. Our research offers a framework for evaluating the performance of MDPD/ML estimators in an extensive range of modeling scenarios. Software developed in this research is freely available online.

Current approaches to training self-driving vehicles utilize simulation tools but are limited by the small size of their rendered images. This restriction hinders the ability to train models in critical situations. A crucial aspect that lacks proper simulation is the creation of three-dimensional traffic scene models. To address this challenge, we present SceneGen, a novel approach that generates both two- and three-dimensional scene models to advance the training of self-driving vehicles. By integrating a text-based layout tool with 3D rendering, SceneGen allows for the creation of large-scale, high-resolution 3D scenes while keeping its image size comparable to real-world images. To validate SceneGen's effectiveness, we compare its results to three alternative 3D scene creation methods and demonstrate its superiority in producing more accurate and diverse scenes. Furthermore, we showcase SceneGen's performance in several evaluation metrics and incorporate it into the Scene Understanding, Object Detection, and Tracking tasks for self-driving vehicles. Our findings indicate that SceneGen yields better results compared to traditional methods of 3D scene creation. Additionally, we preemptively address potential concerns about SceneGen's scalability and robustness. To facilitate research, we make SceneGen available openly at https://github.com/autotram-scene/SceneGen. By providing high-quality 3D scene models and surpassing traditional methods, SceneGen represents a significant step towards refining the training of self-driving vehicles using simulation tools. These models and results can be found at https://autotram-scene.github.io/SceneGen/.

We address two longstanding conjectures in probability theory: the joint ergodicity of IP* and BiIP* processes, and the ergodicity of the BiIP* process alone. To achieve this, we develop an original method for analyzing stationary processes that is broadly applicable. By establishing a key connection between our novel approach and a recent breakthrough by Kalicinski and Szewczew, we gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between these processes. To solve the problems at hand, we primarily utilize this new analysis technique. We also explore its potential by demonstrating its applicability to the BiIP* ergodicity issue, even though that particular problem is already settled. Our primary innovation involves showing that a specific modification of a given process results in a new process with established ergodic properties, and then establishing that this new process possesses the same statistical characteristics as the original process. To this end, we establish a critical identity that may have value in its own right. We conclude by highlighting the versatility of our approach by successfully applying it to a BiIP* variant that has been proposed but never studied before. This novel variant raises an interesting question about the relationship between its own ergodicity and that of the original BiIP* process. Our findings thus contribute meaningfully to the ongoing study of complex systems. Additionally, our method for assessing joint ergodicity may be useful for addressing other, more complex problems related to the convergence of probability distributions. Lastly, we believe that our results have implications for the ongoing exploration of the BiIP* process itself. To facilitate further research, we have made our code freely available for download. By demonstrating the practical utility of our theoretical model, we also aim to encourage interdisciplinary collaboration between mathematicians and computational scientists. Ultimately, our ultimate goal is to use this approach to tackle even more challenging problems. To this end, we invite interested parties to join us in exploring new research questions and identifying new problems waiting to be solved. In doing so, we may uncover new insights that can, in turn, lead to additional breakthroughs. In our quest to address these grand challenges, we propose a series of specific research directions that we believe have significant potential for significant progress. We then illustrate the potential applicability of our approach to these issues through the lens of the BiIP* ergodicity issue. We also invite the broader scientific community to join us in actively working towards a comprehensive understanding of complex systems. Researchers are utilizing hybrid quantum-classical algorithms and machine learning to accelerate chemical state preparation, a crucial process with numerous applications. By training a generative model using a classical computer with data from Monte Carlo simulations, it can learn the underlying structure and create a quantum state that closely mimics this structure. When combined with quantum phase estimation, this enables the development of highly precise, yet complex ground states. Our study leverages the BERT4GAN algorithm to train a generative neural network that generates states on the potential energy surface of LiH, significantly improving its fidelity when subjected to increasing interatomic distances. Notably, the sample states produced surpass the current quantum state preparation capabilities. Utilizing quantum-classical co-design, we further optimized the model using Q-angle optimization, resulting in a 240-qubit simulator from IBM. The resulting state shows an unprecedented 99.4% fidelity after just 100 Monte Carlo iterations. The effectiveness of this approach is evident when comparing its performance to conventional quantum state preparation methods. The co-design process also identifies the key parameters that indicate the potential effectiveness of this approach for larger chemical systems. The potential of this hybrid approach is evident, and it may soon play a significant role in the development of chemical applications for near-term quantum computers. Accurate organ modeling during surgical procedures is crucial for intraoperative real-time guidance. However, registering preoperative models with real-time intraoperative data is challenging due to various issues such as sensor noise and the constantly changing surgical scene. In laparoscopic procedures, the problem is further compounded by limited-field images from the endoscope, which results in distorted views of the organ anatomy from multiple orientations. As a consequence, traditional methods based on likelihood maximization and robust techniques often fail, leading to unsatisfactory results or becoming computationally infeasible. In the context of limited-field range data and real-time processing, a new approach is proposed that leverages the properties of the organ in question – in this case, the liver – to facilitate efficient registration. By assuming the presence of uniform vascular tissues within the organ, a novel metric-based algorithm is proposed to address the registration challenge. Experimental evaluations using both phantom and human patient data demonstrate the effectiveness and computational feasibility of the proposed method. Furthermore, comparisons with conventional techniques highlight the superior performance of the metric-based algorithm in terms of accuracy and robustness. The proposed method demonstrates potential for laparoscopic liver surgery, but requires further optimization to be suitable for real-time processing. While self-supervised flow estimation has achieved notable progress in recent years, several significant challenges remain unresolved. Notably, current approaches continue to struggle to handle situations where objects move behind others and are temporarily obscured from view. This research seeks to address this persistent issue by introducing a novel unsupervised optical flow model that leverages a unique technique to recover hidden flows. We've developed a particular representation for disparity maps that incorporates an "occlusion mask," which essentially pinches off parts of the map where objects are obscured. By introducing this representation, we've established a method to recover hidden flows by manipulating the mask in a way that effectively moves it back into view. To accomplish this, we've designed a specific loss function that enables optimal solutions to be found with a conventional optimization method. Moreover, we've devised an approach to estimate an approximate mask, which in turn enables us to utilize this estimate to improve the mask itself in a self-updating loop. We've tested our proposed model in a variety of scenarios and compared it to multiple state-of-the-art competitors, with results indicating a significant reduction in error rates of around 20-30% according to SRE and FLow metrics. This study explores how a powerful magnetic field influences the quark matter equation of state, taking into account the effects of spin polarization and strange quarks. Our analysis reveals that, to a significant extent, a strong magnetic field can cause the quark matter's pressure to rise and its density to increase, with the impact being more pronounced for spin-polarized quarks. Additionally, our findings suggest that the influence of a magnetic field on the quark matter's behavior can be interpreted through the lens of a "magnetic susceptibility" that applies to the quark's spin polarization and effective mass. Notably, we observe that the influence of a magnetic field is greater for strange quarks than for non-strange quarks. Our research also anticipates that in neutron stars, the impact of a magnetic field would be observable in the form of an irregularity in the stellar's universal relation. Furthermore, the study implies that the equation of state for spin-polarized quark matter shares some resemblance to that of spin-polarized neutron matter. Our research provides a theoretical framework that can be put to the test through comparison with empirical data from neutron and quark star observations, or from experiments that involve interacting quarks in a magnetic field. Even-2-factorable (E2F) refers to the unique capability of a graph to have two distinct 2-factors that intersect only on even-sized connections. The E2F property can be extended to higher-dimensional factors. This study specifically explores the concept of even-2-factorability in cubic graphs. Our research discovers that every cubic graph can indeed possess two 2-factors that share only even-sized connections and proves that the same property also applies to all halved graphs derived from cubic graphs. Furthermore, this implication demonstrates that halved graphs inherently possess the even-2-factorable (E2F) property. To validate this property, a method is proposed that allows identification of any cubic graph's even-2-factorability by verifying the existence of a suitable 2-factor that intersects with previously determined factors on even-sized connections. Ultimately, this method leads to a proof that halved graphs are inherently even-2-factorable. 

Keywords: Even-2-factorable, Cubic Graphs, Halved Graphs, 2-factors. 

This article provides a new approach to recognizing even-2-factorability in cubic graphs through the use of halved graphs, ultimately leading to a proof that cubic graphs' halved equivalents inherently possess this property.

Li recently proposed a modified version of the Bateman-Horn Conjecture, which provides more precise estimates for the number of prime values taken by a specific class of polynomial expressions with rational coefficients. Under certain conditions,  the conjecture predicts that the total number of prime values produced by these expressions over a given range is on the order of $O\left(\frac{R}{\log R}\right)$, where R represents the range in question. In this paper, we explore an extension of this conjecture to polynomial expressions that also contain irrational coefficients from a quadratic field. Under certain technical conditions and with the aid of a density assumption regarding the distribution of prime values, we establish that the number of prime values produced by these expressions under a given range is of order $O\left(\frac{R}{(\log R)^2}\right)$. In addition, we establish a far-reaching generalization of a result by Bombieri and the second named author concerning the distribution of prime values within families of polynomial expressions with rational coefficients. This generalized result is obtained through the application of a recent density theorem by Dietmann. In a related direction, we establish that a certain condition concerning the vanishing of certain arithmetic functions does hold, which provides a result that has been independently obtained by Harman. We investigate the direct detection of dark matter, assuming it is a pseudo-Goldstone boson, and to illustrate this, we analyze a supersymmetric model.  In this model, the dark matter equivalent is a pseudo-Goldstone meson, and we can unambiguously determine its direct detection properties.  Conversely, we can also unambiguously determine the pseudo-Goldstone nature of dark matter by analyzing a given direct detection signal within a supersymmetric framework.  As an example, we examine a scenario with scalar dark matter, and demonstrate that its direct detection can be significantly influenced by the vacuum expectation value of a scalar field, which in turn is affected by the presence of a dark sector Higgs portal.  As a result, we find that the vacuum expectation value of this field, and consequently the dark matter density, can be adjusted through the Higgs portal by modifying the pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone nature of the dark matter is validated.  We also find that the elastic scattering of dark matter with nucleons is reduced due to its pseudo-Goldstone nature, and that this can be made consistent with direct detection constraints such as LUX.  Furthermore, we find that the pseudo-Goldstone nature of dark matter is consistent with the absence of dark matter overabundance in the universe.  We anticipate that investigations of the direct detection of dark matter with a pseudo-Goldstone nature will be relevant to a wide range of theories beyond the Standard Model.  In addition, we find that the influence of the vacuum expectation value of a scalar field on the direct detection of dark matter can also be applied to other types of dark matter, and that this influence is particularly apparent in composite dark matter models that incorporate a pseudo-Goldstone boson.  We hope that this investigation will lead to a reevaluation of the direct detection capabilities of the supersymmetric parameter space that incorporates a pseudo-Goldstone boson.  We also hope that this investigation will lead to a reevaluation of the ability of dark matter to resolve the Higgs naturalness problem, as well as the ability of a Higgs portal to resolve the hierarchy problem, and that it will stimulate further research into the direct detection of dark matter with a pseudo-Goldstone nature.  We anticipate that this investigation will lead to a reevaluation of the direct detection capabilities of the supersymmetric parameter space that incorporates a pseudo-Goldstone boson, and that it will stimulate further research into the direct detection of dark matter with a pseudo-Goldstone nature.

This model, described by a nonlinear parabolic system, was modified to incorporate an external force leading to an asymptotically stable equilibrium point. A new approach involved using the linearized observability inequality to develop a boundary control strategy to drive the population towards a stable equilibrium point. This method effectively managed the population by minimizing the size of the population outside a localized area. To extend this approach to a larger system, a linearized observability inequality was established for a reduced model through a technique called differential embedding. Finally, this method was applied to a rational function reaction-diffusion system where an observable inequality could be derived for a modified system with an observable equilibrium point. This allowed the development of a control strategy to manage the population both spatially and temporally. Due to the challenges associated with the full system, the method was first demonstrated for a related system in which the population was represented by rational functions with an observable equilibrium point. Our method for valuing actions in sports involves analyzing the expected outcome based on the specific action's probability of occurrence. To illustrate this concept, we apply it to a simple scenario of soccer gameplay. For instance, committing a foul or the ball going out of bounds apparently seems less rewarding than shooting on goal. However, our approach shows that in certain game scenarios, gaining free kicks or corner kicks might be more rewarding than shooting on goal. To further validate our method, we consider real-world data from German Bundesliga games, using shot and goal data to create a more comprehensive reward framework. This approach allows us to compare the reward potential of various actions across different game scenarios. For instance, we find that scoring a own goal has a reward value similar to scoring an extra goal, and that committing a foul has a reward value similar to gaining a free kick in certain situations. This method can be applied to any soccer action and facilitates the development of decision-making frameworks for players within a game scenario. Moreover, it facilitates the evaluation of coaching and refereeing strategies. Furthermore, it can be used to create more realistic soccer video games by providing a data-driven basis for in-game decisions. To achieve this, we compare our approach to a widely-used benchmark for soccer game evaluation metrics, TrinamiX Soccer Engine. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted an user study with professional soccer players who evaluated several scenarios that were generated based on our reward framework. The results showed a significant correlation with the expected outcomes, indicating that our approach can provide a data-driven basis for more realistic soccer video games. To validate this concept in a broader context, we applied our method to multiple game scenarios in tennis, considering real-world data from ATP and WTA tours, and developed a reward framework for actions such as serving, forehand, and backhand. This framework enabled us to compare the reward potential of various actions across different game scenarios, demonstrating its applicability to various sports. Ultimately, our approach can be used to create more engaging and realistic sports video games by providing a data-driven basis for in-game decisions, and we propose that this concept be further explored in future research. To facilitate this, we have made our method publicly available for sports game developers and researchers, and we look forward to seeing the innovations that result from its application. In addition, we suggest that this approach could enhance the player experience in sports games by providing greater realism and authenticity, and we propose that future research investigate other aspects of this concept. While this concept holds promise, implementing this method proves difficult due to the difficulty in mapping time-domain data to spectral frequencies required by our mathematical formulation. Additionally, time-domain data misfit functions tend to converge slowly, causing issues with FWI convergence. To address these challenges, we are developing a new time-domain FWI framework that first maps time-domain data to spectral frequencies using a convolutional neural network, and then applies a time-domain to frequency-domain mapping using a spectral transformation formula. This approach allows us to utilize high-resolution time-domain wavefields in our model updates. To handle the slow convergence of time-domain data misfit functions, we are introducing an iterative strategy that converges to a local minimum in a limited number of iterations. This strategy iteratively switches between two wavefield models: a high-resolution time-domain model and a lower-resolution frequency-domain model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this new approach in a numerical example. This new method offers a feasible path for time-domain FWI without requiring significant computational resources or complex deep learning architectures. We analyzed IGRB data from 2019 to study IGR J19294+1816's outburst and its spectral behavior. Our data analysis revealed that the source exhibits a quasi-persistent brightening and a high-frequency cutoff around 0.43 MeV, which is unusually low for accreting high-mass neutron star binaries. Within the 2-10 keV energy range, we observed that IGR J19294+1816's hardness intensity pattern changes direction during the outburst's rise and decline phases, a phenomenon also seen in the persistent brightening of V404 Cygni and the 2007 outburst of V406 Cygni. Additionally, we identified X-ray lines at 5.89 keV and 6.4 keV, which are likely the results of the neutron star's atomic hydrogen and iron absorption during the outburst. Our research suggests that the outburst's spectrum is dominated by the neutron star's atmospheric emission and a disk wind, which may lead to further understanding of IGR J19294+1816's high-energy behavior during quiescence. Furthermore, we detected a high-energy tail during the outburst's early stages, which is reminiscent of the high-energy tails observed in V404 Cygni's 2015 outburst and V406 Cygni's 2007 outburst. We discovered that IGR J19294+1816's outburst's spatial extent and high-energy behavior are comparable to those of the three Cygni sources, indicating that IGR J19294+1816's outburst's unique features are likely a result of the source's high rate of spin. Lastly, we derived an upper limit for IGR J19294+1816's magnetic field during the outburst, which suggests that the source's magnetic field may be too weak to power a significant fraction of its power output during the outburst. Consequently, our research implies that the source's spin power is likely the primary energy source driving the outburst's behavior. Consequently, we anticipate that the study of IGR J19294+1816 during quiescence will reveal a power spectrum dominated by the source's spin frequency and its harmonic, which will pave the way for understanding the source's quiescent behavior and possibly all high-mass neutron star binaries that shine by accretion. This research investigates an asymmetric noisy voter model where two species compete for dominance. The model incorporates a level of randomness and is applied to a regular and random network structure. Our analysis focuses on the long-term coexistence of the two species and finds that the outcome depends on the balance between competitive interactions and noise levels. In a balanced scenario, where the competitive force equals the noise, an irregular fluctuating pattern persists. However, if the competitive force prevails, the more dominant species will displace the other. But if the noise prevails, both species coexist or alternate in dominance. Additionally, the structure of the network can facilitate second-order phase transitions or abrupt transitions, and species may also experience sudden shifts towards coexistence or alternative patterns of dominance. The intricate behavior observed in this model is a result of the interplay between noise-driven equilibrium states and the network's local properties. The model's analytical challenges stem from its discontinuous state updates, making it an interesting example of a complex system that exhibits intricate behavior resulting from non-complicated underlying mechanisms. The study provides a thorough examination of the competitive asymmetric noisy voter model on both regular and random networks. The model considered here can serve as a foundation for exploring more intricate competitive phenomena on complex networks. A DED2D system consists of a single sender that can transfer both data and energy to multiple receivers, who can store received energy and use it to power data retrieval. The DED2D problem involves determining schedules for data and energy transfer to maximize total data output, taking into account user storage capacities and decoding speeds. The resulting schedule is non-preemptive and meets user storage and decoding requirements. The performance of scanning transmission electron microscopes is significantly determined by the quality of the electrostatic phase plates used. To fully understand and optimize the operation of these instruments, a comprehensive finite-element method has been developed to simulate the behavior of phase plates. This behavior is modeled by solving a Laplace equation that takes into account the characteristics of the electron beam and the specific design of the phase plate. The application of this method has been demonstrated through the analysis of electrostatic phase plates with a range of designs, including those with circular, hexagonal, and rectangular patterns. It was found that the size of the electron probe and the current density at the probe center depend critically on the plate's design, with variations of up to three orders of magnitude observed. The method has also been utilized to investigate the effect of design imperfections and material thickness on the phase plate's performance. The developed method aligns with and complements existing simulation approaches, offering a versatile tool for the simulation of electrostatic phase plates that can be beneficial for instrument optimization, education, and the understanding of electron optics principles. The code accompanying this study can be used to simulate a variety of phase plate designs and is available for download at the corresponding website. By running this code in conjunction with the described simulation methodology, this study demonstrates the development of the EPUPOSO 2.0 code, which can be employed to evaluate the performance of electrostatic phase plates in scanning transmission electron microscopes. The code enables the simulation of a wide range of monolithic and multi-layer phase plates, encompassing those comprising circular, hexagonal, and rectangular apertures, as well as applied thin lens simulations. Furthermore, this study presents several novel electrostatic phase plate designs developed through the simulation of this code, showcasing its capability to achieve high current density at the probe center with minimal probe size, and highlights the potential of this code to contribute to the optimization of electron probe performance through the simulation of diverse plate designs. The code's applicability extends to the education and analysis of electron optics principles, in addition to its utility in analyzing the effect of design flaws and material thickness on phase plate performance. Recent breakthroughs in dialogue understanding tasks are largely attributed to deep neural networks like RNNs and transformers. This study analyzes six prominent deep learning architectures used for dialogue understanding, including sequence-to-sequence models and memory-based models. It conducts comprehensive evaluations on three popular tasks and finds that the RNN-based models perform similarly to transformer models in terms of accuracy. However, when optimizing models for shorter inference times, the RNN-based models prove more efficient in reducing model size without compromising accuracy. These findings are significant, given that deep learning models for dialogue understanding often exhibit size explosions in their hidden state dimensions. This research provides valuable insights for practitioners to balance performance and inference times when designing and optimizing deep learning models for dialogue understanding tasks. It also paves the way for further studies on model compression and optimizing model dimensions. Due to the high frequency of loop closures in mobile robot mapping, improving detection and filtering these loops in changing environments is crucial. To enhance loop closure detection, we propose a novel attention-based deep learning method that automatically identifies key sections of LiDAR data for consideration. This approach isolates and evaluates local patterns in 3D point clouds to determine their uniqueness and likelihood of indicating a loop closure. We demonstrate the benefits of this technique by comparing it to a baseline method using data from the EuRoPA dataset. Results show the proposed method significantly outperforms the baseline (F1 score: 0.62 vs. 0.48) and exhibits robust performance even with large speeds and abrupt changes. Moreover, this technique proves efficient with limited training data, achieving a 0.56 F1 score after training on just 5000 loops from the EuRoPA dataset. This method is particularly useful for mobile robots equipped with LiDAR sensors and capable of high-speed operation in changing indoor environments. Additionally, the technique demonstrates loop closure detection prowess when combined with the Particle Filter algorithm, achieving a 0.73 F1 score and demonstrating the potential to complement traditional methods like shape-based methods. The increasing demand for high-quality video streaming is forcing content delivery networks to invest heavily in cloud services. To maintain Quality of Service, CDNs are using dynamic resource allocation to adapt to changing network conditions. This study investigates how cloud-based services can collaborate with peer-to-peer networks to maintain Quality of Service in video streaming applications. We developed an adaptive P2P-Cloud model that monitors P2P network performance and adjusts cloud services accordingly to ensure optimal usage. This model maximizes cloud cost efficiency while maintaining desired Quality of Service. We applied this model to a video streaming application and analyzed its behavior to establish a mathematical framework for optimal cloud allocation. This framework considers various P2P network parameters, including degree, distance, and contribution, to optimize cloud resource allocation. This study provides a theoretical foundation for optimal cloud allocation in P2P-Cloud systems and can be applied to other QoS-aware P2P applications. We also presented a practical solution based on this framework, focusing on a peer-reviewed cloud computing scheduling algorithm called MA-CCP. Experimental evaluations of this algorithm revealed how MA-CCP is affected by P2P network parameters and confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed cloud allocation framework. To further validate the feasibility of this framework, we conducted a real-world test on a live video streaming application over the Internet. The results obtained from this test demonstrated the ability of this framework to provide optimal cloud allocation guidance while the application was in operation. This study offers the cloud computing industry valuable insights on optimizing cloud services for P2P applications and provides a useful approach for solving the cloud allocation problem. To facilitate replication of our results, we have made the source code for our MA-CCP algorithm publicly available. This study is relevant to the growing number of video streaming applications that rely on cloud services and P2P networks, and its findings have implications for other Quality of Service-aware P2P applications. In this study, we develop a new approach that enables the derivation of the Lagranian density in the presence of several stabilizing symmetries. This approach involves modifying the instanton gas method. This new approach accurately predicts the upper bounds on the charge of Q-balls, in line with existing theories, and also successfully calculates the masses of both heavy and light Q-balls. This technique is particularly relevant to theories with multiple stabilizing symmetries, as it provides a meaningful interpretation of the axion potential. Furthermore, we apply this method to investigate the impact of a high-scale supersymmetry on the universe, as well as the evolution of Q-ball densities over time in the presence of both heavy and light stabilizing symmetries. The results of these studies demonstrate the capability of this new approach to accurately predict the characteristics of both heavy and light Q-balls. We investigate an intriguing idea that cyclic universes can be driven by holographic dark energy. To achieve this, we introduce a specific cutoff within a cyclic model inspired by the Granda-Oliveros formulation. However, we discover that this cutoff results in a negative pressure that does not adhere to the requirements of dark energy. Consequently, we modify the cutoff to a general form, r = Lf(L), where f is an arbitrary function, and find that the negative pressure condition is satisfied when the cyclic scale factor is substituted. Furthermore, we find that the EoS parameter's dependence on the cyclic scale factor can be expressed as $\omega = \frac{1}{3}$ for a particular function configuration. Additionally, we analyze the growth rate parameter's behavior and find that it exhibits oscillatory behavior in accordance with cyclic models, with an amplitude influenced by the cutoff's cyclic scale factor variant. Lastly, we investigate the relationship between the cutoff's cyclic and de Sitter variants and identify conditions under which the two behave similarly. Our study demonstrates that cyclic models can be genuinely distinct from those resembling de Sitter spaces. Consequently, this study provides a framework for exploring the fundamental connections between cyclic models and the cosmos' ultimate fate.

We develop a theory of polynomial $L$-functions for graphs, extending the classical Dirichlet $L$-functions to a broader framework. This new framework connects the $L$-functions of a graph to those of its higher-order regular covering graphs, establishing a coherent and extensive conjecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of computing $L$-functions through the determination of covering graphs, and present computational results for small graphs. These results support the conjecture and demonstrate its implications for the nonvanishing of $L$-zeros. Additionally, we identify relationships between polynomial $L$-functions and classical Dirichlet $L$-functions, enabling the application of our theory to apologize results concerning the nonvanishing of Dirichlet $L$-zeros. Our methods also facilitate the derivation of bounds for the least positive zeros of polynomial $L$-functions, and we discuss the related open problem of obtaining bound inequalities in terms of graph properties. Lastly, we introduce the concept of extended Selberg polynomials and present computational examples validating the proposed conjecture. Our research is inclusive of recent discoveries of the authors and is accompanied by publicly accessible computations available at the referred link. Our work is also relevant to but independent of the theories of Chowla's conjecture, the Gelfand-Shirshov method, the Capelli identity, and the Yang-Mills measure.

The question of how a Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ with a non-abelian residue field characteristic in relation to its ramification pattern, specifically with wild ramification, relates to its Galois group's additive structure over $\mathbb{Z}_pG$ for $p=\charac(K)$ has been a subject of research. This study addresses the case of $\mathbb{Q}$-Galois extensions $K$ with a prime $p$ having a specific property: it does not divide the degree of the extension, nor does it divide the order of its Galois group. The main contribution here is the identification of a condition on the Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ that arises from the base field being $\mathbb{F}_p$ and results in the group's additivity over $\mathbb{Z}_p G$ implying that the Galois extension is abelian. This finding generalizes and strengthens previous results by M. Lie, particularly in the context of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[-n]{p})$-Galois extensions. Moreover, the connection between Lie's 'length' and the 'depth' of a Galois extension is clarified, demonstrating that the latter is a more refined inductive measure. The paper also introduces a new concept, 'weak additivity', which is shown to be a key feature of Galois extensions exhibiting Serre's wild inertia lemma behavior. Ultimately, it is demonstrated that 'weak additivity' is equivalent to the combination of 'abnormal' and 'Grosshauptmann's inductive' properties. The discussion is accompanied by a detailed examination of a recent paper by J. Harvey and A. Matsumoto. The paper's final section presents an example illustrating the interplay between additivity, normality, and the field's residue characteristic in a $\mathbb{Q}$-Galois extension with a non-abelian Galois group. The example also highlights the unique circumstances that allow it to exhibit additivity, thereby suggesting that the set of additively structured non-abelian $\mathbb{Q}$-Galois extensions with a finite residue field characteristic has a measure of minimal density over the rational numbers. The paper's concluding remarks propose several research directions related to its main contributions.

As the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) upgrades to the High-Luminosity LHC (HLHC), it's crucial to investigate the effectiveness of future collider searches for neutral long-lived particles (LLPs). LLPs decay meters from the primary interaction point, necessitating a fully integrated detector system to recover particle trails. Despite existing studies on individual detector components, a comprehensive analysis across the entire LHC detector suite in the HLHC context has yet to be conducted. This research employs highly advanced simulated data to evaluate the sensitivity of a fully integrated LHC detector system in the HLHC to several types of neutral LLPs, utilizing thermally stressed detector materials to account for radiation damage. The study assesses the optimal recovery strategies for LLPs based on their decay lengths and focuses on the detection efficiency and momentum reconstruction accuracy across various radiations scenarios. The findings demonstrate a significant enhancement in the LHC detector system's sensitivity to LLPs, with the optimal search strategy varying significantly due to the increased radiation exposure at the HLLC, and the importance of incorporating radiation effects in future LLP sensitivity simulations. The study's results can guide the development of new search strategies and reinterpretation of existing sensitivity claims in the context of LLP models. Furthermore, the research provides detector physicists with actionable advice to enhance the effectiveness of future LHC LLP searches. The publicly accessible code accompanying this research is available online.

Our findings reveal that a model's performance on future tasks relies on the interplay between the variance of its outputs and the varying meanings within its vocabulary. Furthermore, we demonstrate that future models can be anticipated to behave similarly to existing models when the context's semantic variance is constant, leading to testable implications for models of future performance and the nature of semantic shifts. In compressive sensing, the stability and effectiveness of signal recovery heavily rely on the underlying structure of the sensing matrix. Recent research has shown that forming a sensing matrix with low mutual coherence can significantly enhance the performance of image reconstruction tasks. This paper explores an intriguing phenomenon where certain natural image collections exhibit organizational hierarchies that mirror the multi-scale properties found in wavelet transforms. Inspired by this connection, we propose modifying traditional random sensing matrices to incorporate wavelet packet decomposition hierarchies. Through concrete numerical examples and extensive experiments with both synthetic and real images, we demonstrate the outstanding precision and robustness of our approach in reconstructing natural images collectives. Furthermore, this method offers a valuable framework for accurately evaluating the coherence of large-scale matrices. Our code is openly accessible for replication and further exploration. This work is also backed by theoretical analysis and a practical implementation using the C++/MATLAB/Python combination. This research provides an innovative solution to an age-old problem in compressive sensing and may also provide insights for other hierarchical signal processing applications. It is currently available on arXiv.org. This work is also presented at CVPR 2021, one of the top conferences in computer vision. We investigate the scalability of active suspensions by considering a general
hydrodynamic model and employing Monte Carlo simulations, and find that the model
exhibits distinct scaling patterns in dimensions 2 to 4 that diverge from linearized
hydrodynamics, with the difference becoming especially pronounced in the context
of shearing instability in dimensions 3 and 4. In dimensions 2 and 4, the deviations
appear in a non-linear manner, whereas in dimensions 3 and (to a lesser extent)
4, they manifest linearly. We demonstrate that linearized hydrodynamics may yield
stable circles in dimensions 3 and 4, and provide a minimal condition for this
to occur in the latter dimension. We also identify that the hydrodynamic model
displays unstable rings in a broader parameter range than the linearized theory in
dimensions 3 and 4. To facilitate Monte Carlo simulations, we introduce a new
algorithm that significantly reduces correlation between particle positions. This finding
suggests that linearized hydrodynamics overestimates the stable radius of circular
aggregations by a non-negligible amount in dimensions 3 and 4. The discrepancies
we observe highlight the need to thoroughly validate linearized hydrodynamics
against numerical simulations and empirical data in various active suspensions. The
research presented here offers a framework for analyzing the scalability of active
systems through Monte Carlo simulations, and provides novel insights into the
scalability of a general hydrodynamic model in dimensions 2 to 4. The study also
identifies distinct scaling patterns in low-dimensional active systems and reveals
the limitations of linearized hydrodynamics in these settings. The methodological
approach outlined in this work can be applied to any active system in which particles
interact forcelessly, expanding our understanding of active suspensions in low-dimensional settings. The research further highlights the value of utilizing both analytical and numerical approaches to actively investigate the scalability of active systems. The framework outlined in this work can be applied to any active system characterized by pairwise interactions that do not involve force, and may provide a foundation for similar studies on the scalability of active systems in higher-dimensional settings. The high-profile email service providers for research institutions are not adequately safeguarded. If breached, these institutions' email users would be jeopardized, potentially enabling hackers to send phishing emails in the name of respected professors, threatening the integrity of various research projects and potentially hindering the institutions' ability to secure vital grants. In this research, we demonstrate that multiple prominent email services can be compromised using publicly available information about their employees, exploiting poorly secured data such as birthdates and job titles that can be easily acquired through social engineering. Furthermore, we discovered that several of these institutions conform to standardized practices when it comes to account security, utilizing outdated methods such as question-based verification that can be easily bypassed, allowing hackers to gain unauthorized access to accounts. Through a series of targeted phishing campaigns, we were able to gain unauthorized access to multiple high-profile accounts, succeeding in one out of every four attempts. We were able to compromise accounts belonging to senior researchers, department heads and executives with responsibility over research budgets, in addition to several prominent faculty members whose email addresses are widely recognized and often the target of phishing attacks. In some cases, we were able to obtain the passwords to these accounts, either by being informed the password by the account holder himself, or by being given temporary access that allowed us to record the password entered, thereby allowing us to use these passwords to log in to the accounts at a later time. We were able to maintain access to these accounts for an average of 141 days, sending out hundreds of phishing emails during this time, resulting in the compromise of numerous email accounts, in addition to successfully obtaining access to one account on LinkedIn, one account on Google and one account on Dropbox. We were able to achieve these breaches without spending any money on them, demonstrating that security breaches of high-profile email accounts can be accomplished with a minimal amount of effort and resources. We were able to accomplish these breaches due to the inadequate security provided by these email services, coupled with the inadequacy of the account security employed by these institutions, leading to the belief that a more thorough assessment of security measures for high-profile email accounts is necessary. In this research, we are providing all the data used to carry out these breaches, in addition to the methods employed, in the hope that this will result in the implementation of more secure methods to prevent similar breaches from occurring in the future. In cuprates, we propose that the unique behavior of electrons at the (π/2,π/2) point drives a Lifshitz transition, and this effect is amplified by the special characteristics of this material's Fermi surface. A significant increase in the coupling between electrons and the long-range phonon field is found, which is attributed to an unusual van Hove singularity caused by the intricate shape of the Fermi surface. As a result, this singularity induces a Lifshitz transition, contributing to the rise in phonon coupling and an anomalous increase in the carrier effective mass with decreasing temperature, ultimately influencing the material's electrical conductivity near the transition point. Estimates suggest this phenomenon could explain the sudden disruption in the $T$-linear resistivity near the transition point if the corresponding enhancement in the phonon coupling is also considered. Furthermore, this theory also provides a possible explanation for the onset of superconductivity at the magnetic point (π,0) by phonon-mediated interaction between electrons. The necessary conditions for this model to hold are discussed, and it is suggested that the essential features of this theory may be applicable to other materials exhibiting Lifshitz transitions near their superconductivity onset points. The proposed model is supported by a numerical solution to the self-consistency equation for the spectral function, obtained using the Dynamical Mean-Field Theory for a 2D tight-binding model with a Lifshitz transition, and it is anticipated that this theory has implications for a broader range of electronic systems experiencing sudden changes in their band structure. The associated DMFT equations are also provided for the spectral function, and this solution may be useful for interpreting and analyzing experimental data, such as ARPES measurements, particularly in the vicinity of a Lifshitz transition. The availability of this solution is also relevant to the development of more refined methods for solving DMFT, such as the Numerical Maximum Entropy method, and the associated Monte Carlo sampling technique. The utility of this solution is demonstrated by comparing the obtained spectral function to results from numerical simulations, and it is found that the DMFT phase diagram, obtained using this solution as the trial function, accurately reflects the topological changes occurring in the Fermi surface as the electron filling is varied. The proposed solution is also applicable to studying the impact of Lifshitz transitions on the electronic properties of materials, and it is anticipated that this solution will contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying physics governing these transitions and their connection to superconductivity. To increase the efficiency of neutron detection in STIC at the SENSEI experiment, researchers are investigating a novel approach by adding a compound containing Gadolinium to the liquid scintillator. Computational modeling analyzes the interaction between neutrons and this optimized scintillator system, demonstrating a substantial enhancement in detection sensitivity, particularly for slower neutrons, and confirming the feasibility of this method for identifying dark matter signatures in future experiments. A comprehensive analysis of the relationships between star systems and planetary systems within a mass of $10^{2}M_{\odot}$ and an angular size of $10^{-4}$ arcseconds has been conducted using the latest astrometric data from Gaia and radial velocity measurements from spectrographs. This study gathers relevant astrometric and radial velocity information for 1,583,419 stars from the second Gaia data release and identifies 1,084,880 exoplanet candidates through a parametric model. A cometary distribution model is applied to distinguish planetary systems from star system noise and identify distinct populations based on star characteristics. The most prominent population consists of compact, Earth-like systems, but there are also broader systems resembling the Kepler-11 and HAT-P-7 configurations. Systems with large orbits are also identified, often featuring super-Jovian planets and resembling the Uranus and Neptune architectures. These planetary configurations are often linked to multiple-planet systems. A significant percentage of stars with large radial velocity stability have small, compact systems similar to 55 Cancri and Tau Ceti. This research provides the most extensive analysis of extraterrestrial systems to date, offering insights into the relationships between star systems and their planetary companions and shedding light on the underlying processes that shape planetary architectures. This study may serve as a foundation for future astrometric missions aimed at discovering thousands of exoplanets candidates. This work is also accompanied by a public database that enables researchers to visualize and analyze individual star systems and planetary systems through an online web interface. This database is continuously updated as new radial velocity measurements and Gaia data become available. This study is designed to inform and shape the scientific objectives of future radial velocity missions like PLATO and ESA's Radial Velocity Mission, as well as astrometric missions like Gaia II and VEGA. This work is further aimed at inspiring the development of new generation ground-based radial velocity instruments with improved sensitivity and stability that can optimize the discovery potential of these missions. The task of automatically extracting information from identification cards has been around for decades and remains a persistent challenge in the field of Computer Vision. Despite significant progress in recent years, precise and accurate extraction results often fall short due to the presence of distorted IDs. Our research diverges from the conventional path by incorporating Natural Language Processing as a complementary technique to enhance extraction accuracy. We propose an innovative approach that leverages NLP to identify crucial words on IDs, effectively prioritizing the extraction task. By integrating a simple yet robust word-embedding based method, we locally refine the extraction results to obtain optimal outcomes. The proposed framework has been thoroughly tested on two diverse ID datasets containing both English and Chinese IDs and has yielded remarkable results, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin according to our assessment. Moreover, our technique has been applied to improve the extraction of IDs with distorted characters, showcasing its versatility and practical applications. We have openly shared the code and dataset used in this research to stimulate further advancements in this area. Additionally, our team invites researchers to collaborate and share their own ID extraction datasets to facilitate overall field improvement. Together, we can collectively achieve greater success in this field.

The long-term behavior of driven quantum systems in equilibrium can be effectively understood through a variety of exact statistical methods that bypass the need for a full microscopic description. This set of techniques, rooted in the equilibrium theory of driven systems and generalized Wigner functions, enables us to recreate the steady-state spectrum, correlation functions, and scattering matrices solely by analyzing the stationary phase of the Wigner distribution in phase space. This strategy has previously been successful for isolating the long-term spectra and correlation functions for specific system sizes, but its implications for finite systems have not been thoroughly explored. Using this approach, we demonstrate that the long-term behavior of driven quantum systems in equilibrium is characterized by a universal set of curves that are independent of the specific system size and provide a complete description of the system's dynamics. Furthermore, we identify a crucial role for coherent states in this context and demonstrate that the system's behavior can be predicted solely on the basis of its semiclassical equivalent. This breakthrough offers a major advancement in our comprehension of driven quantum systems and paves the way for the application of these exact statistical methods to a broader range of systems. Additionally, we highlight potential applications of this understanding to other statistical descriptions, including the Lindblad equation and scattering theory. By reconciling quantum mechanics and classical physics in this way, we gain a more unified perspective on the dynamics of quantum, classical, and mixed systems. This newfound insight is illustrated through a driven harmonic oscillator, scattering in a quantum billiard, and the dynamics of a quantum rotor in a magnetic field. This study is concluded by proposing several innovative research paths that can further expand our knowledge in this field. The discovery of increased acceleration in the movement of certain near-Earth asteroids is a subject of interest, and to investigate this phenomenon, researchers analyzed a group of small asteroids orbiting the Sun in a similar path to Earth. This study examined the orbital patterns of approximately 1,700 objects within 1 astronomical unit of the Sun, using data from Pan-STARRS1 and LEIDT-2. A more sensitive limit was set for the minimum detectable size, at 100 meters, and the research focused on detecting instances of enhanced acceleration among asteroids with a semi-major axis less than 1 au. The study found that none of the detected objects exhibited enhanced acceleration and conformed to the established parameters of the solar system. The absence of evidence supporting enhanced acceleration in these asteroids suggests that the previous findings were the result of methodological limitations. The most likely explanation for enhanced acceleration in previous findings was the contamination of smaller asteroids, and the research demonstrated that a more advanced method, known as a Richardson-Kent filter, can produce cleaner results. The most accelerated asteroid detected in the study was (99942) 2000 AO$_{28}$, with an acceleration ratio of 1.38, and the research revealed that this object, along with several other asteroids, were part of a larger group with accelerated orbital movements. The acceleration in these asteroids is consistent with the possibility that they originated from a broken asteroid that has since dispersed. The discovery of additional group members is necessary to confirm this theory, and the research also highlighted the importance of using advanced filtering techniques and a comprehensive astronomical catalog when studying this phenomenon. The most suitable candidates for further study based on existing data include (4443) Brthor, (5276) Pollington, (5429) Shawneee, and (6559) Marishita. The study demonstrated that LEIDT-2 and LEIDT-2S can detect the movement of small near-Earth asteroids, and the collaboration between LEIDT-2 and the orbital system can be utilized to enhance the accuracy of acceleration measurements. The most accurate measurement obtained in the study had an uncertainty of 0.05 m/s$^2$, and the research demonstrated that a collaborative approach between ground-based telescopes and LEIDT-2 or LEIDT-2S can significantly improve the quality of these measurements. The study also analyzed the potential sources of enhanced acceleration in asteroids, and the findings suggest that the previously proposed explanation for the existence of ToO objects is the most likely explanation. Determining whether a set of rational functions evaluates to a constant value or is entirely distinct from constants can be a challenging problem, especially when considering its connection to computational complexity classes. In this study, we investigate decision problems related to rational functions in one variable, and these decision problems surprisingly lie at the intersection of algebraic decision problems and computational complexity classes like PSPACE and BPP. Our research reveals that deciding if a system of rational functions is continuous or disconnected over the complex plane is a PSPACE-complete problem, whereas determining if a single rational function separates it from constant values or reconnects it with itself requires a more complex calculation that is equivalent to solving a system of linear differential equations under specific constraints, a process that is known to be a non-uniform BPP problem. Additionally, our work shows that deciding if two rational functions have identical roots or if they share a common root with a given rational function over the complex plane are also PSPACE-complete problems. We also examine decision problems related to rational functions that are restricted to being non-residues or having specific values for particular prime factors, and our results show that these problems also hold a high computational complexity. We believe these results provide a deeper understanding of the computational properties of rational functions and their connection to computational complexity classes. These results are achieved by linking decision problems related to rational functions to problems related to polynomials and linear differential equations, and they are also applicable to functions that are analytic continuations of rational functions. Our research also reveals that deciding if a system of rational functions evaluates to a constant value or is entirely distinct from constants is a non-uniform BPP problem, and this result is achieved by linking this problem to the connection between linear differential equations and rational functions through the non-uniform BPP algorithm of Hermann and Ko. These results are also extendable to a larger class of functions known as pre-Jacobi polynomials and provide them with similar computational complexity properties. These results are of particular interest as they bridge the gap between algebraic decision problems and computational complexity classes like PSPACE and BPP. Moreover, our research also considers decision problems related to the evaluation of systems of rational functions at different algebraic points, and our results show that these problems are also related to computational complexity classes like EXP and its variants. Additionally, our work also explores decision problems related to the connectivity of systems of rational functions that are defined as the intersection of sets defined by several rational functions, and our results show that these problems are also related to computational complexity classes like NP and its variants. Complex systems, characterized by multiple time scales and competing dynamics, pose significant challenges for prediction and control. While reservoir computing has proven highly effective for temporal pattern recognition, its application is generally limited to systems with relatively simple dynamics. This study introduces an unconventional reservoir architecture, inspired by the fractional order Lowell oscillator, which inherently captures diverse time scales. The proposed reservoir model is then demonstrated for two demanding scenarios: predicting multi-stable and scale-free dynamics in a nonlinear system similar to a Kuramoto network, and modeling cross-frequency dynamics in a fractional order phase oscillator. The architecture's performance is compared to a conventional Lowell oscillator reservoir and an established Echo State Network for both scenarios, showcasing the new design's superior or comparable performance. The proposed approach provides a reservoir computing framework capable of addressing a broad spectrum of applications featuring a wide range of time scales. This is achieved without the need for careful tuning of the reservoir's connectivity or update rate parameters. The introduced methodology is versatile, allowing incorporation of external information and prior knowledge, which can facilitate the solution of real-world problems requiring the integration of numerical data with theoretical models. The code for the new architecture and the associated examples is available online at an open-source repository. The results of this work are also supported by numerical simulations conducted with MATLAB, and the related code has been included as part of the repository mentioned above. A common challenge in bias-reduced estimation arises when an initial estimation step fails to meet the required smoothness conditions, necessitating a new approach. To mitigate this limitation, a alternative bias reduction method is proposed, characterized by increased flexibility that relaxes the traditional smoothness constraints. The proposed estimator leverages a distinct representation of the bias component, enabled by a change-of-variables transformation, allowing for a more general expansion that is free from constraints on the parameters' values. The benefits of this approach are two-fold: first, the estimated bias exhibits the desired cancellation property; second, the flexibility accommodates non-differentiable cases. Theoretical properties of the proposed estimator are established through asymptotic normality results, and a practical application is demonstrated using a threshold model from labor economics. The accompanying simulation evidence highlights the estimator's superior performance relative to its counterparts. The proposed method is made readily available through an R package that can be accessed via an R function included in the supplementary materials. The results obtained from implementing the estimator in a research setting are also presented. The research paper includes an illustration of the estimator's application in a labor economic context and the accompanying code is provided in the supplementary materials. We introduce an advanced model to study the spread of diseases within enclosed environments, building upon traditional epidemiological models by incorporating super-spreader events. We examine how the dynamic transmission of COVID-19 within a conference center can be understood and potentially mitigated through this enhanced model. Furthermore, we analyze how modeling assumes no prior knowledge and can be applied to analyze various epidemic scenarios. We investigate the influence of super-spreader events on infection dynamics and find that a small group can cause widespread illness due to their exponentially increased transmission rate. We explore the impact of isolating infected individuals, discovering that this can significantly reduce the peak infection rate. We also find that vaccinating a group can lead to a smaller group of infections among the unvaccinated individuals. We analyze how modeling assumes no prior knowledge and can be applied to analyze various epidemic scenarios. We discovered that this model can be a powerful tool for understanding and mitigating the spread of diseases through analysis of the model's dynamics and its application to real-world scenarios. We believe that this approach can be used to study the spread of diseases in various closed environments and advocate for a more general adoption of this model in epidemiological research. We made our calculations publicly available to facilitate further research and encourage scientists to build upon our study.

A $C_0$-semigroup of operators $\mathfrak{A}$ on a Banach space $\mathfrak{X}$ is considered codiskcyclic if there exists a closed invariant subspace $\mathfrak{M}$ with a codimension of 1, where the restriction of $\mathfrak{A}$ exhibits surjectivity. In this research, codiskcyclic $C_0$-semigroups are analyzed in the context of Banach space applications. Specifically, we investigate codiskcyclic operator semigroups on Banach spaces of continuous functions, demonstrate codiskcyclic properties for a notable example, and explore related concepts of supercodiskcyclicity and diskcyclicity. Furthermore, we provide codiskcyclic characterizations for single-server Phillips function maps and a related periodic evolution equation. These analyses contribute to a deeper understanding of codiskcyclic operator semigroups within Banach space frameworks. The accuracy of solar surface magnetic field observations relies heavily on vector magnetic field measurements, which are typically inferred from spectropolarimetric analysis and the assumption of force balance. However, the magnetic field's true strength and direction may be underestimated if the used inversion techniques do not account for the fill fraction properly, especially in strong field regions. We present a method to directly consider the magnetic filling factor during the inversion process with regular least-squares optimization techniques. This approach uses a single parameter to model the magnetic energy density and the thermal one, effectively eliminating the need for separating filled and void areas. We demonstrate that by doing so, the assumptions about magnetic pressure balance can be reliably recovered with increased precision, especially in strong field regions. This precision improvement becomes apparent when comparing maps created with and without considering the fill factor, as well as between different inversion codes that employ similar physics. We also find that using the fill factor directly yields more realistic values for magnetic field strength and direction when applied to synthetic data. This method is compatible with current spectropolarimetric inversion techniques and can be implemented using existing codes with minor adjustments. We suggest utilizing this method to create reference maps for assessing the performance of end-to-end solar spectro-polarimetric inversion simulations.
