Topological entropy in subshifts is a highly researched topic, particularly regarding recognizable and ultimately recognizable subshifts. This study explores the interplay between these concepts and morphisms. By defining recognizable subshifts as those whose extensions are ultimately recognizable, our investigation confirms that recognizable subshifts exhibit increased topological entropy when subjected to certain morphisms, which can result in an enhancement or deterioration. Additionally, our findings indicate that applying recognizable morphisms to subshifts may either elevate or diminish the topological entropy, depending on the underlying subshift. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that using recognizable morphisms can raise topological entropy from a lower bound to the maximal possible value. This study also reveals that using ultimately recognizable morphisms has a similar effect, but only when the initial subshift has an elevated topological entropy. These outcomes illustrate the complex relationships between recognizable subshifts, morphisms, and topological entropy. Moreover, these results highlight the distinct implications of using recognizable and ultimately recognizable morphisms. Ultimately, this research underscores the multifaceted nature of these relationships.

Contrastive learning in unsupervised conditions involves generating contrasting samples from a single stimulus. This technique is often limited due to the complexity of contrasting sample generation. We introduce ReCross, a contrastive learning approach that uses a single strong positive sample and multiple weak negative samples to significantly simplify the process. This method is highly versatile and can be applied to both traditional contrastive learning and recent pre-trained language models like BERT. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ReCross by conducting extensive experiments on both the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks, achieving notable improvements and establishing new state-of-the-art benchmarks. Additionally, our method is remarkably easy to implement and requires minimal adjustments to existing code. This ease of use, coupled with the substantial gains achieved, makes ReCross a highly accessible and convenient solution for enhancing the performance of language models in unsupervised conditions. We have made our code and models available for public access.

Hyperparameter optimization is a critical task in machine learning, often hindered by time constraints or computational expenses due to costly function evaluations. While techniques like grid search are impractical for expensive-to-evaluate models, we find that even the most sophisticated modern methods can fall short when confronted with private datasets that cannot be shared with remote evaluators. To address this challenge, we present a novel algorithm that efficiently tunes the hyperparameters of a model while keeping the dataset private. Our method leverages a private intermediate representation of the optimization problem to facilitate cooperative optimization with remote evaluators, significantly outperforming conventional methods on several private dataset benchmarks. Notably, our approach boasts a mere additional evaluation cost of 1.5 times the cost of a single-pass stochastic gradient descent. Moreover, our method is versatile and adaptable to a range of optimization algorithms and problem domains. We showcase its effectiveness on hyperparameter optimization problems in private settings for both machine learning and language model applications. To bridge this gap, we present the performance evaluation of LifeStream, our recent compiler-based approach that converts general-purpose, float-based programs to their corresponding integer programs for arbitrary precision arithmetic. To assess LifeStream's validity, we compared its performance to that of hand-optimized numerical libraries for three key scenarios: numerical linear algebra, real-world dataset analysis, and a physics engine. Our results show that LifeStream's precision-sensitive variants match the performance of hand-optimized libraries in numerical linear algebra and the hand-optimized variants of BLAS/LAPACK, and even surpass them by 1.5-3.5 times for certain operations. We extend the concept of a Bertrand curve to a higher-dimensional space of constant curvature in the setting of Euclidean space. Bertrand curves have been thoroughly explored in two-dimensional Euclidean space, especially in its standard form, and also in its simplified form within the space of all plane curves. Furthermore, Bertrand curves have been analyzed in the context of a space with constant curvature, and even in the scenario where the curve itself has a constant non-negative value. However, despite the significance of such research, the term 'Bertrand curve' is often misunderstood as referring to a specific type of curve that is unique and definite in both 2D and 5D Euclidean space, and even in the complex plane. This misunderstanding needs to be addressed through clarification and a review of the applicable definition of a Bertrand curve in both 2D and 5D Euclidean space, and the complex plane. We then establish a new, general approach to identifying Bertrand curves in a space with constant curvature, and demonstrate this method's effectiveness through analysis of curves within this context. Additionally, we recognize that certain types of curves which satisfy the Bertrand criterion do not exist in either the 2D or 5D Euclidean space, or the complex plane. Our research also involves exploring the relationship between curves that satisfy the Bertrand criterion and their associated dual curves. We demonstrate that in a space with constant curvature, a curve's dual curve will also satisfy the Bertrand criterion, and that this dual curve can be expressed as a Bertrand curve in the context of that specific space. We then analyze specific types of curves to demonstrate the applicability and usefulness of our new approach. We conclude by establishing a connection between curves that satisfy the Bertrand criterion and their associated tripls and quadruplets of curves, and identify opportunities for further research in this area. 

Keywords: Bertrand curve, curve geometry, dual curve, triplex and quadruplex spaces.

The evaluation function used in training models significantly impacts their performance, yet some loss functions are employed less frequently due to limited understanding of their behavior or practical difficulties. To shed light on underrepresented loss functions like KL Divergence, we investigate a theoretical loss landscape that encompasses both logistic regression loss and KL Divergence. Our analysis reveals that, in this setting, a variety of loss functions, including those typically utilized such as cross-entropy, can be viewed as minimizing a more general function in a restricted domain. To illustrate this concept, we derive an alternative interpretation of KL Divergence in this theoretical loss landscape. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that, even in modern settings with modern optimizers and vast datasets, using KL Divergence as the loss function yields models with lower test accuracy compared to using cross-entropy. This suggests that models may benefit from incorporating loss functions beyond those commonly employed in the data they are trained on. Additionally, we show that this benefit may extend to unsupervised domain adaptation, demonstrating improved test accuracy when using an unsupervised loss function tailored to the source domain. This indicates that loss functions have value as tools, enabling adaptation of models to new domains with minimal additional data. 

This research is influenced by the work of Y. Wang, J. Liu, and H. Liu, which suggests that overfitting may occur when using certain loss functions due to the complexity of the model, and that this issue can be addressed through techniques like regularization. Building upon this, we explore a more complex scenario in which the loss function's behavior is shaped by an underlying distribution, and investigate how this distribution impacts the model's performance when a different evaluation function is used. 

Our analysis is set within a theoretical scenario that combines elements of both supervised and unsupervised learning, utilizing a general form of the logistic function to model decision boundaries, and a specific type of distribution to govern the data generation process. This framework allows us to examine how different loss functions evaluate models by controlling the underlying distribution, effectively dictating what models are learned. 

Specifically, we first demonstrate that cross-entropy loss can be viewed as a constraint on an optimization problem that includes logistic regression, and that this results in models that learn the data distribution. Conversely, we show that KL Divergence loss can be seen as optimizing a similar problem, but with a different evaluation function that places models in a distinct set. 

Our experiments validate our analysis by evaluating models trained with these loss functions on unseen data, and also explore their application in unsupervised domain

To assess the validity of the grand canonical ensemble, it's crucial to regulate the system's compressibility at a given pressure. Unfortunately, thermal fluctuations force the compressibility to be positively infinite in the grand canonical ensemble. This complication arises because the number of particles is randomly varied according to a Poisson distribution. As a result, the system's ability to expand infinitely to minimize pressure forces the grand canonical ensemble's validity to be limited by the finite size of the system. In contrast, the pressure derivative of the system's free energy exhibits a minimum value, which can be used as a compressibility proxy. In this research, we analyze the relationship between this compressibility and the bulk properties of systems modeled by Ising and Lattice Gas, and we propose a similar approach for spin glass and hard core bosons. Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach can be applied to finite temperature phases by using the spin wave approximation. Furthermore, we investigate the phase coexistence in the Lattice Gas and show that the proposed compressibility not only distinguishes the coexistence state but also accurately measures the volume fluctuation in the same manner as it does in the bulk. This understanding of compressibility is subsequently utilized to improve the Metropolis-Hastings sampling method. We find that by combining the proposed compressibility with the acceptance ratio, we can identify and avoid unfavorable sample configurations more effectively. As a result, this research offers a novel strategy for adjusting the compressibility of the system during Monte Carlo simulations, which can enhance the efficiency of Metropolis-Hastings sampling. This efficiency improvement is universally applicable to all Monte Carlo algorithms that exploit the system's equilibrium properties to evaluate proposal distributions. Moreover, this research introduces a new method for detecting phase coexistence in finite temperature systems. The proposed compressibility measure provides a precise indication of the phase coexistence state, allowing for the accurate measurement of the fluctuation of a specific volume. The discovery of a precise indicator of phase coexistence is a significant breakthrough, as this issue has been a persistent challenge in the simulation of multi-phase systems. In rain removal image processing, establishing a precise relationship between rain pattern formation and dissipation is considered a key challenge. Current methods primarily focus on analyzing the rain pattern through traditional image segmentation techniques, yet they fail to capture the underlying physics. This research introduces an innovative model that redefines rain droplets as semi-transparent ellipsoidal objects, allowing for both generation and removal processes to be modeled through physics-inspired methods. Specifically, rain generation is represented by an advection differential equation, while rain removal is captured by a diffusion equation. These approaches enable not only accurate estimation of rain-free images but also simultaneous removal and estimation of background images. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over state-of-the-art techniques in terms of both subjective visual quality and objective metrics. Moreover, our model facilitates the learning of physics-based processes without manual parameter tuning, instead relying on learned parameters that adapt to diverse datasets. Comprehensive comparative evaluations on multiple public datasets consistently rank our method at or near the top in terms of PSNR. The code for our research is available online at https://github.com/zhengzheng420/PHRain.

The existing model performance is enhanced when the models are trained to recognize not just a particular relation type but also the most general one it belongs to. As a result, the models are compelled to understand the hierarchy by learning the most specific relation type for a given sentence, thereby potentially leading to better comprehension of the sentence's core "if-then" content. In our research, we introduce a novel hierarchical relation type classification task that allows neural models to not only identify specific relation types but also the more general ones they belong to. Quantum algorithms like HHL's estimation method for matrix inverses are highly promising but often hindered by NISQ hardware limitations. To overcome this, the NISQ-HHL algorithm was developed to offer an efficient and roughly equivalent solution for matrix inversion. Building upon this work, our proposal goes beyond the original HHL algorithm, allowing it to be executed on modern quantum hardware while also providing a more precise result. Although the modified version may not match the original algorithm's overall performance, it still represents a significant enhancement for the specific applications where the algorithm spends a considerable amount of time in the amplification phase. We demonstrate the advantages of this approach through an example involving the calculation of a matrix inverse in a chemical system's Hamiltonian matrix. This illustrates an imaginary scenario in which a quantum computer has access to a limited number of highly reliable and reconfigurable logical qubits. The algorithm yields a notable improvement in its scalability and could have implications for the development of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. These advancements could potentially lead to breakthroughs in areas like the simulation of chemical valence bonds and quantum machine learning's data preprocessing stages.

Recent advances in single-view video prediction have been significant, but most existing methods are limited to predicting short-duration videos. To overcome this limitation, we draw inspiration from the concept of relative viewpoints in the field of image synthesis. Unlike previous approaches that solely focus on individual time steps, our proposed framework, Relative Video Transformer, leverages a dual representation and incorporates relative viewpoint information to enhance the prediction of videos from novel perspectives. This approach is particularly beneficial for longer-duration video prediction tasks. We evaluate our method against the current state-of-the-art techniques for single-view video prediction on the SSO dataset and achieve superior performance, with an average PSNR improvement of 0.16 across various time scales. This indicates that incorporating relative viewpoint information is critical for accurate prediction of extended video sequences. To facilitate comparative evaluations, we have released the code and model weights for our proposed Relative Video Transformer on the MMAction2 repository.

This research paper builds upon an idea proposed by unclonable encryption and copy-protection for unlearnable functions in cryptography. Specifically, it explores the potential for a broader application, which we term "functionally unclonable extraction," enabling an original owner to prevent unauthorized replication of a diverse range of functions by multiple users. These functions can be both cryptographic and non-cryptographic in nature. We demonstrate the feasibility of this concept through two distinct constructions. First, we show that even if several users have access to a random number generator used to create multiple authentic copies of an original input, it is computationally impossible for them to combine these inputs to create a new, distinct input. We also present an additional construction, which allows an original owner to prevent multiple authorized parties from simultaneously reproducing a diverse range of original images protected by a particular pattern of lines. These constructions demonstrate the feasibility of "functionally unclonable extraction" and contribute to a broader understanding of the potential for copy-protection in cryptography. Building upon this foundation, we propose several potential future directions for this area of research. Lastly, we highlight a connection between this work and an open problem in cryptography known as the direct product theorem for circuits. A fundamental concept in coding theory is the relationship between channel capacity and reliable communication. However, this research investigates an alternative framework where communication is achieved not just by conveying information, but also by maintaining a connection with the receiver. In this framework, a portion of data is allocated for'syncing bits,' which ensures that the receiver can maintain contact with the sender. These syncing bits serve a purpose analogous to that of pilot signals in modern wireless communication systems. By leveraging this framework, a novel problem of channel authentication is formalized. The goal of this problem is to develop methods that can ascertain the origin of information while maintaining a connection with the receiver. The research demonstrates that by utilizing this framework, various coding techniques such as polar codes and LDPC codes can be adapted for authentication purposes. The adaptations demonstrate that the coding rate required for authentication can be made arbitrarily small, thus aligning with theoretical expectations. The research also introduces a novel metric known as the authenticated rate, which represents the coding rate necessary for both reliable communication and verification of the source. The development of polar code and LDPC code ensembles in this context is presented through comprehensive derivations. The findings of this research have the potential to contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental limitations and trade-offs involved in the use of communication resources with verification capabilities. We utilize large supercells to account for lattice relaxations and doping effects on plasmons in twisted bilayer MoS$_2$. Our calculations indicate that lattice relaxation significantly impacts plasmon characteristics, with varying twisted angles resulting in distinct trends in plasmon energy and dispersion. Doping, considered through carrier concentration adjustments, reveals a notable reduction in plasmon energy with increasing twist angle, ultimately converging to a doping-induced limit. Notably, lattice relaxation exhibits a more complex dependence on twist angle compared to the doping effect, and our findings also reveal that doping can be comprehended through a shift of the band structure rather than band filling. Furthermore, our study identifies that the plasmon energy versus carrier concentration relationship follows a universal path that is independent of the twisted angle, which we propose results from a uniform electron gas within the central region of the twisted sample. This central area, having a uniform Mo atomic density close to that of single-layer Mo, dictates the plasmon energy versus carrier concentration curve, and its characteristics resemble those of single-layer MoS$_2$. Additionally, our research highlights the importance of lattice relaxation in understanding plasmon phenomena in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides.

This research paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of almost conformal Ricci solitons in the context of complete, non-compact Riemannian manifolds. Our primary objective is to establish a condition that can identify whether an almost conformal Ricci soliton is indeed an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton when the soliton has a non-constant scalar field. To this end, we first establish a crucial condition that can determine if an almost conformal Ricci soliton is an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton when the manifold has a compact parameter. This condition is key to proving the more general case for non-compact manifolds. Notably, our argument for the non-compact case relies on an analytical technique that involves the separation of variables. We also prove the equivalence between almost conformal Ricci solitons and almost conformal gradient Ricci solitons in compact manifolds that have a non-constant scalar field. Additionally, this equivalence holds for complete, non-compact manifolds with a compact parameter. Lastly, we identify a necessary condition for the soliton's scalar field to be harmonic. Furthermore, we establish that this condition, coupled with the compactness of the manifold or the compactness of the manifold's parameter, is sufficient to imply that the soliton's scalar field is a conformal gradient Ricci soliton. This conclusion is already known for compact manifals, but it represents a significant advancement for non-compact manifolds. Moreover, this research reveals that a recent publication is actually addressing a special case of our findings. In essence, this research is an extension of a discussion on the soliton's harmonic scalar field in a specific setting to a broader context. Both stellar and planetary magnetospheres are significantly influenced by the reconnection of magnetic field lines at their boundaries, but the underlying processes that shape these environments differ greatly. In the case of stellar magnetospheres, the impact of magnetic reconnection is clouded by the vast extent of the wind's plasma, which masks local changes. In contrast, planetary magnetospheres are characterized by the profound effect of magnetic reconnection on their motion of geophysical shocks, revealed through recent simulations. This talk will discuss recent numerical modeling of the interaction between solar wind and the Martian magnetosphere, specifically focusing on how magnetic reconnection influences the planet's shock waves and magnetospheric boundaries, and will also explore the implications of these findings for other terrestrial planets within the solar system.

Recent research demonstrated that a neural network's Lipschitz constant can be limited during training using a modified objective function. This approach allows us to train neural networks with controlled sensitivity to input changes without needing explicit differentiation or Jacobian monitoring. Our study investigates how the choice of $p$-norm influences the model's accuracy and robustness. We show that the choice of $p$-norm affects the model's performance, and provide a theoretical justification for this observation through the lens of Lipschitz-penalized empirical risk minimization. Our analysis also highlights the benefits of using the infinity norm, and supports experimental findings indicating improved performance when $p=1$. We demonstrate that this choice yields models with comparable accuracy and substantially improved robustness in the face of $l_2$-attacks. Our research implies that the choice of $p$-norm is a critical consideration in such penalty-based methods, and highlights the potential for further optimization strategies. Deep neural models for sentence comprehension have made significant progress in recent years. Despite achieving impressive performance on individual sentences, many sequential models struggle to capture the hierarchical organization of sentences. To overcome this limitation, we draw inspiration from the success of tree search algorithms and incorporate local heuristics into neural networks to leverage their combined strengths. By recursively applying a simple sorting algorithm to inter-syntactic dependencies, we demonstrate the ability to derive hierarchical tree structures from neural network representations and showcase this capability on local and long-distance dependencies in English. Moreover, our method's extensibility to other languages is highlighted through an analysis of relative clauses in German and Japanese. Furthermore, we showcase sequential models that can accurately predict sentence embeddings and demonstrate substantial gains in semantic similarity tasks on the SemEval 2012 task 2 and the STS benchmark. The code and data for our work are openly accessible online.

The ultra-short period exoplanet HD80606b, orbiting a G-type star about 411 light-years from Earth, has been studied through NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope observations in 2004. Researchers analyzed high-resolution spectra of the star HD80606, obtained by the Keck telescope, to estimate the planet's mass and a key characteristic of its atmosphere. Due to its close orbit to the star, the planet experiences a scorching surface temperature, changing dramatically over its 111-day orbital period. When passing its closest point, its surface temperature spikes to around 4700 degrees Fahrenheit, only to drop to around 2000 degrees Fahrenheit when it's at its farthest point. To understand this extreme temperature fluctuation, scientists needed to determine the planet's mass, which in turn required pinpointing the star's velocity during the closest point of the orbit, known as periastron. To do this, researchers analyzed the star's light during the periastron in 2004 and 2005 using the Hubble Space Telescope, showing the star was moving at around 110 miles per second. Based on this data, scientists calculated the mass of the planet, finding it to be about 1.78 times the mass of Earth, significantly narrower than previously estimated. Additionally, they determined the planet's atmosphere likely contains a extensive hydrogen envelope, likely the result of the star stripping it away during a close approach about 100 million years ago. This unique planet offers a fascinating opportunity to study the effects of a close celestial approach on a planetary atmosphere.

A deep-neural-network (DNN) approach known as low-dose PET-MRI image synthesis was proposed in a previous study to enhance the quality of low-dose PET images by utilizing MRI information. This work extends the initial research by comparing various techniques for combining MRI and low-dose PET information in the synthesis process. A new method that combines complementary aspects of the maps was also introduced to improve the accuracy of PET-MRI image synthesis. Through cross-validation and a cohort of 12 patients with prostate cancer, the proposed method was evaluated against baseline methods. Results showed that the new technique surpasses the baseline methods, with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 11.432%, significantly improving MAPE scores of 13.537% (baseline method 1) and 12.135% (baseline method 2). The proposed method's accuracy can serve as a benchmark for further research in this area. Additionally, a user-friendly graphical user interface was designed to facilitate easy access to the proposed method for healthcare professionals. The enhanced PET images demonstrated excellent agreement with clinical standards, as evidenced by mean coefficients of variation of 0.253 (early phase) and 0.275 (late phase). The proposed method's accuracy, combined with its user-friendly interface and the ability to handle whole-body images, makes it a valuable tool for clinical applications. Nevertheless, the technique is still in its developmental stage and requires refinement to rival cutting-edge DNN methods. Furthermore, the method's ability to handle diverse types of tumors needs to be explored in future research. The proposed technique's code is available online for the benefit of the scientific community.

We investigate the operator growth phenomenon in the SU(1,1) Witten model by employing symmetry. It is established that the operator growth follows a continuous pattern, characterized by an exponential increase in a twisted sector. Additionally, we derive exact expressions for the average and standard deviation of operator dimensions, confirming that they adhere to expected scaling properties. These results are validated through explicit calculations of entanglement properties in a corresponding context. Furthermore, we highlight the significance of employing symmetry in calculations, as it significantly reduces the necessary computational effort compared to generalizing from previously known results. Our findings also reveal that the SU(1,1) Witten model exhibits behavior akin to that observed in certain higher-spin conformal theories, and we anticipate that our methodology may be applicable to additional symmetry settings. Moreover, this analysis indicates that the twisted sector, which has an exponential operator growth pattern, may be distinguishable from the rest of the spectrum by means of a Hermitian operator derived from entanglement thermalizes slowly. If this operator also characterizes the distinction in other contexts remains to be seen. Our study employs a recently introduced method for computing operator dimensions and standard deviations, which is applicable to any parity-breaking, one-dimensional system that can be mapped onto a SU(1,1) representation and may have implications for understanding operator growth in other settings. Lastly, this analysis underscores the significance of symmetry in operator growth studies and suggests that the twisted sector may be relevant for studying phase transitions in quantum systems.

Recently, deep learning-based approaches have enhanced signal fingerprint-based localization by leveraging a medium to large number of reference points, but they have largely focused on static locations and underrepresented culture and physical diversity. A novel deep learning framework is introduced for wireless localization, characterized by its simplicity, low data requirements, and ability to account for geospatial distance between signal samples. A convolutional neural network is utilized for initial feature extraction from WiFi signals, followed by a proprietary use of relative positioning information via spatial temporal graph neural networks to estimate relative distances between locations. The model's performance was evaluated on a dataset containing diverse reference points and users, demonstrating superior results compared to baseline methods and the model's ability to extend to new locations within a specified range. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework can accurately estimate distances of less than 10 meters with high precision and extends to locations up to 5-7 meters beyond the training range with reasonable accuracy. Additionally, the model's ability to incorporate diverse reference points and users was found to be beneficial. Furthermore, the evaluation of extending the model to new locations without fresh training showed promising results, with an accuracy of 0.97 or higher within the trained range and 0.80 accuracy at 5 meters and 0.68 at 7 meters beyond the trained range. The code for this research is available online at https://github.com/kuichun75/STGNN-Localizaton. Through this work, this research aims to encourage the development of efficient deep learning methods for wireless localization that can be applied to a wide range of settings.

A vast array of exotic energy sources is being considered for the purpose of propelling an interstellar civilization across the vast expanse of the cosmos. To evaluate the effectiveness of these sources, a new framework is introduced that assesses their capability based on the principle of conservation of energy. This approach is applied to analyze the potential of stars, black holes, dark matter, dark energy, supernovae, and cosmic strings. The study reveals that dark energy offers the highest energy output, followed by supernovae, dark matter, cosmic strings, stars, and finally black holes. It is interesting to note that the most energetic of these sources can be localized, such as supernovae, in contrast to the often diffuse nature of the others. This distinction leads to the possibility of detecting a civilization located near a supernova through its increased flux, even if the civilization is not utilizing this energy. This study sets the stage for exploring detection methods in future research.

As energy recovery linacs (ERLCs), like future multi-pass (MP) SRF-based light sources, face increasing energy recovery thresholds due to growing user demands, it's becoming essential to manage beam-RF interaction limits by filling patterns. This algorithm uses an approximate solution to a 1D matrix equation and leverages the unique structure of MP ERLC transfer matrices to achieve a significant computational advantage. By applying this algorithm to a simple test case and a more realistic benchmark derived from the proposed FAIR ERLC design, it demonstrates the ability to find optimal filling patterns that minimize beam-RF interaction in interaction regions, resulting in a threshold current reduction. The results obtained with this algorithm are also compatible with the findings of more sophisticated general-purpose beam dynamics codes like MAD. Accurate neutron cross section measurements are crucial for understanding the composition of stars and stellar interiors. To facilitate this, a comprehensive study of neutron cross sections across a broad energy range is necessary. This research extends previous measurements of the total neutron cross section in scintillator from 2 to 40 MeV and adds new data between 98 and 688 MeV. The total neutron cross section in carbon was also reevaluated from 250 to 661 MeV and the results from both energy ranges are consistent. The research is significant as it addresses a major limitation in the calibration of neutron energies for stellar neutrino detection. The new cross section measurements in scintillator are accurate to 1.5% and those in carbon are accurate to 2.4%. The research is also relevant to ongoing and future neutron cross section measurements that will improve the accuracy of neutrino flux and energy spectrum determinations. The new cross section measurements in scintillator are 14.27 +/- 0.20 (stat.) +/- 0.17 (sys.) barns at 100 MeV, 16.72 +/- 0.22 (stat.) +/- 0.20 (sys.) barns at 200 MeV and 13.99 +/- 0.21 (stat.) +/- 0.18 (sys.) barns at 600 MeV. The new cross section measurements in carbon are 1064 +/- 25 (stat.) +/- 84 (sys.) millibarns at 252 MeV, 541.0 +/- 13.5 (stat.) +/- 10.5 (sys.) millibarns at 385 MeV and 434.6 +/- 5.8 (stat.) +/- 4.2 (sys.) millibarns at 672 MeV. The research is based on neutron cross section measurements obtained by neutron scatters and detectors made of scintillator and carbon. The research is further supported by data from neutron scattering off hydrogen, helium, carbon, oxygen, neon, magnesium and silicon. The new cross section measurements are consistent with existing data and enhance the precision of neutron cross section measurements across a broad energy range. Our previous model indicated that planets similar to Earth form through a process called planetesimal formation, which occurs when small particles stick together in a solar system. However, further research revealed that the model fails to account for the growth of planets in a high-accretion-rate and high-temperature environment typical of the protoplanetary disk. In order to address this limitation, we modified the model by considering the effects of temperature on the sticking forces between particles. Specifically, we found that in a temperature range of approximately 20-40 Kelvin, sticking forces increase significantly due to the presence of condensible species such as water and silicate vapors. This "optimal" temperature range, where the increase in sticking forces is greatest, is around 25-30 Kelvin. Within this range, we found that the growth of particles follows a self-similar pattern, characterized by a power-law size distribution. This result is consistent with observations of the Earth's building blocks in the solar system. Ultimately, our modified model suggests that planetesimals form through a continuous growth process, starting from small particles that stick together in a narrow temperature range. This process is governed by a power-law size distribution, where the slope depends on the sticking forces and the particle velocities. According to the model, the point of transition to planetesimal formation occurs at a radius of approximately 1 kilometer. Above this size, particles begin to accumulate mass through gravitational influence and settle at the center of the solar system due to their low velocity compared to smaller particles. Our findings provide a foundation for investigating how the growth of particles influences the development of the solar system. Additionally, we expect this model to be applicable not just to the Earth's formation but also to other planetary systems and potentially even exoplanets. Furthermore, we anticipate future research to refine our model through further modification of the sticking forces and consideration of additional factors such as magnetic properties and the influence of other solar system bodies. Ultimately, our model offers a new perspective on planetesimal formation, one that could ultimately reveal the underlying processes that shaped our solar system. In the future, we plan to utilize this model as a starting point for exploring how the growth of particles influences the evolution of the solar system and its planets. Consequently, we expect this model to contribute meaningfully to our understanding of how the solar system and its planets formed over four billion years. The concept of truncated distance in graphs was initially explored in relation to metric dimension. This study further investigates how the graph's structure changes when a maximum geodesic distance is applied, often referred to as a G$k$ graph. We aim to examine the metric dimension of these graphs when the same shortest path is considered, focusing on a specific subcategory of G$k$ graphs known as H$t$ graphs. Specifically, we seek to identify how the metric dimension of H$t$ graphs is impacted when the same shortest path is applied, and we establish a threshold value $t \geq 3$, beyond which the metric dimension of these graphs remains consistent at 1. This finding extends a prior discovery by Furer and Raychaudhuri. We also introduce an efficient algorithm for determining the metric dimension of H$t$ graphs, albeit restricted to instances with dimension 1. This algorithm leverages a parameterized version of the recognition problem for H$t$ graphs. Additionally, we explore upper and lower limits for the metric dimension of H$t$ graphs, and these limits may help inform future research on this topic. Lastly, several instances of the metric dimension of specific H$t$ graphs are calculated, and these examples may provide alternatives or complementary data to existing metric dimension values as reported in graph database collections. This study is an early step towards a broader investigation of the metric dimension of G$k$ graphs. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) possess variables on all temporal scales, from hours to decades, which poses analytical challenges due to data sets spanning extensive periods and incorporating multiple time bases. To address this issue, a unified framework for long-term variable analysis has been proposed, which involves a combination of forecasting and "post-mortem" analysis to extract meaningful insights from both short-term and long-term variability manifestations. This approach has been successfully applied to analyze the variability of the quasars GRK 339, GRK 472, and GRK 529, which are part of a larger sample set. To efficiently discover binary asteroid candidates from large datasets, our research proposes an expedient method for the point spread function (PSF) analysis that leverages machine learning. By applying a convolutional neural network to astronomical images, we can quickly identify patterns that correlate with the presence of asteroids and accurately determine their rotation periods. These rotation periods are crucial for identifying binary asteroid candidates, especially in situations where the companion asteroid's brightness is too low to be detected through traditional means. By utilizing this method on data from the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System (Pan-STARRS), we extracted a list of 341 binary asteroid candidates and validated the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a smaller dataset of 1,500 known binary asteroids. The technique for rotating PSFs was recently patented by one of our study's authors. Our research demonstrates a cost-effective approach for finding binary asteroid candidates and can be adapted for other applications in asteroid science, such as detecting small asteroids or identifying potential danger to near-Earth objects. By integrating this method into existing detection algorithms, we believe it has the potential to significantly enhance the discovery rates of binary asteroid candidates. The technique also raises interesting questions about the potential use of machine learning with data from upcoming wide-field surveys, such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Sky (LSSS). The full dataset derived from this research has been made publicly available through the Small Body Mirror website maintained by the NASA's Near Earth Object Program Office. The data include the 341 potential binary asteroid candidates identified and a subset of 1,500 confirmed binary asteroids used for validation. The research was supported by the NASA's Near Earth Object Program and the Pan-STARRS consortium. The code developed for this research has been openly shared on GitHub in an effort to encourage the further development of this approach and its potential applications in asteroid science. Economic research frequently examines the impact of network connections on individual behavior. However, pinpointing the influence of specific network connections is a complex task. This paper introduces a novel estimation technique to assess peer effects within networks by reconfiguring network positions and analyzing resulting changes in behavior. We apply this method to an experiment in which participants were given monetary incentives to display cooperative behavior in a strategic setting. The findings show that the estimated peer effects are substantial and accurate, confirming the technique's validity. Furthermore, the method can account for diverse network structures and identify the specific network connections that influence individual behavior. Ultimately, this method can be an invaluable tool for dissecting the impact of network connections on individual behavior in various settings.

To establish a reliable performance benchmark for future MIMO systems with correlated noise and arbitrary channel dimensions, we develop an optimal Bayesian detection method in this research. However, this approach's error rate is impractically difficult to compute due to the high dimensionality of its likelihood function. As a result, we investigate a simplified, yet efficient detection algorithm that outperforms the industry standard MMSE detection method. Specifically, we evaluate the performance of this optimal detector, derived from the Generalized Likelihood Ratio Test and assuming Gaussian signaling and Rayleigh fading, in MIMO systems with correlated noise and large channel dimensions. Our analysis reveals that the optimal detector's error rate lies within the bound set by the diversity order and the coding gain, providing a reliable performance benchmark for future MIMO systems. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the proposed detection method's error rate performance approaches that of the optimal Bayesian detector when accounting for the impact of channel dimensions. Finally, our research demonstrates that one of the considered detection methods, characterized by an optimized signal-to-noise ratio and moderate complexity, is comparable to the MMSE detection method in terms of error performance in large-scale MIMO systems with correlated noise and moderate to high SNR levels. Consequently, we propose this detection method as a reference for future MIMO detection research. To facilitate future research, we provide our derived optimal detection formulas and associated error bounds for practical evaluation purposes. Additionally, numerical computations verify the theoretical error bounds and demonstrate the detection method's scalability to large channel dimensions. The Gondwana supercontinent's breakup history involved an extensional system with diverse direction and velocity changes, which significantly impacted the development of passive marginal structures.  Our analysis of the South Atlantic margin in West Africa and Brazil aims to investigate how changes in extension direction and velocity affected the tectonic and stratigraphic evolution of rift basins.  We built a 2D numerical model simulating the extension of a lithospheric plate with varying direction and velocity to better understand its implications for rift basin evolution.  Results show that when the extension direction changes from perpendicular to parallel with respect to pre-rift paleostress fields, there is a sudden shift from symmetrical to asymmetrical rifts, with significant consequences for tectonic evolution and stratigraphic patterns.  We observed that high-extension-velocity rifts exhibit synthetic and anti-symmetric faults, whereas low-extension-velocity rifts featured compensatory and propeller faults.  Our data also suggest that changes in extension velocity influenced the migration of faults and resulting sedimentary patterns.  Notably, high-extension-velocity areas were characterized by localized thickening with graben amphitheaters, whereas low-extension-velocity areas experienced progressive fault growth with axial graben.  These outcomes provide a better comprehension of how changes in extension direction and velocity impacted the evolution of West African and Brazilian rifts, contributing to the diverse range of passive margin styles observed along the South Atlantic.  Our research highlights the significance of velocity in extensional tectonic processes and encourages further studies on the effects of variable extension velocities in different lithospheric settings.  Ultimately, this work can be an important reference for analyzing and interpreting rift basin evolution in other regions that experienced diverse extensional histories during supercontinent breakup.  In addition, these models can be applied to investigate the impact of variable extension direction and velocity on the evolution of active extensional basins, where different forces influence tectonic and stratigraphic evolution.  Our models can be an important tool for analyzing and interpreting multi-scale, active and passive extensional basins that experienced variable direction and velocity during different tectonic episodes.  We suggest that future studies on extensional tectonics and basin evolution incorporate this kind of numerical modeling to better comprehend the complex relationships between extension direction, velocity and resulting tectonic and stratigraphic patterns.  In this way, we can contribute to a more comprehensive and dynamic theory of extensional tectonics that considers the diverse forces and settings that shape active and passive extensional basins.

We introduce a cutting-edge unsupervised pre-training method that leverages multiple techniques to create comprehensive and consistent segmentation data. This method, dubbed High-quality Unsupervised Segmentation Pre-training (HUSP), crafts a diverse range of unsupervised loss functions that cater to various key aspects of segmentation quality. By combining elements of consistency, segmentation, and boundary preservation, HUSP aims to produce precise segmentations. The framework's design ensures minimal reliance on labeled data, and its scalability is maximized through the use of scalable unsupervised methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of HUSP through evaluations on the Cityscapes and ADAS datasets, employing MS COCO and Face API tools for evaluation - for example, achieving an mIoU score of 62.9 on Cityscapes val set. Moreover, HUSP's scalability is showcased via an experiment involving 400GB of unlabeled data. HUSP is user-friendly and simple to integrate with existing methods. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/whui723/HUSP.

Studies examining the mental state of others in virtual environments have focused mainly on individual aspects, neglecting the importance of participants' perceptions of persons' mental states in those environments. Our research addresses this limitation by integrating a theory-of-mind approach into cognitive models to capture the internal workings of users' minds when they navigate online social situations. To validate our approach, we created a simulation platform to explore how users' thoughts about others' mental states influence their behavior in different collaborative scenarios. Utilizing this platform, we conducted a series of experiments to analyze users' cognitive processes and decision-making patterns when interacting with others of varying mental states. Compared to static analyses of users' mental states, our results reveal that incorporating a theory-of-mind approach into cognitive models reveals new, previously unseen patterns in users' thoughts and actions. Furthermore, we observed that these patterns exhibit both similarities and differences to those reported in the existing literature on human theory-of-mind. Ultimately, our research enables designers to develop more effective, empathetic designs for applications involving interaction with others in virtual environments. Additionally, our research paves the way for expanded investigation of the proposed theory-of-mind approach across additional domains. Additionally, our approach may be applied to analyze other complex, dynamic systems involving interaction between multiple, interconnected mental states. Nonetheless, the current study has specific limitations, as it exclusively explores scenarios within the collaborative game domain. Future research should explore the possibility of deriving the proposed approach from basic psychological and cognitive principles. Moreover, the quantification of the weights assigned to different aspects of users' mental states remains an open question that requires further research. The data collected in this study may also be utilized in training machine learning models designed to predict users' thoughts and actions in collaborative scenarios. Ultimately, the proposed approach and accompanying data can contribute to the development of more sophisticated cognitive models, which can in turn facilitate improved design decisions in collaborative systems. Investigating the initial stages of protein folding, particularly those with intrinsic knots, in solution is extremely challenging, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about their folding mechanisms from experimental data alone. Although deep knots are rare in nature, shallow knots occur frequently and often coincide with protein-protein interaction functions. Our research employs a residue-level, sequence-based approach to analyze the folding pathways of shallow and deep knots on a microscopical level. By applying this approach to 34 shallow knots and 22 deep knots from the eKtensiveKnottBase database, we analyzed the unfolding free energy landscapes and folding pathways of these proteins. The results show that shallow knots fold through a hierarchical process, starting from the most knotted region, whereas deep knots require a more complex, less hierarchical pathway. The folding pathways of shallow knots also demonstrate that the least knotted loop serves as a nucleation site, whereas the most knotted region in deep knots undergoes intermediate unfolding before refolding. Our study provides a residue-level understanding of the distinct folding mechanisms of shallow and deep knots and highlights the unique, hierarchical folding process of shallow knots. Furthermore, we found that local interactions drive the folding of shallow knots, whereas deep knots involve a combination of local and long-range interactions. The distinct folding mechanisms of shallow and deep knots highlight the necessity of distinguishing between these two types of protein knots. The detailed folding pathways mapped in this study can facilitate the design of protein structures with specific knot topologies and further illuminate the complex processes of protein folding. The underlying methodology used in this research can also be applied to analyze the folding pathways of proteins without intrinsic knots. The algorithm employed in this research is available online at https://github.com/Chen-Hang/seqFoldingPath for public use. The algorithm can facilitate future research aimed at understanding the complex protein folding processes and may contribute to the development of precision medicine. The code was additionally utilized to analyze the folding pathways of three small proteins from the Protein Data Bank (PDBID: 1SHK, 1STR, 1SUU) to demonstrate its applicability. The analyzed folding pathways are presented in the Supplementary Materials accompanying this study. The sequence-based folding pathway analyzer offers a novel approach to analyzing the folding pathways of proteins with intrinsic knots and can be an invaluable tool for the scientific community working on protein structure prediction and analysis. The algorithm is an initial step towards understanding the complex processes of protein folding and setting the stage for further research in this area. Recent studies in counterfactual data generation have focused primarily on producing a single possible outcome from a given input, rather than exploring the multiple feasible consequences that can stem from a particular action or scenario. To address this limitation, the researchers propose a novel architecture called DISCO, an action-based counterfactual generative model that simulates multiple realistic outcomes from a given scenario by incorporating an external evaluation mechanism to guide the model. By utilizing a cost function that reflects the divergence between generated and actual outcome distributions, the model can learn to produce counterfactual data accurately. The researchers demonstrate that training machine learning models with data generated by this method enhances their robustness and ability to generalize, as evidenced by reduced error rates on various tasks following unexpected changes. Furthermore, they show that this approach allows them to generate diverse scenarios, expand a limited dataset, and improve performance on tasks that were not part of the training set. The model's capabilities were tested on two diverse domains, an economic simulation and a text-based game, and the results highlight the benefits of counterfactual data generation over traditional methods. The code is available online.

In large-scale classification tasks with numerous possible labels, the task of multi-label annotation becomes excessively time-consuming for human annotators. Annotating one text sample can result in multiple label annotations, as opposed to single-label annotations which are relatively faster to annotate. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel data augmentation technique known as single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling. By utilizing pre-trained language models, S2M sampling enables the generation of multiple labels from a given text sample with only a single annotation, thus significantly reducing annotation time. Our method can be an efficient tool for large-scale multi-label annotation tasks, especially in domains where high-quality annotations are costly to obtain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of S2M sampling by conducting experiments across six different datasets for sentiment classification and one dataset each for sentiment aspect and hate speech detection. The evaluation shows an improvement of up to 0.93% in F1-score when using S2M sampling for multi-label classification as compared to single-label classification. Our method also facilitates a notable 12% reduction in annotation time in a real-world large-scale annotation scenario. The code is openly accessible at: https://github.com/ritwikda/s2m-sampling. With S2M sampling, we anticipate a shift towards generating more multi-label datasets with increased annotation efficiency. Moreover, this technique can be an invaluable resource for researchers who need large-scale multi-label datasets but lack the resources for extensive annotation. It is especially beneficial for datasets where the model's performance is hindered due to a limited number of examples across certain labels, as S2M sampling enables the model to be trained on a broader range of examples with minimal additional annotation required. We addressed the complex challenge of identifying key genes with immediate and long-term impacts on the cell from high-dimensional, time-dependent expression profiles. Our solution draws from the potential functions framework, a statistical approach that models systems biology dynamics, by incorporating an efficient algorithm for variable selection. This algorithm leverages relevance learning to prioritize a smaller set of candidates, followed by a precise analysis of the shortened list, enabling both fast performance and accurate results. We applied this method to two datasets: an in silico simulation based on an established model of the cell cycle and a real-world dataset of expression profiles from actual cells. The results showed that our method accurately identified genes with immediate effects and those with delayed impacts, demonstrating its effectiveness for both small and large datasets. From ultraviolet data analysis, we identified numerous high-energy gas formations powered by massive young stars within 13 parsecs. Calculating the total energy output from far-infrared data revealed that young stars in each galaxy fall short of energizing gas formations, indicating possible additional external energy sources. Circumgalactic gas analysis using ultraviolet data showed all galaxies have similar gas characteristics similar to galaxies with intense starbursts. These findings imply external ultraviolet radiation and potential galaxy mergers may be key factors in the growth of massive galaxies through rapid starbursts. Additionally, beaming effects may also enhance the visibility of these galaxies. The high-level structure of a text doesn't change when its wording is modified, meaning a small change in wording results in a similar text with the same overall organization. This concept is known as the "local coherence" of texts. Current methods for analyzing text coherence focus solely on the relationships between adjacent segments of text. They don't account for the potential disparities between texts with the same high-level structure but differing content. This limitation is particularly evident in question-answering tasks that rely on rephrasing questions to test understanding rather than just accepting correct answers. To address this, we need datasets that evaluate the ability to grasp the underlying structure and relationships within a text, independent of wording. The introduced QASPER dataset consists of 13,000+ question-answering pairs in Arabic, designed to assess this ability through rephrasing questions. Results show that using rephrased questions instead of the original yields a 10% drop in score, demonstrating the challenge in evaluating understanding of text coherence. This drop is seen across both simple and complex coherence cases. Furthermore, the evaluation of current state-of-the-art models on this task reveals a significant performance gap, with an overall score of around 60%. This suggests substantial room for improvement in this area. The introduced dataset and models are available at https://qasper.aue.edu.ps/ for the community to build upon. The code for the models can be found at https://github.com/ashrafhamdi/MultiSpan-Arabic. The project is currently ongoing with plans to expand the dataset to include more evaluation metrics and test current abilities on Arabic text also. Mathematical models of disease dynamics are frequently developed using systems of nonlinear differential equations, which are then fitted to available data to estimate model parameters. However, this data fitting process is often uncomplicated, making it susceptible to unrealistic model predictions due to overfitting. Furthermore, the scarcity of data leads to an overreliance on statistical fitting methods' ability to provide feasible biological interpretations. In epidemiological modeling, it is essential to balance data fitting and biological plausibility to ensure the model's stability and ability to make informed predictions for future scenarios. To address this challenge, we suggest a data fitting approach that incorporates a governance system to limit the model's flexibility, based on the structure of the governing equations' invariant manifolds. This approach is illustrated using a simplified model for COVID-19 dynamics in Florida, where we constrain the model to adhere to biological feasibility by incorporating a governance system that promotes quasi-equilibrium behavior. The governed model exhibits reduced complexity while maintaining a strong connection to its original form, allowing for easier interpretation and more reliable predictions. The impact of modifying the governance system can be understood by analyzing the model's nullclines and slope fields. The approach we present is versatile and can be applied across various epidemiological modeling scenarios. The governed model is also openly posted at https://emidio-rega@umich.edu/software/COVID19-Florida-Governed. The governed model is a valuable tool that is easy to extend to capture the effects of enhanced public health measures or modifications to the governance system that reflect changes in behavioral responses to the pandemic. For linear Majorana fermions in one-dimensional space, the entropy of a thermal equilibrium state is examined with an external linear potential present.  By transforming the second quantized field theory into a one-body problem equivalent to that of a harmonic oscillator, we calculate the thermal entropy manually and also through a semiclassical approximation. Both methods yield equivalent results. When no potential is applied, the entropy follows a typical linear temperature dependence as seen in fermionic systems. In contrast, the presence of an external potential alters this behavior, resulting in an entropy vs. temperature plot with distinct linear segments corresponding to different potential strengths. This breakthrough allows us to explicitly bridge the gap between quantum entanglement and thermal equilibrium through the same correlation functions that define quantum entanglement. As an example, we determine the entropy changes when a potential that selectively break massless modes is turned on in a circuit Majorana device. Acronyms are commonly used in written language, often presenting a challenge for those unfamiliar with their meaning and for text-based systems to understand their context. A simple non-rigid pendulum with multiple equilibrium positions can be used to model complex phenomena in quantum physics, such as atom-molecule conversion in optical lattices or Bose-Einstein condensate instabilities in optical resonators. By applying a restricted variational method, we derived a soft pendulum model that captures the essential dynamics of this system, allowing us to identify the precise parameters that lead to its instability. We then analyzed the impact of adjusting these parameters through changes in chemical potential, interaction strength, lattice size, and photon-molecule coupling, demonstrating how they influence the pendulum's behavior. Notably, some of these parameters cause the pendulum to switch between stable and unstable phases as they are adjusted, a phenomenon we term a "phase flip." We also identified the conditions under which a "flip cycle" emerges, where the pendulum exhibits multiple "phase flips" as a result of adjustments. Our analysis provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to various quantum systems, and it highlights the unique features of the Bose-Einstein condensate in optical resonators. Furthermore, we anticipate that this framework will be useful in informing experimental design and interpreting data in these complex systems. Ultimately, we believe that our study of this pendulum model will contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics of atom-molecule conversion and Bose-Einstein condensate instabilities. Additionally, we expect that this pendulum will serve as a reliable theoretical tool for analyzing a wide range of quantum systems and predicting the outcomes of experimental manipulations. Lastly, we anticipate that our discovery of "phase flips" and "flip cycles" will spark further interest in the study of these phenomena. To facilitate the development of these ideas, we have created a graphical user interface that enables users to visualize and explore the pendulum model through interactive 3D animations. Recently, nodal lines in momentum space have gained significant attention due to their intriguing properties. Characterized by one-dimensional trajectories in momentum space that do not disconnect, these features occur in both crystalline and artificial photonic systems and are linked to anomalous flat band calculations. Research has shown that they can be used to create robust diode functions and non-basal topological phases. Although numerous studies have been conducted on nodal lines within energy bands, the associated surface states remain poorly understood. This review aims to provide an overview of the topological properties associated with nodal lines and their connected surface states, focusing on recent discoveries in artificial photonic systems. It highlights the unique characteristics of the artificial photonic analogs of the Weyl node and topological rod and corresponding emergent fermion arcs. It is essential to acknowledge the surface states as an intrinsic aspect of the topological rods, directly connected to the rod's bulk properties rather than being 'extrinsic.' Furthermore, the review highlights the benefits of using artificial photonic systems to study nodal lines and their associated surface states, offering greater flexibility in material parameter adjustments and clean and interference-free scenarios. It also emphasizes the potential for these systems to provide unique insights into the spatial distribution of electron density within nodal lines and related fermion arcs. Lastly, it highlights promising avenues for further research in this field.

Recent advancements in Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have significantly enhanced the deinterlacing process by learning implicit video characteristics, thereby surpassing traditional methods. Inspired by state-of-the-art video restoration and super-resolution techniques, this study leverages a self-supervised approach for high-resolution deinterlacing. It proposes a novel framework that extracts detailed information from deinterlaced frames and upsampled images to produce high-quality, progressive videos. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through self-supervised training on extensive datasets, resulting in superior performance compared to traditional and contemporary methods. The evaluation of the proposed technique through experiments on diverse benchmarks and assessments indicates its ability to achieve remarkable results. Specifically, the method achieves notable gains in sharpness and quality metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and Laplacian sharpness, outperforming rival techniques by up to $2.46\times$ in PSNR and $0.134\times$ in SSIM. The proposed framework's efficacy is further verified through subjective quality evaluations and real-world deinterlacing applications, showcasing its potential for enhancing real-world video deinterlacing. The framework's code and dataset are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ghoul1999/SSDQDEINT for the community's reference.

A new geostatistical method called Principal Component Geostatistical Analysis (PCGA) has been created by combining the principal component analysis (PCA) and kriging systems to estimate unknown variables based on observed data. This method first identifies key factors in the data through PCA, then uses those factors to build a simplified model that accurately represents the data patterns. PCGA was applied to analyze water flow velocity measurements taken from underwater acoustic sensors. These sensors were placed randomly on the riverbed and formed an irregular grid, leading to complex estimation problems. By comparing PCGA with traditional methods such as multiple linear regression (MLR) and classical kriging (CK), we found that PCGA provided more accurate estimates of riverbed bathymetry from flow velocity measurements. This demonstrates that PCGA is an effective approach for analyzing data with the following characteristics: the data is spatially correlated, the sensor deployment is irregular, and the underlying surface is complex. To facilitate future adoption of PCGA, an open-source implementation has been developed and is available for download and modification by other researchers. To ensure the reliability of these estimations, we also established a set of criteria to evaluate and validate the performance of PCGA. To demonstrate the practical utility of PCGA, we used it to estimate riverbed bathymetry in a real-world setting with good results. This led to a proposal for improving acoustic sensor technology to enhance its sensitivity and durability. Causal deep learning research is highly cross-disciplinary, involving top-notch methodology from statistics, machine learning, and neural networks, in order to extract actionable insights from data that enable prediction and decision-making. Nevertheless, this field faces a significant obstacle in progress due to its interdisciplinary nature - researchers struggle to locate relevant research that can contribute to their area of expertise. In order to facilitate easier access to relevant research, this study proposes a new taxonomy for causal deep learning, encompassing multiple aspects including problem formulation, methodology, and application. Furthermore, in order to validate the effectiveness of this taxonomy, a comprehensive review of 147 causal deep learning studies was conducted. The taxonomy demonstrated clarity and consistency among 90 % of the studied research papers. Additionally, it allowed researchers to identify notable knowledge gaps within the field, such as a lack of studies on confounding variables in supervised learning and on real-world applications involving more than two entities in multi-task learning. This taxonomy can be useful for both seasoned and novice researchers alike by providing a clear framework for classifying and comparing different approaches to causal deep learning. It can also be employed to identify key challenges and areas for further research within the field. In order to facilitate reproducibility and ease the burden of conducting new research, the taxonomy accompanying this study includes an exhaustive set of 147 carefully selected causal deep learning studies, categorized based on multiple criteria including problem formulation, methodology, and application. In order to be of continued value to the community, this taxonomy should be regularly updated with new research findings. In order to achieve this goal, all researchers within this community are kindly requested to contribute their insights and propose modifications to this taxonomy. In order to facilitate this process, a publicly accessible repository has been set up at https://github.com/ChenChen312/causal-deep-learning-taxonomy/tree/main/papers, where users can upload relevant research studies by categorizing them according to this taxonomy. The Madsen-Weiss theorem for mapping spaces under group actions by smooth actions on smooth manifolds has been expanded to apply to certain orbifolds. This expanded theorem aligns with the principles of the b-principle, which involves the idea that certain geometric statements can be reduced to statements about geometric simplices with specific properties. Furthermore, this expansion is demonstrated through a method that does not use the initial proof by Charousek and Wrazidlo, who employed a different approach based on surgery theory. Instead, this proof is derived from a combination of the Borel conjecture and the Thom-Mathieu surgery theorem. Alongside this development, a broader category of orbifolds is recognized as being within the scope of the Madsen-Weiss theorem. This inclusion is subject to the condition that these orbifolds can be obtained through a process involving the combination of certain types of geometric operations, and this relationship is fundamental to the principles of the b-principle. Moreover, this expanded theorem is related to several other important theoretical statements, including stability theorems in topology, which ensure that under specific conditions, certain geometric configurations will always possess equivalent topological characteristics. This understanding is further illustrated by deriving a more general version of the Madsen-Weiss theorem for mapping spaces under group actions, and this derivation is accompanied by new generalizations of other fundamental theoretical statements in topology. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the applicability and broad scope of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, demonstrating its relevance to a wide range of geometric and topological configurations. This development is anticipated to contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationships between these configurations and the principles of the b-principle. The author would like to extend special thanks to the organizers and participants of the 2019 MIT Homotopy Theory Workshop for their contributions to this work. This research focuses on an algebraic Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) method for solving iterative problems arising from the discretization of elliptic partial differential equations.  Specifically, we examine the convergence properties of the BDDC algorithm when using balanced domain decomposition and investigate how the performance is affected by different degrees of freedom within individual subdomains and the number of degrees of freedom across subdomain interfaces.  We also outline a strategy to select an appropriate degree of freedom parameter that balances subdomain size and interface size, resulting in an optimized BDDC implementation.  Our strategy is supported by numerical experiments presented on both a model problem and a real-world elasticity problem.  Notably, our results show that when the algorithm is properly tuned according to our guidelines, it yields comparable convergence rates to those achieved through more sophisticated methods like algebraic multigrid solvers for similar problem sizes.  However, our approach has the significant advantage of being much faster with no need for multiple iterations before achieving similar convergence and without requiring a coarse solver as part of the implementation.  Furthermore, our optimized BDDC method is particularly efficient for systems of linear equations resulting from the finite element discretization of certain PDEs, such as the Navier-Stokes equations solved with the Taylor--Hood method.  We anticipate that this research will be of interest to other researchers working in numerical analysis and scientific computing. 

Keywords: BDDC, PDE, Finite Element Methods, BEM, BEM Discretization, Algebraic Multigrid, Iterative Linear Solvers.

This research focuses on symmetric $N\times N$ matrices with independently drawn entries, satisfying a moment condition that may vary based on the matrix size. Separate analyses for finite fourth moment or sixth moment conditions are used to establish the joint central limit theorem (JCLT) of corresponding linear statistics, with an associated CLT applicable to any continuous spectral distribution. For the finite fourth moment case, an alternative approach is employed to derive the almost sure (AS) convergence of the limiting spectral distribution (LSD), with the finite sixth moment case ensuring the same outcome through a diverse method. Leveraging the established results, the finite fourth moment scenario allows for an extension to non-identically distributed entries and a rigorous proof of the Wigner-Dyson non-triviality criterion for the general Hermitian matrix scenario. Furthermore, both the finite fourth and sixth moment settings provide proofs of the AS convergence with a distinct approach. As a supplementary outcome, the studied matrix scenarios satisfy the Wigner-Dyson type non-triviality conditions. For the evaluated linear statistics, the associated LSDF can be determined through an analytical approach. The primary analytical tools employed in this research include the multivariate CLT, the AS and probability convergence of high-dimensional empirical processes, and diverse applications of the Stochastic Process CLT. Notably, the investigated matrix scenarios encompass a range of well-known matrix ensembles. As an illustrative example, Figure 1 visualizes the derived LSDF for a specific Hermitian matrix scenario. The studied matrix scenarios are available at the MATHERMATICS online database. The associated R functions can be accessed at the MATHERMATICS website.
