To address the issue of imbalanced data distribution in medical severity detection, we propose a novel 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network, which incorporates contrastive learning and a custom loss function to handle both data imbalance and potential errors in severity annotation. To compensate for the lack of direct supervision in unsupervised severity learning, our approach leverages the information extracted from the supervised segmentation of anatomical structures. This is achieved through a multi-task network that simultaneously performs unsupervised severity detection and supervised anatomical structure segmentation. To rectify the data imbalance issue, we introduce a custom mixup technique that applies a spatial mixup and a channel mixup to both data and features respectively. This is accompanied by a method to automatically identify and prioritize rare severe cases for enhanced learning. The evaluation of our proposed method on two publicly available datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to prominent baseline models. Moreover, the evaluation of our technique for annotating severe cases yields promising results with high consistency levels. All code and data utilized in this research are publicly accessible for replication and further development.

Recent studies have achieved significant progress in Generalizing to Errorful Corpus (GEC) by combining pre-trained models and employing neural sequence-to-sequence architectures. Nonetheless, these models generally rely on extensive training data and suffer from an overfitting problem when given inaccurate annotated text. To overcome this limitation, we propose a technique to adapt GEC models using imperfectly annotated data by leveraging labeled and unlabeled data simultaneously. This proposed method utilizes both source and target data in a joint training process with a sequence-to-sequence model, employing an encoder with contextualized representations. Moreover, we employ a simple yet effective technique to manipulate the source data's annotation noise level. Our experimental results on three datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms traditional multi-task transfer learning approaches while yielding a notable improvement in performance when compared to training GEC models with clean source data. In theory, the allocation resulting from the Round-Robin mechanism is at least as fair as the cut-and-choose algorithm. However, the practical fairness of these methods depends on the number of agents and their speeds in relation to the number of items. A faster agent with a smaller share can still allocate their portion quickly, potentially allowing them to grab multiple items before other agents have a chance to act. To address this issue, the fair division process is typically restricted to taking place over a fixed number of rounds equal to the number of agents. The purpose of this research is to examine how the Round-Robin method and the cut-and-choose algorithm perform under different delimiting structures in relation to deadlocks and efficient allocation. The focus will be on cyclic structures derived from both the Round-Robin and cut-and-choose algorithms. The study shows that both the Round-Robin and cut-and-choose algorithms lead to similar deadlock thresholds in cyclic structures. The research also explores the impact of delimiting structures on allocation efficiency in relation to both the Round-Robin and cut-and-choose algorithms. The study finds that the efficiency of delimiting structures is essentially the same for both methods. When attempting to reduce the reliance of target domain adaptation on labeled data by using pseudo-labeling, one potential issue arises from relying solely on predictions from a single image translation. To address this limitation, our research proposes an alternative approach called "Multi-View Pseudo-Labeling" for target domain adaptation. The core idea revolves around utilizing pseudo-target data predictions from various translations of a single target image to produce a single accurate pseudo-target sample. To achieve this, we first gather diverse target domain samples by applying different adaptation models and regularization techniques to a single target image translation. These translations are then combined using different weight calculation methods including simple averaging, weighted averaging, and fusion of multiple neighbors. Our experiments conducted on real-world image classification and segmentation benchmarks reveal that our proposed approach outperforms traditional pseudo-labeling techniques by a significant margin and demonstrates sensitivity to the weight calculation method, particularly on larger benchmarks. The evaluation also highlights the effectiveness of utilizing multiple translations and different adaptation models. Our code is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository indicated in the paper's citation.

The increasing use of modern databases that handle rich data, including images and audio, has given rise to sophisticated attacks on machine learning models due to their detailed update histories. This threat is mitigated by the application of differential privacy, which adds random noise to the data to prevent unauthorized access. Although research on differentially private machine learning has been extensive, there is a lack of understanding on how to securely update deep neural networks, particularly in real-time applications. This paper addresses this challenge by presenting a novel algorithm that securely updates deep neural networks through a process of iterative refinement, allowing previous knowledge to be leveraged for improved accuracy. This algorithm can be used in a variety of settings, including when the data provider has limited communication with the machine learning model, as demonstrated by a concrete example. The results show that this algorithm can achieve comparable accuracy to non-private methods while providing strong protection against unauthorized access due to its noise-tolerant design. The proposed algorithm can also handle a wide range of data types, including images and audio, as demonstrated by its application in a real-time deep neural network. This marks a significant advancement in the secure development of machine learning models and has the potential to shape the future of private machine learning. Recently, concise and essential subsets of rules have gained significance in explaining artificial neural networks through interpretations. In our research, we extend this concept to machine learning models that utilize probability distributions rather than logical rules. By leveraging the principles of minimal unsatisfiable cores from logical reasoning, we develop an algorithm to identify the most compact and critical configurations of model parameters that lead to incorrect predictions. This set of configurations serves as a vital set of features that can help us comprehend the underlying reasons behind the model's errors. We apply this approach to extract fundamental knowledge from complex models in classification and generative tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate the advantages of our method by comparing it with alternative techniques in both task types. Our results reveal that our approach not only facilitates the reduction of model sizes but also improves performance in both settings. We also showcase the fundamental components extracted through our algorithm on several image recognition tasks, demonstrating its practical applications. Our method is readily available online for download.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity in the automated detection and segmentation of surgical instruments within endoscopic images. To enhance the accuracy of these methods, attention-based networks have been successful in focusing on critical regions. Building upon this success, a novel Dual decoder attention network (DDANet) was proposed, where two identical encoder modules share a codebook to combine unique attention mechanisms in both decoder modules. In this study, DDANet was tested on public datasets, achieving a 0.841 ADE20k score and outperforming other deep learning methods (e.g., semi-supervised models) by a significant margin of 11.5%. Furthermore, DDANet demonstrated superior performance on the Endoscopic Instrument Dataset (EID), with an average score of 0.836, surpassing state-of-the-art methods by 7.2%. The proposed network's reliability was validated through experiments on data augmentation, where a notable increase of 14.5% was observed. Moreover, semi-supervised versions of DDANet were developed and demonstrated exceptional performance on datasets with limited annotated data, showcasing great potential for solving instrument segmentation challenges with only a few annotated images. The code for this study has been made publicly available on GitHub https://github.com/ChenChen0920/DDANet, and the dataset used in the experiment can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1x6T4s2T6T6T6T6T6T6T6T6T6.

Recently, deep learning methods for Re-identification have flourished due to significant breakthroughs in image representation learning. In an unsupervised setting, contrastive learning has emerged as a prominent approach for ReID, primarily leveraging local dissimilarities and global similarities to enhance model performance. However, existing contrastive learning-based unsupervised ReID methods still rely on labeled data for learning, which hinders their practical applications. To address this issue, we propose a novel, fully unsupervised contrastive learning-based ReID approach called Bidirectional Contrastive learning for ReID (BCReID) that learns from both similar and dissimilar data without relying on labeled information. By exploring the contrastive relationships between samples of the same and different identities, our method enhances the model's ability to distinguish identity differences and reduce intra-class disparities. To overcome the limited scalability of traditional contrastive learning on ReID datasets due to excessive memory requirements, we introduce a technique to efficiently batch similar and dissimilar samples through bidirectional contrastive learning. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our proposed method, demonstrating superior or on-par performance with state-of-the-art unsupervised and supervised ReID methods on various evaluation metrics. Moreover, our method achieves notable efficiency gains in terms of model size, parameter reduction, and training time. Additionally, the scalability of our method is demonstrated by its capacity to extract feasible and discriminative features from a large dataset of 1 million images. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/AugmentUS/BCReID.

Recent advancements in machine learning, coupled with enhanced computational capabilities, have made deep learning an attractive option for processing high-frequency financial series and forecasting Value-at-Risk (VaR). While researchers have explored various deep learning approaches to VaR forecasting, integrating these models with optimization frameworks has been lagging. This study addresses this gap by developing a non-parametric deep learning VaR forecasting framework that minimizes backtesting errors according to the Expected Backtesting Size (EBS) criterion. Moreover, this framework is mathematically equivalent to a time-series GARCH model, providing a connection between deep learning and traditional financial modeling techniques. Our empirical analysis utilizing S&P 500 index data reveals that the proposed model outperforms both a conventional GARCH(1,1) model and a more recent deep learning VaR forecasting model. An investigation into how variations in the masses of quarks and the spacing of a lattice affect the properties of mesons can be carried out by performing a systematic analysis of lattice QCD data. This study examines the sensitivity of the masses and decay constants of the lightest mesons within the $SU(3)$ flavor symmetry to the quark mass and lattice spacing, with a particular focus on the influence of isospin breaking on the neutral pion. Deep learning systems rely heavily on data to perform effectively but often incorporate massive, hard-to-manage datasets that necessitate a data-centric approach to their design. Despite the significance of data debugging, the typical process remains labor-intensive and inflexible for both human and automated practitioners. We introduce DataScope, an innovative system designed to automate and optimize the data debugging process for machine learning pipelines by leveraging optimisation techniques and data debugging as a search process. By combining domain-specific knowledge with automated trial and error, DataScope outperforms traditional methods by reducing data debugging time, and also enables the detection of multiple relevant data bugs at once. Experimental evaluations using real-world datasets demonstrate DataScope's capabilities to be 2-5 times more efficient than human practitioners and 8-20 times more efficient than automated methods. Additionally, DataScope can identify an average of 5-10 data bugs per hour, a significant improvement over human practitioners' average of 1 data bug per hour. The system's effectiveness in combining domain-specific knowledge with automated trial and error has been proven to yield results that are 10-20% more accurate than those produced by the base machine learning models on their own. DataScope can be applied to a wide range of machine learning pipelines, including those employing neural networks, and supports various data sources and debugging algorithms. This thesis will specifically examine and review low-dimensional laser research, focusing on the underlying physics governing the intrinsic photon emission characteristics of planar, wire, and box lasers. The review will also present the concept of laser mode evolution with size and the implications it has on photon emission properties. The presented analysis is supported by theoretical and experimental findings from previous research. The review is further expanded to discuss the implications of the intrinsic photon emission characteristics of low-dimensional lasers on the total spontaneous emission factor and the phenomenon of laser threshold. The discussion is then expanded to encompass higher-dimensional laser cavities and outline the potential future research directions in this field of study. We investigate how the two-time second-order correlation function of light emitted from an atomic medium behaves under random phase fluctuations. Initially, we consider a system of $N$ independent atomic resonators generating uncorrelated coherent states of light, and show that the two-time second-order correlation function of the total system displays periodic variations in field amplitude, in stark contrast to the atomic ensemble's typical behavior of maintaining correlation-free over time. Furthermore, we find that the periodic variations cease as the number of independent resonators increases, and offer a general expression for the two-time second-order correlation function in this scenario. Building upon this, we apply this understanding to atomic interferometry, revealing that random atomic fluctuations cause undetected shifts in phase differences, and propose remedies to overcome this limitation. Additionally, we propose using the two-time second-order correlation function as a functional indicator of atomic phase fluctuations, potentially enabling atomic interferometry to operate with unprecedented precision. Lastly, we outline the potential for our findings to be extended to atomic systems interacting with photons.

This leads to a significant reduction in data requirements. We demonstrate that offline learning with a single sample path per agent can achieve the same level of performance as learning from multiple individual trajectories by applying the SIT framework, which involves augmenting the state space through an action-value function transformation. The theoretical findings are supported by empirical evaluations on various complex tasks, confirming the benefits of the SIT framework. We investigated the relationship between single-particle entanglement and nonlocal behavior in quantum systems that consist of multiple spatially distributed sites. This was accomplished by examining the entanglement between a specific system site and the remainder of the system. Our study revealed that this single-party entanglement effectively captures a system's nonlocal properties, particularly its ability to be steered and demonstrate paradoxical effects in correlations with other systems. Notably, we found that in equilibrium, single-particle entanglement is insufficient and cannot fully describe a system's nonlocal behavior when in contact with a thermal bath. Conversely, in isolated systems and out-of-equilibrium scenarios, our proposed measure accurately captures the essence of nonlocal effects arising from single-party entanglement. To further illustrate this, we considered two scenarios: (i) a system that undergoes sudden cooling from a state of high entanglement, and (ii) a network where a system site experiences persistent growth in entanglement with the remainder of the system over time. In both instances, our analysis effectively captures the development or persistence of nonlocal effects, steering, and paradoxical correlations, underscoring the utility of single-party entanglement as a governing principle governing these phenomena. Ultimately, this work establishes a fundamental connection between single-particle entanglement and nonlocal properties in multiparty systems. Additionally, our findings are relevant to controlling the propagation of entanglement in quantum networks. To facilitate practical applications, we also developed a simple, effective method for measuring single-party entanglement in complex systems through a minimal system interaction. This is particularly advantageous because many-system entanglement can now be efficiently diagnosed by measuring the entanglement between a single system site and its complement. Our research provides a clear, universally applicable framework for understanding the role of single-particle entanglement in complex quantum systems. This will have a positive impact on the development of practical applications for controlling the propagation of entanglement in quantum networks. Furthermore, this research is complemented by publicly accessible numerical tools that enable the single-party entanglement of out-of-equilibrium and isolated systems to be efficiently calculated, and can also be adapted for use with other isolated systems. A Nova-like system's binary configuration is revealed through the analysis of high and low orbital sidebands in extreme spectra, created when a massive star's overflow hits its companion, leading to accretion disks and beams of energy.  V392 Persei's binary nature was studied using the Discrete Fourier Transform of extremely broad spectra, covering both high and low sidebands, obtained with the RXTE and the XMM-Newton.  Its 16.58 hour orbital period was confirmed, along with the confirmation of both white dwarfs in the system and the direction of the orbit.  V392 Persei's binary configuration was further defined by detecting both high and low orbital sidebands in its spectra, showing that the accretion disks and beams of energy are oriented at an 18 degrees angle.  This angle caused the nova-like system to display bi-stability, where its high mass loss rate was produced during the transitions from sub-critical to super-critical accretion, resulting in the sudden eruptions characteristic of this type of system.  This study shows that the nova-like system's binary configuration can be a major factor in its eruptions, with the direction of the orbit possibly influencing the direction of the eruptions.  This finding may provide a possible explanation for the sudden eruptions of V392 Persei, as an Earth-stable binary configuration could lead to the accumulation of matter on the star's surface.  This study also demonstrates the capability of the RXTE and the XMM-Newton to detect the sidebands in Nova-like systems' binary configurations, paving the way for further research in this area.  Finally, V392 Persei's binary configuration serves as an ideal subject for the study of the magnetic fields of white dwarfs, making it a crucial asset for this area of research.  This study was conducted in accordance with the recommendations outlined in the 2011 IUE Legacy Archive Workshop, which suggested that the analysis of extremely broad spectra, created when a massive star's overflow hits its companion, leading to accretion disks and beams of energy, could provide valuable insights into the binary nature of these systems. In urban settings, automated vehicles can optimize their journey by connecting to roadside infrastructure and obtaining real-time information about traffic signals. However, determining safe speeds to maintain during approach and specific phases of traffic signals poses a computational problem that needs rapid solutions. To address this challenge, we developed a traffic signal phase prediction model that uses historical data and machine learning to estimate phase durations with reasonable accuracy (±25%). This model was created with scalability in mind to accommodate applications across various city sizes. To evaluate the efficacy of this model, we conducted experiments on three distinct datasets, showcasing its ability to accurately predict phases for at least 80% of intersections on the same road network during a 500-second window. Furthermore, we demonstrated that a derived speed prediction model adheres to real-world speed patterns. To facilitate seamless integration with existing traffic management systems, our model and associated speed predictions were designed to be lightweight and easily extensible to any city by incorporating the few estimated parameters into a numerical solution. To facilitate autonomous vehicle planning, we incorporated these speed predictions into a lookup table to provide safe speeds for automated vehicles to maintain during approach and specific phases of traffic signals, thereby enhancing the computational efficiency of trajectory planning algorithms by at least 10 times. The outcome of this method is a streamlined trajectory planning process for connected automated vehicles that can be computed in real-time, aligning with the temporal constraints of traffic signal phases. To validate this approach, we conducted experiments on three distinct datasets, comparing the performance of the proposed method against a state-of-the-art algorithm, and the results indicate that the proposed method achieves a higher success rate (above 80%) in achieving planned distances within the same road network during a 500-second window. Additionally, we conducted a supplementary experiment to demonstrate the efficacy of the traffic signal phase prediction model in scenarios with varying city sizes and traffic signal cadence. To facilitate the adoption of this method by the autonomous vehicle industry, we created a prototype of the automated vehicle planning process using the model, and the code is available for public review. To further this research, we suggest enhancing the traffic signal phase prediction model using deep learning techniques and exploring the application of this model to predict traffic signal phases in real-time through direct communication with traffic management systems. Additionally, we propose comparing the performance of this method against more advanced algorithms and validating the speed prediction model against real-world data. To accelerate the adoption of this method by the autonomous vehicle industry, we recommend collaborating with industry partners to integrate this method with existing trajectory planning algorithms and develop autonomous vehicles that can communicate with traffic management systems.

Our results are relevant to ongoing discussions regarding the Weak Binding Principle and the holographic bound in anti-de Sittter space.

To investigate extended scalar sector interactions with a Higgs boson at a TeV-scale, our research proposes utilizing precision tests of the Higgsstrahlung process, specifically measuring the differential cross-section or polarization of the emitted boson. However, this study suggests that a more comprehensive approach is possible. We show that, along with the differential cross-section or polarization, it is also necessary to consider the vector-boson scattering process and modify the Higgs self-coupling to thoroughly examine the underlying scalar sector. Furthermore, we illustrate this multi-faceted approach by evaluating the impact of an extended scalar sector on the $h\to \gamma\gamma$ decay rate, which is currently constrained to a deviation of less than $2.5\sigma$. Ultimately, our findings suggest that a comprehensive, precise study of the Higgs boson in the $t\bar t h$ process at future $pp$ colliders with TeV-scale energy will be crucial in uncovering clues about the fundamental underlying scalar sector.

The past year has seen significant advancements in the study of Saturn's polar atmospheres through the analysis of data from the Cassini mission. Researchers have made detailed observations of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV) and the south polar stratosphere during Saturn's southern summer, the latter of which exhibits a polar vortex similar to the NPSV but in a more stable form. In contrast to the NPSV, the south polar stratosphere shows minimal changes throughout the seasons. Studies have identified the presence of C$_2$H$_6$ in both the NPSV and the south polar stratosphere but at much higher concentrations in the former. Furthermore, the distribution of this polar solvent in the NPSV is highly irregular and closely mirrors the vortex's temperature structure. In the south polar stratosphere, C$_2$H$_6$ is found in significantly lower concentrations and displays a more uniform distribution. It is hypothesized that the unique appearance of the NPSV and the differing chemical compositions of the two polar regions are a result of the unique wind patterns found at Saturn's poles. The NPSV's irregular shape is thought to be caused by the interaction between the planet's atmospheric circulation and the surrounding vortex walls, a phenomenon not observed in the south polar stratosphere due to the latter's greater stability. The distinct chemical composition of the NPSV and the south polar stratosphere can be attributed to the varying levels of mixing between these regions and the lower latitudes, which are influenced by the different wind patterns. The discovery of the significant concentration differences of C$_2$H$_6$ in these two regions highlights the importance of further studying the chemistry of these areas. The unique appearance of the NPSV and the distinct chemical composition of the two polar regions make the north polar region of Saturn a fascinating area for further research and analysis. This survey highlights the growing body of research in commutative algebra, specifically focusing on the interplay between characteristic-zero results and their positive-characteristic counterparts. Rather than presenting a comprehensive overview of the latest developments, our goal is to illustrate the emerging theme of characteristic-zero results having positive-characteristic analogues, often with characteristic-zero proving methods applicable in positive characteristic. We will explore this relationship through a few selected areas within commutative algebra, also identifying potential directions for future research in this engaging field of study. No new theorems are introduced in this survey, and the discussions are supported by relevant examples. We will examine the interplay between characteristic-zero results and their positive-characteristic analogues in the following areas: local algebra, algebraic geometry, and commutative algebra itself, also briefly touching on topics like graded rings and algebras of finite representation type. No new theorems are introduced in this survey, and the discussions are supported by relevant examples. We will explore future research directions that could further illuminate the similarities and differences between characteristic-zero and positive-characteristic results. We investigated the metal-insulator transitions in strongly correlated systems with the help of dynamical spectral weight distributions, which were obtained through functional renormalization group methods. Our study focused on the interplay between interaction and bandwidth within tight-binding models, and it allowed us to systematically analyze the structural changes to the electronic spectrum as the system transitioned between metallic and insulating states. Through this process, we identified distinctive features in the spectral weight distribution in both the metallic and insulating states. Furthermore, we confirmed that certain "sum rules of spectral weight" hold true in the metallic state but break down in the insulating state. The breakdown of these sum rules was further confirmed through symmetry-analyzed spectral weight distributions and through comparisons with exact diagonalization results for small systems. Our study demonstrated that the dynamics of correlated systems cannot be understood without considering the spectral weight distribution, which provides a degree of freedom that can be adjusted to test different theoretical models. This is particularly relevant given the diversity of metal-insulator transitions in strongly correlated systems and the need for a universal theory to explain them. The methods employed in this study can also be applied to investigate other phase transitions and spectral weight structures in correlated systems. The data obtained in this study has been made publicly accessible to facilitate comparisons with other theoretical models and to advance our understanding of the electronic structure of correlated systems. The results reported in this study are relevant to the ongoing research on materials such as doped Mott insulators, cuprates, and ruthenates, where the interplay between different types of electronic interactions and electron filling gives rise to diverse metal-insulator transitions. The methods employed in this study can be extended to include the effects of lattice vibrations and magnetic impurities, which are essential for an accurate description of the electronic structure in these systems. This relationship also reveals that the preimages of certain cohomology classes under the symplectic form's map will correspond to the pullbacks of certain differential forms. By utilizing this correspondence, we can define the concept of characteristic classes for symmetric double vector bundles by using their images and the preimages of these classes. Taking the Lie algebra of a reductive group $G$ with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{h}$, we examine a continuous, bi-invariant measure on the adjoint orbit $G'$ for a semisimple element $e\in G$. This investigation leads us to a deeper exploration of Kirillov's measure, and in doing so, we establish a connection between geometric measure on the orbit $G'$ and Kirillov's measure. In particular, we show this relationship holds when the underlying field is $\mathbb{C}$, and our proof relies on a broad application of harmonic analysis to extend earlier results specific to the action of the Weyl group. In the case where the field is $\mathbb{R}$, we make analogous discoveries within the context of the real Lie algebra of $G$ and its associated Euclidean space. Here, our findings enable us to extend Kirillov's measure and demonstrate its equivalence to geometric measure on the orbit $G'$. In addition, our proof includes a broader application of harmonic analysis to extend earlier results specific to the action of the Weyl group in the real case. Furthermore, our discoveries also reveal that Kirillov's measure can be locally defined through an integral involving logarithmic polynomials, and in doing so, we establish an intriguing connection to classical results of Bernstein and Gelfand on the representation theory of unipotent groups. Lastly, our discussion concludes with a discussion on generalizing these measures to irreducible representations of Schr\"{o}dinger pairs.

Quantum error-correcting codes, particularly those from the stabilizer class, share an intriguing connection with classical disordered statistical mechanics models. A notable example of this connection is the mapping between the toric code and Edwards-Anderson Ising model in an external magnetic field, or the 2D Z2 gauge model and the 2D random-bond Ising model. This correspondence facilitates the utilization of exact statistical mechanics methods for the analysis of these classical systems to study quantum error-correcting properties. Conversely, insights from quantum systems can be applied to classical disordered statistical mechanics. As such, there is a potential for leveraging the advances made in the study of quantum error-correcting codes to further understand classical disordered statistical mechanics and vice versa. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the stabilizer-code/ statistical-mechanics correspondence, covering both the physics and mathematics underlying this connection, as well as discussing both the quantum and classical aspects. Furthermore, we will discuss the benefits and limitations of employing this mapping for computational purposes. As an illustration, we have conducted a computational trial by applying quantum Monte Carlo simulations to the toric code after converting the problem to the corresponding Edwards-Anderson Ising model, in an attempt to simulate the robustness of topological order against the influence of isolated quantum quench errors. As expected, the results from this combined approach closely align with the established outcomes for the toric code itself. This trial serves to showcase the feasibility of employing classical statistical mechanics methods for the study of quantum error-correcting codes through the mentioned correspondence. Additionally, this method may also be used to compute the free energy of these codes by utilizing the available exact statistical mechanics results, a computation that would otherwise be extremely challenging for the codes themselves. As such, we propose that this combined approach can provide a useful computational tool for the rapid evaluation of the free energy of these codes across their phase diagrams. This review is based on the authors' existing research published in various studies. Specifically, the proposed computational scheme for the rapid evaluation of the free energy of these codes has not been previously explicitly outlined in a comprehensive manner within the existing scientific literature. As such, the review is considered original in this context. As for the trial mentioned above, the associated numerical data has not been included within the review text for the sake of clarity, but is available in the accompanying source code for the calculations. As for the scientific literature that the review is based on, the authors have not received any financial or non-financial gains for their published research

Recent breakthroughs identifying Tellurene and Germanene have sparked significant interest in 2D group-V semimetals. However, both Tellurene and Germanene are extremely difficult to stabilize as free standing quantum wells. A quantum well made from SnTe, which shares similarities with Tellurene but is slightly easier to obtain, is proposed as a more feasible alternative. By engineering the lattice structure of this well using applied stress, it is possible to create a substantial non-trivial gap, and the optimal stress for this purpose is determined as $\sim$4.5 kBar, which yields a gap of $\sim$0.23 eV when considering a well 10 atomic layers thick. This proposed well has the additional benefit of being compatible with the lattice structure of a variety of functional materials that can be grown on the SnTe substrate. Through comprehensive band structure and scattering simulations, it is demonstrated that introducing strain to these wells results in significantly reduced conduction and effective mass, which can be as low as $\sim$10$^{-25}$s, making this a promising candidate for improving channel velocity in 2D quantum wells used in field effect transistors. The compatibility and the possibility for adjusting band structure through applied stress also make this well an attractive platform for the direct conversion of electrical strain to photonic strain, which could be applied to light sources such as lasers. Finally, the potential for this well to be used in the direct conversion of electrical strain to photonic strain in optical modulators is also highlighted. These proposed strain-controlled 2D semimetals offer a new path for the development of a variety of high-performance, compact and reliable optoelectronic devices that can be a key component in photonic data processing systems. These devices have the potential to outperform current technology by at least an order of magnitude. Moreover, they could also serve as a foundation for the development of new sensing and energy applications that can be a crucial step towards the advancement of photonic and quantum technologies. Ultimately, further research is necessary to fully explore and realize the capabilities of these proposed 2D semimetals.

To model blocking fractures in fractured porous media, researchers have approached this issue by extending the single-phase problem to a multiphase problem. The authors propose a different strategy, drawing on the capabilities of the Dirac delta function to represent blocking fractures through a set of concentrated limits. This method aligns with previous work by Mikelian and Rassasse in 1986. By leveraging the weak formulation, the proposed model can be computed using a finite element method. The authors demonstrate that their model exhibits the required physical properties typical of Darcy flows and prove the convergence of a discrete problem to a continuous solution. Ultimately, the proposed approach enables the simulation of blocking fractures within the context of Darcy flows. The authors also examine the impact of blocking fractures on pressure by means of numerical experiments. The method described here has the added benefit of facilitating the effortless incorporation of blocking fractures into more complex multiphase simulations. The authors further explore the potential of this approach to be applied to other PDE systems that incorporate concentrated singularities. To illustrate this potential, the authors consider a simplified adaptation of the Biot model. When dealing with multiple hypotheses in an uncertain environment, it's common to use a set of hypotheses that encompass all possible scenarios. Determining the best hypothesis involves evaluating each hypothesis based on its expected value, which is calculated by applying a utility function to the expected outcome. However, most traditional methods assume the utility function is known and consistent across all hypotheses. In practice, different hypotheses might have distinct utility functions that cater to their specific objectives. To address this issue, we propose a method that enables the use of diverse utility functions in hypothesis selection. By associating a utility function with each hypothesis, the proposed approach allows for an objective evaluation of the expected value of each hypothesis. Hypotheses are then ranked based on their expected values. To maintain computational efficiency, we use a simplified formulation that is refinable for more accurate results. The proposed method is applicable to any uncertainty representation and can handle a wide range of utility functions, including those with nested minimization and conditional statements. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness by applying it to two real-world scenarios: one in engineering and the other in economics. The results show that the proposed approach yields the exact same output as state-of-the-art solvers for simple cases and provides a significant speedup (by at least an order of magnitude) for more complex scenarios. Moreover, the method can handle large numbers of hypotheses (in the thousands). The proposed method is particularly useful when the number of possible hypotheses is substantial and evaluation time is a concern. The method has a linear complexity and can be highly beneficial for expensive-to-evaluate hypotheses. The proposed approach is also relevant to the broader context of uncertain decision-making. The code for this research is available online.

Using a semi-classical model, we analyze the Mott-Seitz theory to understand the non-radiative decay of excited states in metal clusters and nanoparticles. By making the impact of electron-electron interactions more explicit, we simplify the model to a one-dimensional scenario to reveal that its non-radiative decay mechanism is similar to that of Jahn-Teller theory. We calculate the energy required for a metal cluster to undergo non-radiative decay and find it to be comparable to the energy used in optical experiments, thus suggesting that this energy can also be utilized to control the non-radiative decay process through electron configuration adjustments, a concept that is corroborated by recent research findings. Additionally, we propose that this method could be applied to any system where the Mott-Seitz model is relevant. We also examine the possibility of optical control over non-radiative decay in gold nanoparticles by considering the effect of local electric fields on the electron configuration and how this might influence cluster symmetry changes. We conclude that field control of these clusters could provide an effective means to manage their non-radiative decay processes. We further suggest that the principles we have derived from this analysis may be applicable to other systems subject to local environmental influences and governed by similar dynamics. Inspired by biological learning mechanisms, unsupervised training algorithms for neural networks have been developed using neural activity and synaptic plasticity rules. However, these algorithms typically require multiple trials and a large number of neurons to achieve a level of accuracy comparable to supervised learning. In contrast, a novel training algorithm for linear neural networks is presented, where an individual can learn an exact match in just a few trials. The algorithm involves computing an error signal as the dot product of observed output and desired output, subtracting the actual output, and then applying this error to adjust the weights. When applied to an unsupervised setting with redundant inputs and output variables, the algorithm surprisingly yields sparse representations and accurate decoding. The underlying mechanisms are further illuminated through excitable neural networks and the algorithm's connection to Hebbian plasticity is explored and confirmed by additional simulations. Notably, the algorithm allows for robust performance even when infected by random neural responses, providing a potential basis for future infection-resistance algorithms. The Hartree-Fock method's convergence can be influenced by the strength of the electron-electron Coulomb interaction, with stronger interactions leading to greater convergence challenges. This difficulty may stem from the choice of basis functions rather than the Hartree-Fock method itself. In this research, the convergence issue within the Hartree-Fock framework is re-examined by simultaneously selecting basis functions and solving the Hartree-Fock equations. This approach forms an optimization problem which can be minimized using a method like Least Squares. This study presents a new algorithm for this minimization problem and evaluates it through simulations of atomic calculations. The proposed method consistently displays better convergence compared to the standard Hartree-Fock method and is robust against diverse initial conditions. Furthermore, this study determines an optimal threshold for the basis function addition criterion which can be as low as 10^-6. The proposed algorithm has been implemented into an atomic Hartree-Fock code available under request. This research paves the way for a similar study on the convergence issue within the Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory framework. In matrix optimization, where the objective and constraint are factorized and share a similar inexact form, we investigate the geometric structure of an associated submartingale with decreasing weights. Under mild conditions of strong convexity and smoothness, being non-degenerate and having a unique minimum, we discover that the geodesic distance between any two nearby points converges in a linear manner. This linear convergence rate can be expressed in terms of the eigenvalues of a matrix derived from the factorized objective and constraint, enabling us to establish a linear convergence rate for an inexact proximal aggregate reflection method. Moreover, this method can be an efficient approach for certain matrix optimization problems, particularly when solving large-scale systems that involve multiple coupled variables within complex matrices. To support the theoretical findings, we include numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the inexact proximal aggregate reflection method across a range of scenarios. Additionally, we highlight how this approach can be applied to solve optimisation problems arising from the construction of Lanczos methods and the approximation of matrix functions.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread extremely fast over 2020-2022, infecting nearly every corner of the globe, and has become one of the most severe medical crises in the 21st century. To slow the virus dissemination, understanding how it transfers from one person to another is crucial. Since infected individuals release massive amounts of COVID-19-contaminated droplets into the air when coughing or sneezing, studying their behavior is essential. Droplet size significantly influences the virus dissemination, with larger droplets falling to the ground quickly but still posing a significant infection risk if they fall onto people's faces, whereas smaller droplets remain suspended in the air for an extended period, potentially spreading the virus over longer distances but also evaporating rapidly and reducing their size to potentially infectious levels. Furthermore, the behavior of these droplets is affected by numerous factors including temperature, humidity, air movement, and human activities which complicates the virus dissemination model even more. Due to the unique characteristics of COVID-19 that allow it to remain infectious on surfaces for an extended period and be transmitted through indirect contact, a comprehensive model must also consider the virus's ability to spread through surface contact. Consequently, developing an accurate model for the virus dissemination requires a holistic approach that takes into account the behavior of droplets in the air and on surfaces, the virus's survival capabilities on surfaces, and how they are cleaned and disposed of. In this research paper, a comprehensive model for the virus dissemination in indoor environments is presented. The model accounts for the behavior of droplets in the air and on surfaces, the virus's survival capabilities on surfaces, and how they are cleaned and disposed of. The model includes probability functions for indirect contact infections and face-to-face contact infections and can be applied to various indoor settings such as offices, restaurants, and public transportation. The model was verified using numerical methods and a Monte Carlo technique. The influence of several factors including the initial number of infected individuals, droplet size, surface cleanliness, and disposal practices on the virus dissemination was examined. The results show that the model can effectively track the spread of the virus and the number of infected individuals. The model can be an invaluable tool for public health officials and policymakers as it allows them to evaluate the impact of different control measures such as increasing cleaning and disposal frequencies, improving surface cleanliness, and implementing face masks. Inverse problems are inherently challenging to solve, often requiring significant assumptions and prior knowledge for a feasible solution. Conventional methods, while providing valuable insights, can be insufficient for complex, ill-posed inverse problems. The introduction of Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) has revolutionized the field of inverse problems by enabling the learning of inverse procedures. This research focuses on employing ANNs in tandem with Bayesian learning techniques to develop an adaptable tool for solving diverse inverse problems. This method leverages the strengths of both approaches: the flexibility of ANNs in modeling unknown forward processes and the Bayesian framework's ability to quantify uncertainty. This framework is exemplified through a deblurring problem, where a neural network learned to invert a stochastic and nonlinear imaging process. This work showcases the potential of this method by demonstrating the ease with which the method can be modified to accommodate varying levels of noise and system disturbances. This research is an early exploration aimed at stimulating discussion and further investigation into utilizing ANNs within Bayesian learning frameworks for inverse problems. This approach may provide a foundation for solving a broad range of complex and dynamic inverse problems.

Our goal is to explore the underlying structure of this graph class and establish a key relationship with the equality between standard and symbol powers of ideals. Our approach involves utilizing the recently introduced concept of oriented graph filtration and the associated graded object, as well as the equalities between standard and symbol powers of ideals in relation to its properties. We intend to identify and characterize the oriented graphs that meet the desired equality condition through this framework. Our findings reveal a key connection to a specific subclass of oriented graphs termed as'monotone oriented graphs'. Our main contribution involves showing that the equality between standard and symbol powers of an edge ideal WI,r) holds true if and only if the weighted oriented graph (W,r) exhibits a specific combinatorial property rooted in the subgraph G0 and the ordering of the weighted vertices in G0. Neural networks deploy significant amounts of data but face a critical threat: silent data corruption (SDC). Even a single corrupted value can lead to entire model failures and, in some cases, reduced performance. To mitigate this, researchers have proposed various techniques for detecting and mitigating SDC, including uniform range testing for in-depth data analysis. However, applying these methods uniformly or randomly to check for SDC across large datasets is inefficient. Therefore, this work introduces non-uniform range testing methods that prioritize high-risk data locations to optimize the detection process. Specifically, it leverages techniques from sensitivity analysis and numerical stability to develop data-dependent testing ranges. By fine-tuning these ranges through an iterative process called range refinement, it significantly improves the detection rate while minimizing tests. The proposed approach is versatile and applicable to a range of loss functions, including cross-entropy loss. Experimental results on large-scale datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness, achieving a 5-10 times increase in SDC detection compared to uniform testing and demonstrating the method's applicability to a range of neural network architectures. Furthermore, the work is accompanied by an open-source framework that enables the introduction of SDC into training data and facilitates a range testing library for various functions. Our research focuses on examining the connection between the fundamental topology of transport networks in cities and the emergent dynamics of collective behavior. We utilized two prominent civil unrest datasets from Nigeria and India to conduct a joint analysis with the underlying transport networks in these cities. Our results reveal that cities exhibit distinct relationships between topological features and the dynamics of unrest, depending on their specific characteristics. Furthermore, we observed a notable difference in the influence of network topology on unrest dynamics when comparing the two cities. We applied a simplified model to bridge the gap between temporal unrest patterns and network topology, demonstrating that the model's parameters reflect the fundamental properties of civil unrest spreading. We found that the model can capture the diverse relationships between unrest dynamics and network topology found in the data sets. Moreover, we found that the model can distinguish between the different temporal unrest patterns observed in the two city datasets. Additionally, we used the model to predict unrest behavior on various networks, showing that its predictions align with actual unrest patterns. Our research offers a theoretical framework that can be utilized to analyze the spread of civil unrest on transport networks in other cities. Furthermore, this model can provide policymakers with insights to inform their strategies to mitigate unrest. We make the model's code publicly available to facilitate its use for analyzing the spread of civil unrest in other networks.

Recent deep learning-based Visual-Inertial-Odometry (VIO) models have achieved impressive performance in simulating and real-world environments, yet there's a significant gap in understanding how these models work compared to traditional VIO algorithms. Through the application of a specific operator, we can transform the parafermion vertex operator algebra into one with a $q$-deformed structure. By employing these screening operators, we can develop a conformal field theory on the torus. We've developed a new framework that allows a student model to be efficiently trained on a set of diverse data by incorporating the insights of a pre-trained expert model. Instead of employing traditional optimization methods, our approach identifies and highlights the crucial salient samples that are likely to aid the student's knowledge amalgamation. The expert model's task is then modified so that it generates a more refined output for these salient samples, effectively fine-tuning its performance. We demonstrate that the expert's enhanced ability to handle key cases can significantly benefit the student's training, showcasing substantial gains in accuracy across various evaluation metrics. The devised method has far-reaching implications for the development of student models, particularly in scenarios where the expert model lacks explicit supervision. The framework's applicability is further highlighted through the improvement it brings to a model undergoing regular training on large-scale datasets, such as ImageNet. The code for the proposed framework is openly accessible on GitHub, showcasing the benefits of salient sample generation using our approach. The project also includes the code used to analyze the influence of the expert model's type and the sampling method in the experiment section. Previous research suggested that grid cells, a key component in the brain's spatial coding system, are largely independent of external cues. However, our findings indicate that many rodents' grid cells are significantly influenced by sensory inputs from visual and tactile sources, often in alignment with environmental features such as walls and floors in rooms. Furthermore, the periodicity of grid cells can shift in response to changes in external cues, such as being placed in rooms with different floor dimensions. Our study reveals that the brain's temporal place cells integrate spatially-modulated sensory information with ambiguous path integration signals to convey the rodent's position, and that the influence of external cues on grid cells is a ubiquitous feature of the brain's navigation system. This is demonstrated through electroencephalogram recordings made in the rodent's parietal cortex while navigating various environments with different sensory characteristics, combined with behavioral data showing that the brain's temporal place cells rely on the accuracy of their grid cell inputs to correctly locate food sources. This is highlighted by the fact that rodents can only accurately find food when the grid cell input to the place cells is precise, but this precision requires the ability to learn the rodent's starting location in a room. This insight challenges the current understanding of the brain's spatial coding system and suggests that external cues play a more significant role than previously thought. This perspective is further supported by the fact that many environmental features in animals' natural habitats likely map to the grid cell frequency, and therefore it is likely that animals' ability to navigate these environments relies heavily on the external cues available to them. The discovery of solar-like cycles in smaller, cooler stars like Kepler-29 has been limited due to lack of data. Our research focuses on detecting cycles in stars with surfaces similar to that of the Sun, but that are 0.5 to 1.5 times the Sun's size. We used magnetic field measurements from the Kepler spacecraft's spectroscopy, taking into account all possible cycle periods from 150 to 400 days. Cycle detection was possible for the 10 hottest targets in the study through a technique called the Hann window method. The findings showed that kinematic dynamos, which produce short-term cycle variations, are prevalent in the smallest stars, while magnetic cycles similar to the Sun's are common in medium-sized stars. The detection of cycles in the largest stars in the study was less clear due to instrumentation limitations. Overall, we found that magnetic cycles are common in small and medium-sized stars. The study included data from Kepler up to 41.8 days before its shutdown. The approach used in the research offers a new way to study stellar cycles through magnetic field analysis. The method may be applied to studies using data from the Kepler successor, Kepler EBS, which starts operations in 2024 and includes a capability for measuring stellar magnetic fields. The research identified six potential long-term cycle targets and confirmed the detection of cycles in 10 of the 32 hottest targets with surface temperatures similar to that of the Sun, also confirming that cycles exist in stars that are 0.5 to 1.5 times the Sun's size. The study demonstrated the effectiveness of the technique with artificial data sets and established an optimal window size for cycle detection of 2.5 to 3.5 solar cycles, which was validated by analyzing data sets that included the Sun. The discovery of cycles in the Sun-sized stars KIC 82806, KIC 10279247, KIC 2991261, and K2-25b were the first of their kind at the time of publication. We establish an unlimited family of non-hyperelliptic genus three covers of the projective line in the genus four case, with the base being a quartic in $\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Q}}$. These families are generated by quadratic extensions in $S_4$, with some restrictions on the rational rank of associated elliptic curves to prove the statement. Additionally, we demonstrate that there are an infinite number of quartic extensions in $S_4$, with a rational point group being isomorphic to that of a non-Serre curve mentioned, for a particular type of bounded rational rank. Furthermore, under certain conditions, we prove that an infinite number of these covers won't have an enhancement to a genus two cover, with a rational point group being $D_4$ or $S_4$. Moreover, we show that there are an infinite number of degree two Galois extensions in $S_4$, with an associated rational point being an equivalence class of an irreducible polynomial, for a specific type of bounded rational rank. Lastly, we assert that an infinite number of these covers, with a rational point group being $D_4$ or $S_4$, won't gain rank when associated elliptic curves are defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, with a particular combination of rational and 2-rational coefficients. This is based on recent research by K. Dat, J. Huard, and C. Scharber, with additional conclusions drawn. This work is a continuation of that research. We investigated the time-twirling of a system that interacts with an environment, starting from an initial state that is symmetric under time-reversal. Our analysis reveals that the time-twirling state is non-exponential in both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. In unitary dynamics, this time-twilling state is related to the time-winding number and is represented by a uniform superposition of time-wrapped states. In non-unitary dynamics, this time-twilling state exhibits a non-unitary exponential decay and is represented by a uniform superposition of time-wrapped states with lost phases. Notably, this time-twilling state can be used to measure the distinguishability time, which marks the point at which the system's state becomes distinguishable from its time-reversed state. This concept is demonstrated through a study of a system subject to continuous and discrete decoherence. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of time-twilling states in understanding the time-evolution of open systems. Furthermore, we propose that this approach could be applied to study the emergence of time-irreversibility in complex systems evolving from chaos to structure. Ultimately, our analysis of time-twilling states may provide new insights into the fundamental issue of time's arrow in physics. Our study introduces several new concepts, including the time-twilling operator, time-twilling state, and distinguishability time, which are applicable to both continuous and discrete systems. These concepts are not only theoretically relevant but also have practical implications, as they can be applied to design new measurement protocols that leverage the coherences of time-twilling states. These protocols could potentially enhance the performance of quantum sensors, such as those based on atomic interferometry, electronic spin sensing, and optical metrology. Moreover, our study paves the way for exploring the connection between time-twilling states and other non-equilibrium phase-sensitive properties, such as superconducting device critical current and charge order in cuprates. Ultimately, our research introduces time-twilling states as a powerful tool for studying the non-equilibrium physics of complex systems and highlights their potential to drive new breakthroughs in this field. Our approach is broadly applicable to both discrete and continuous systems and can be used to analyze systems in contact with thermal reservoirs, such as Caldeira-Leggett models, as well as systems based on spin-boson interactions, such as superconducting qubits mounted on vibrating micro-mirrors. The evolution of a planet's atmosphere may be shaped by a recurring cycle between its internal and external components. This model suggests that a habitable planet's atmosphere has gone through an eternal process of transformation, with multiple phases sparked by the interior's heat and tectonic activity. This paper explores the potential for an atmospheric "nitrogen lock" to occur on these worlds, where a significant nitrogen-rich compound forms and cannot be broken down due to changing chemical conditions. This "lock" might lead to a stable greenhouse effect, causing the atmosphere to retain heat and lead to further evolution. To investigate this concept, we must consider the complex interactions within these planets's systems and how they influence their atmospheres. This work focuses on one aspect – the potential for an atmospheric lock – and suggests future studies should investigate other consequences of this lock-locking mechanism. This lock-locking mechanism has the potential to significantly impact a planet's atmosphere over billions of years. This model predicts multiple lock events and suggests that a habitable exoplanet like Kepler-452b, with a secure solid surface and extensive atmosphere, could have experienced this cycle of atmospheric transformation at least once. This work also introduces computational tools for modeling these planetary systems and their atmosphere evolution and identifies key processes that these codes can help investigate. Ultimately, this study raises questions about the long-term implications of this lock-locking mechanism and other similar processes and encourages further research into the complex interactions within these planetary systems. Our research involves computational methods to analyze the interactions between water molecules and olefin fragments in their ground and excited states. Using 1,3-pentadiol (1,3-PDO) as a model, we investigate the effects of hydroxyl group placement on π-olefin and NBO orbital structures. Furthermore, we investigate the energy changes and mechanisms for methyl cation and proton transfers within these complexes. To understand the significance of 1,2-pentadiol (1,2-PDO) compared to 1,3-PDO, we also consider the consequences of hydroxyl group positional error, revealing distinct differences in molecular geometry, methyl cation production, and proton transfer pathways. While both molecules exhibit protonated enediol structures, the proton transfer mechanism in 1,2-PDO is concerted and endothermic, in contrast to the exothermic, stepwise transfer in 1,3-PDO. These computational results provide a theoretical basis to explain the observed preference for 1,3-PDO over 1,2-PDO in base-induced reactions. Additionally, we extend our study to 1,2-hexadiol (1,2-HXD) and 1,3-hexadiol (1,3-HXD) to explore the effects of ring size on the molecular geometry, methyl cation production, and proton transfer pathways, revealing that both 1,2-HXD and 1,3-HXD exhibit protonated enediol structures and exothermic, stepwise proton transfer mechanisms. Notably, the preferred protonation site shifts from C2 in 1,2-PDO to C5 in 1,2-HXD, and both 1,2-HXD and 1,3-HXD exhibit similar proton transfer mechanisms. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between water molecules and olefin fragments and have implications for the theoretical description of base-induced reactions. Moreover, they highlight the significance of computational methods in analyzing these reactions computationally and predicting the outcomes, which can be verified through future experiments. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of theoretical calculations in understanding complex biochemical reactions and the need for further experimental validation. Tensor network methods have successfully applied various disciplines, yet they're often challenging to prepare as quantum circuit parametrizations. Our research introduces a universal framework for converting a wide range of tensor networks into qubit circuits, expanding the reach of quantum circuit theory. This approach allows us to leverage TN physics beyond the limitations of circuits. As an illustration, we transform the matrix product state into a qubit circuit, revealing that this representation captures entanglement properties. Utilizing this framework, the quasiprojectivity degree can be quantified as the minimal number of unitary operations required to prepare a given state using this circuit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this transformation retains the physical properties of the original tensor network state. As an example, we investigate the entanglement properties of a matrix product state exhibiting fractal behavior. Our research introduces a universal framework for converting tensor networks into qubit circuits, expanding the reach of quantum circuit theory.

In cancer research, classification and diagnosis are frequently supported by quantitative analyses of tissue samples. Deep learning methods combining computer vision and graph neural networks have shown great promise in this area by accurately distinguishing between tumor and normal tissues. Our novel framework, RAGNet-DA, leverages a region-based approach and combines graph neural networks with data augmentation to significant improvements in Generalizability and Robustness. RAGNet-DA's key innovation is a region-based graph neural network that uses object masks to select distinct regions within an image, building a class-specific graph to classify tissues. To enhance generalizability, the model is trained on multiple datasets and is reinforced by robust graph classification capabilities. The inclusion of data augmentation techniques and training on multiple datasets further improves performance by capturing a broader range of tissue appearances and reinforcing the model's generalizability. Experimental results on the prospective, industry-led MICCAI Grand Challenge dataset showed RAGNet-DA's superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its potential as a reliable and generalizable approach for unsupervised tumor-normall tissue classification. Additionally, our model's robustness and generalizability were validated through various experiments, demonstrating its capability to accurately classify tissues after being trained on a different dataset and data augmentation techniques. Moreover, an analysis of the influence of graph construction and neural network architecture on the model's performance was conducted, revealing that distinct components can lead to different levels of generalization. Moreover, an evaluation of the model's performance across various datasets showed a notable correlation between tissue hardness and classification accuracy, suggesting that the model may be employed to assess tissue hardness as a complementary aspect. Furthermore, an assessment of the model's robustness in the presence of hard tumors revealed that it is capable of accurately classifying tissues even in the presence of tumors with low probability. Lastly, an analysis of the model's performance in challenging scenarios, such as classifying tissues with uncertain boundaries, demonstrated its potential as a robust and generalizable approach for this task.

Point processes that evolve in time in accordance with specific rules, known as Hawkes processes, have been employed to model interaction-driven phenomena in various fields. To capture more intricate interactions, researchers now utilize nonlinear relationships between the processes and their conditional intensities. A study has been conducted to analyze a recently introduced variation of the nonlinear Hawkes process, specifically the Shi-Cui-Ma-Zhang version, when the underlying functions are smooth and have limited growth. To estimate the model parameters, a variational Bayes approach was developed and demonstrated to yield high accuracy when compared to traditional methods. The accuracy of the proposed method was evaluated through simulations, revealing a strong correlation between the estimated and true parameters, alongside a notable decrease in estimation error when compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the method was successfully applied to real-world data sets originating from finance and telecommunications, resulting in an insightful analysis of the detected interaction phenomena. Additionally, the study investigated the convergence rate of the variational Bayes estimator, demonstrating a square root relationship with the time horizon. Implementing accurate and high-performance simulations of astrophysical systems is a complex challenge, particularly when it comes to N-body simulations of large clusters of stars and dark matter. To tackle this issue, we integrated the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) into the ARTYPE 2.0 code to leverage its computational benefits. By converting the pairwise Newtonian interaction formula into an algorithm that utilizes the FMM, the code's performance is significantly enhanced when simulating a range of scales, from a few to millions of objects. The FMM-based algorithm demonstrates speedups of up to 100 times compared to a straightforward brute-force method and retains the same level of accuracy. The new algorithm also provides a smooth transition between the direct and multipole approaches, offering greater flexibility in simulations, the ability to handle a large number of particles, and a substantial reduction in memory usage. The enhancements to ARTYPE 2.0 make it an ideal platform for conducting extensive, high-resolution N-body simulations in the realm of massive clusters of stars and dark matter. The code's advanced performance, coupled with its modular design and scalability, allows it to tackle a diverse range of computational astrophysics challenges. The current version of the code has been utilized to create billions of time steps in simulations of up to 1.9 billion objects and has a credit in the development of the IllustrisTNG500 flagship simulation. The code is now an open-source contribution as part of the Responsibility Research project. Current medical segmentation models primarily focus on fine-tuning pre-trained models within a single domain and do not adequately address the challenge of annotating multiple anatomical domains. To address this issue, this paper introduces Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA), which employs contrastive learning to semisupervised data across different domains. By incorporating a contrastive loss function along with a general domain discriminator, CS-CADA enables the separation of domain-specific information and the adaptation of multiple domains through a single contrastive learning step. This allows for seamless adaptation to any target domain with only a few labeled samples. The resulting theory is characterized by a finite BRS anomaly and does not include any auxiliary fields related to the algebra of general coordinate transformations. This effective action may be employed to investigate the dynamics of 3+1 dimensional supergravity. We examine the electric dipole moment (EDM) of the tau lepton within a Type-II two-Higgs doublet model, incorporating minimal supersymmetry. Employing constraints from $K^0 \bar K^0$ mixing and the Higgs mass, we find a significant potential for the model to explain the observed $T$-parity paradigm's success. However, even without it, the tau EDM can surpass the present experimental limit with the minimal model, while the most constrained scenarios require a substantial number of additional degrees of freedom to reconcile the discrepancy. Furthermore, we found that the model can also effectively address the cosmological moisture problem. Nonetheless, the solution poses a challenge for the model. Additionally, we found that the $K^0 \bar K^0$ mixing constraint already significantly limits the parameter space that could resolve the hierarchy problem. We also found that the most feasible pathways for the model to resolve the hierarchy problem involve new contributions to the Higgs mass from interactions with other scalar fields. Lastly, we found that even without additional degrees of freedom, the model fails to meet the requisite for naturalness in the Higgs mass, largely due to the constraint from $K^0 \bar K^0$ mixing. In this research, we explore a diverse set of rank metric codes, specifically those that can correct errors, for both low and high code rates. Our investigation reveals an intriguing distinction in the error-correcting abilities of these codes, with a significant gap in performance occurring at code rates equal to or above or below 1/2. This distinction highlights the importance of considering code performance across various utilization scenarios. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that certain rank metric codes, such as Generalized Reed-Muller codes and the previously unstudied Extended Generalized Reed-Muller codes, exhibit optimal error-correcting capabilities when compared to other codes in certain scenarios. Additionally, we establish upper and lower bounds for the minimum rank of codes within the Reed-Muller code family, providing a measure of their complexity. These findings, accompanied by explicit examples and a comprehensive overview of related topics, are presented in this study. Our discoveries are anticipated to contribute meaningfully to the field of rank metric codes and code theory.
