Building upon the observations made by Li, Song, and Yang in "AdS$_2$ Geodesic Operators, OPE Blocks, and Three-Dimensional SCFTs", we extend our analysis to the realm of $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories in two dimensions. We establish a precise connection between the conserved current block operator in these theories and its equivalent representation in $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ Chern-Simons theory, set within the context of AdS$_2$ geometry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the latter expression yields a novel two-dimensional conformal block, accessible through the AdS$_3$ geodesic operator of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ Chern-Simons theory. Interestingly, this block exhibits a distinct spin representation compared to its counterpart derived from AdS$_2$ geodesic operators. Additionally, we utilize this relationship to derive the four-point function of stress tensors in $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal gravity on AdS$_3$, with results consistent with prior analyses utilizing the bootstrap method. Moreover, we obtain explicit expressions for scalar and tensor four-point functions in $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories on AdS$_2$, thereby revealing a richer spin representation than previously understood. Lastly, we establish that AdS$_2$ geodesic operators, encompassing both scalar and spin conserved current blocks, are an exhaustive set of boundary CFT$_2$ operators capable of recreating AdS$_3$ geodesic Witten diagrams. Consequently, our findings provide a foundational framework for investigating generic AdS$_3$ CFT$_2$ relationships via geodesic Witten diagrams.

Using the DES-Y3 shape catalogue and a corresponding sample of approximately one billion galaxies, this study employs neural networks to analyze the large-scale structure and gravitational field in the DES footprint. A deep learning model, specifically a convolutional neural network, is trained to identify distortions caused by gravitational lensing, and is integrated with traditional methods to create a combined estimator. Comparing to traditional approaches, we find that neural network-based method yields a mean squared error of approximately 0.25 arcseconds, demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, when applied to specific galaxy populations, we observe a notable improvement of up to a 15% reduction in estimation error. Leveraging this method, we estimate the stellar mass power spectrum and a key non-linear scale, R0.1M*, with reasonable accuracy, and identify potential sources of discrepancies relative to theoretical predictions. The techniques employed in this analysis also provide a framework for analyzing other extrinsic astrophysical properties. Through this analysis, we gather valuable experience and skills in using machine learning to address complex scientific questions, and the associated code is openly available for future applications. Ultimately, this study lays the groundwork for enhanced analysis, such as confronting stellar mass function models and estimating the scatter in mass-to-light ratios. In 1975, Gelfand and MacPherson defined the notion of combinatorial differential manifolds through a set of basic rules, demonstrating their theory's equivalence to traditional differential manifolds. Building upon their work, Finsler manifolds can now be accurately described using the rules Gelfand and MacPherson established. Furthermore, their rules enable the development of a meaningful framework for measuring volumes in the context of differential manifolds. In particular, this framework allows for the computation of correct volumes in the presence of singularities, thereby extending the approach of Gelfand and MacPherson in their landmark paper from 1975. In addition, it becomes clear that the definitions of combinatorial differential manifolds and singular homology have a strong, mutually enriching relationship. As a result, many long-standing open questions in the field are resolved, while new intriguing problems arise. For instance, the inability to define combinatorial differential manifolds in a manner compatible with Finsler structures raises the question of whether there exists an even more fundamental framework that underlies both concepts. The introduction provides an overview of the key developments in the field, accompanied by a new perspective that reexamines the relationship between combinatorial differential manifolds, singular homology, and Finsler structures. Moreover, novel, groundbreaking ideas are introduced in relation to the computation of volumes, the definition of combinatorial differential manifolds, and the determination of homology, all of which are supported by concrete examples and theoretical frameworks. Ultimately, this work is a testament to the enduring legacy of the groundbreaking work of Gelfand and MacPherson in 1975. In conclusion, this research paves the way for a fresh exploration of the field, fueled by numerous, previously unanswered questions. We've obtained early spectra of the Type II supernova SN~2020jfo, obtained just one day following its initial detection, allowing us to analyze the absorption lines in an exceptionally narrow time frame. Our analysis of the SN~2020jfo's spectra revealed the presence of numerous neutral metal absorption lines, originating from the expansion of the outermost layers of the star and spanning approximately 1500 km/s. The spectra also displayed prominent absorption features of hydrogen, which, when compared to other Type II supernovae, exhibited a distinct pattern of line widths. By correlating the line widths with line identification, we observed an unusual relationship between line widths and ionization levels, which deviated from expected outcomes. Furthermore, the relative abundances of several elements in SN~2020jfo, including iron, nickel, magnesium, and silicon, were determined and showed a consistent pattern of increasing abundance with ionization level. This pattern, combined with the expansion velocities of these elements, revealed that SN~2020jfo's progenitor star exhibited an irregular pattern of shell ejection, with outer regions velocities ranging from 10,000 to 21,000 km/s. A detailed analysis of the spectra using the P-Cygni profile indicated that the absorption lines were shaped by a combination of the supernova's expanding envelope and the movement of the supernova's progenitor star's circumstellar material. The comparison of the relative abundances of nickel and iron in SN~2020jfo showed a significant anomaly, with a ratio exceeding the solar value by a factor of at least 10. This exceptionally high ratio suggests that the supernova's explosion destroyed a significant portion of the iron, while also implying that SN~2020jfo may have generated a substantial amount of 56Ni, with the potential to produce a neutron-capture element enhancement in the surrounding interstellar medium. The discovery of SN~2020jfo, along with other recent Type II supernovae, highlights the importance of early high-resolution spectroscopy in understanding the physical processes governing these explosions and the impact they have on their surroundings. Ultimately, this knowledge will be crucial in using supernovae as cosmological tools.

A type of highly sensitive and wide-view optics found in lobsters and crabs, lobster-eye optics offers unparalleled performance in detecting polarized and anisotropically scattered light. Its intricate design consists of equilateral-triangle arrays that trigger optical super-resolution and nearly 360-degree field-of-view capabilities. Reversing the optical system into a camera configuration requires determining the optical paths and identifying the detection areas within the device. Although researchers have proposed several methods to decode the optics, these methods are either impractical without additional components or fail to accurately detect specific segments. To address this challenge, we investigate how rotating a cross-like image by a specific angle can reveal the inner workings of the lobster-eye optics. Utilizing the symmetry of the equilateral-triangle arrays, we analyze how the rotated cross interacts with the optics and develop a practical method to identify distinct segments of the device. This method provides a feasible solution for deciphering the optics without complex manufacturing or third-party components. To validate our approach, we apply it to a real-world lobster-eye optics model and demonstrate its accuracy through numerical simulations and experimental verification using a photonic crystal lens as the optics component. This approach opens up possibilities for the development of a universal camera-coding method that can decode a wide range of complex optics designs. Moreover, we propose that this approach could be extended to other optical systems that exhibit rotational symmetry, enabling the decoding of such systems through a simple cross-pattern test. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of innovative cameras that can mimic the sensitive vision of arthropods.

This article presents an investigation into the level set method's potential to enhance the analysis of second-order fully nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). To illustrate the method's viability, we solve a singular fully nonlinear Hessian equation using a level set approach and leverage the technique to derive a new proof for a specific boundedness theorem within the context of these types of equations. Additionally, this method suggests an alternative way to investigate the uniqueness of solutions to fully nonlinear equations. This methodology also naturally extends to equations defined over Clifford surfaces and similar manifolds. Furthermore, this approach prompts an inquiry into the level set method's potential to contribute to the analysis of stochastic fully nonlinear PDEs. Lastly, this strategy may provide an alternative to the existing approach to boundedness theorems as demonstrated in the companion paper.

The analysis focuses on the predictions of haloes with $M_h\ge10 12h^{-2}\mathrm{M_\odot}$ at a redshift of $z=0$. The research finds that there is a strong correlation between halo mass and the amplitude of initial cosmological density fluctuations. To simplify the many parameters in the model, a sub-set of highly correlated variables is identified using a principal component analysis. Interestingly, it is observed that using a density-only model, instead of one that accounts for both density and velocity, yields a similar level of accuracy in predicting halo mass, even when the parameters in question have been optimized separately. This implies that there may be a limit to how accurately haloes can be distinguished based on large-scale cosmological conditions. This study introduces a semi-supervised Convolutional Matrix Factorization (CNMF) technique for automatically transcribing piano music from audio recordings. Based on the successful applications of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Matrix Factorization (MF) in music information retrieval, we developed a CNMF framework that combines a Convolutional Neural Network with two complementary low-rank factorization methods, Alternative Multi-kernel Factorization (AMKF) and Supervised Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (SNMF), to optimize piano transcription accuracy using both labeled and unlabeled data. Our research first provides a comprehensive review of recent piano transcription research, then thoroughly evaluates the proposed semi-supervised CNMF approach against a diverse set of  15 state-of-the-art low-rank factorization techniques and 5 supervised deep learning methods on three publicly available piano transcription datasets. Our evaluation reveals that the proposed semi-supervised CNMF method achieves significantly higher Mean Opinion Score (MOS) scores than existing low-rank factorization and deep learning methods on three publicly available piano transcription datasets. Additionally, our research demonstrates that incorporating limited labeled data and sophisticated factorization methods can substantially enhance piano transcription accuracy. Moreover, our experiments confirm that both the applied CNN architecture and factorization methods are critical components of the proposed semi-supervised CNMF framework. Furthermore, our method successfully leverages unlabeled data to significantly improve piano transcription accuracy, highlighting its primary advantage. Our research also provides a useful evaluation framework consisting of a diverse set of 15 state-of-the-art low-rank factorization techniques that can be used to compare and evaluate the performance of other piano transcription methods. This research introduces an original approach to assigning mean properties such as mean specific angular momentum and mean mass to fluid elements within rotating stars, deviating from conventional methods. By utilizing a set of conserved quantities specific to the star's equilibrium configuration, we can establish local volume-averaged property values that accurately represent the overall characteristics of the star's rotation and composition. This novel framework is demonstrated through a hypothetical rapidly rotating Polytropic star and reveals distinct patterns in the spatial distribution of these mean properties, which exhibit pronounced diagonal symmetry in alignment with the star's rotation axis. The assigned mean specific angular momentum and mean mass display intricate patterns across diverse rotational scenarios. Notably, our method reveals an unexpected correlation between the star's mean specific angular momentum and mean mass, which was previously overlooked, and this correlation holds significant potential for further exploration in the study of rapidly rotating stars. Additionally, this approach facilitates an examination of the entropy patterns within these stars, showcasing how they adapt to various rotational forces that shape their interior structures. As the star's angular momentum increases, there is a noticeable shift in the entropy distribution across different fluid layers, accompanied by a notable tilt in the entropy patterns' symmetry axes. This study provides an opportunity to reevaluate the entropy patterns observed in rapidly rotating stars through oscillation mode analysis, offering valuable insights that can contribute to a deeper understanding of these celestial bodies' dynamics. Ultimately, this research paves the way for utilizing the assigned mean properties in numerical solutions to the advection equation, which can help reveal the complex patterns of chemical elements within rapidly rotating stars. Despite the theoretical nature of this work, it is position to lay the groundwork for future numerical applications and can be extended to cover stars in polynomial gravity potential. To facilitate efficient training of deep convolutional neural networks with limited labeled data, we've developed a method for cost-effective selective labeling. By prioritizing and focusing labeling efforts on the most informative and difficult-to-learn images, we've achieved a notable reduction in labeling costs without sacrificing model performance. Our approach combines a data-driven prediction model and a statistical analysis method to identify and label the most challenging cases. The model we developed, named selective labeling network, excels in two scenarios: one where the labeling process is repeated to refine the model, and another where the model is optimized for a specific labeling budget. Through thorough experimentation on ImageNet and Places365, we demonstrated that selective labeling leads to significant cost savings (around 5 times) without a performance drop, and with repeated labeling, even better performance can be achieved. Moreover, our method is versatile and applicable to a range of deep convolutional neural network architectures. The code is available at https://github.com/zhunghong/Selective-Labeling-Deep-Network. The paper has been accepted by CVPR 2019 and awarded the Best Paper Award.

The detection of gravitational waves from the merger of neutron stars or black holes allows researchers to locate potential electromagnetic counterparts. However, the traditional method of identifying counterparts, which involves comparing observed electromagnetic data with theoretical models within a fixed time frame and spatial error radius for the electromagnetic event, may be optimized by considering the electromagnetic data's temporal and spatial relationship to the gravitational wave event even if no counterpart is observed. This approach can be implemented by creating a comprehensive electromagnetic sky map that is aligned with the possible location of the gravitational wave event and can be used to assign a probability value to each electromagnetic source. To illustrate this concept, we use a neutron star merger event, GW190425, to create a distribution of possible locations and corresponding electromagnetic source probabilities. These probabilities are then applied to existing catalogs of high-energy sources and notable astronomical events, resulting in the re-interpretation of several sources within the 50% confidence error radius of the possible location of the gravitational wave event. This process is performed for a range of time windows preceding, during, and following the gravitational wave event. The resulting study suggests that the neutron star merger event GW170817 may be re-interpreted by considering the possibility of pre-merger activity. The method described here can be readily adapted to any future gravitational wave detections that may be of interest. The code developed for this study is openly accessible by integrating the GWCatalog into the general catalog analysis framework called SExpress. The re-evaluation of existing neutron star and black hole discoveries through this method is also feasible due to the low computational requirements of the code. The new insight gained from this study can motivate multi-wavelength observations and further analysis of the electromagnetic data, in addition to informing the development of more targeted models that can be used to identify possible counterparts in future neutron star and black hole merger events. The approach presented here can be expanded to consider additional information about the gravitational wave event's properties, such as the masses of the merging objects, the spin of the objects, and the characteristics of the gravitational wave signal, in order to provide even more precise predictions for the possible locations and corresponding electromagnetic source probabilities. The re-evaluation of existing discoveries through this method may also contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationships between these high-energy sources and the gravitational wave events that are associated with them. Understanding the living conditions and social environment of patients is crucial for improving health equity, but many patients' conditions go undetected due to a lack of relevant information in their medical records. This research aims to enhance the detection of social determinants of health by leveraging natural language processing and machine learning to extract information from clinical notes. Our study utilizes the SHARPen framework, which combines highly performing models and facilitates future advancements in the field, to demonstrate the benefits of incorporating auxiliary tasks in model training. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that extracting information from clinical notes can significantly boost the detection of social determinants of health, both with and without the aid of existing standardized data, indicating substantial potential for future applications. Ultimately, our findings highlight the potential for natural language processing to play a key role in addressing disparities in medical diagnosis. To facilitate future research, our model selections, training settings, and performance data are openly accessible. By providing model examples and training settings that yield these results, we hope to encourage researchers to pursue related goals and contribute to the advancement of the field. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to equitable medical care by empowering detection of social determinants of health through natural language processing. We investigate the problem of minimizing the cost of moving a passive swimmer with variable velocity under external currents in a three-dimensional space. This cost is represented by the time it takes to transition the swimmer from one fixed position to another. Assuming the swimmer's motion follows a stochastic process described by a Brownian motion with occasional changes, we make assumptions about the frequency and magnitude of these transitions. Our analysis of online forums reveals that many communities are still recovering from the social impacts of the pandemic, which drastically reduced diversity in urban areas. We investigate whether restrictions on gathering sizes contributed to this effect by comparing the diversity of discussions on Reddit. Our results show that, although restrictions were responsible for the initial decrease in diversity, the greatest loss was incurred during the community-building period that followed. This period saw a significant increase in diverse discussions that lasted over a year. Furthermore, we found that some cities experienced increased diversity in discussions after restrictions were implemented, which suggests that physical distancing may have facilitated diverse online interactions. However, our data does not support a clear connection between diversity and the severity or duration of lockdown measures. A comprehensive framework for developing scattering theory is created by an asymptotic algebra and a scattering matrix, which dictate the behavior of operators and their convergence at infinite times and spatial distances. This foundational structure is already present in established theories like CFT$_2$. Our research focuses on identifying the intrinsic properties of this underlying framework and developing a systematic approach to constructing scattering theories. We establish a key relationship between the asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix, which can be used to determine the entire algebraic structure given the asymptotic algebra. This relationship is then utilized to build scattering theories from first principles by combining the asymptotic algebra with freely generated unitary representations of solvable Lie algebras, which emerge in finite-dimensional form at infinite times. We apply this method by constructing a scattering theory based on the Weyl algebra, which parallels the properties found in $2$D conformal field theory, specifically associated with Virasoro algebra. The resulting scattering theory exhibits algebraic structures analogous to those found in massless chiral CFT$_2$. The asymptotic representation of the Virasoro algebra, which includes central charge, is derived using this construction method for the first time. The obtained scattering theory also contains an algebraic $Z_2$ grading, related to the holomorphic weight operator known as $L_0^{\rm ph}$. The developed approach allows for an abstract understanding of scattering theories and can be utilized to analyze more intricate algebras, such as those present in $3$D conformal field theory. The resulting theories may serve as models for describing scattering in higher-dimensional spacetimes. The proposed construction method also raises fundamental questions about the nature of scattering theories and their relationship to conformal field theories. The derived theories can be viewed as conformal field theories with undefined couplings, suggesting that coupling constants play a crucial role in defining a conformal field theory. The ultimate goal of this research is to deconstruct the algebras found in finite-dimensional form and apply this knowledge to resolve open problems in mathematics and physics. The proposed approach to scattering theories can be extended to non-compact algebras, such as those present in $2$D conformal field theory, using the construction method described above. The resulting theories feature asymptotic representations of non-compact algebras at infinite times and spatial distances. The spread of false information on social media has become a pressing concern, and Twitter is no exception. Given the microformat nature of tweets, previous studies have demonstrated substantial success in detecting false information by utilizing contextual information from adjacent tweets. Nevertheless, it is unreasonable to assume that contextual knowledge from nearby tweets is consistently beneficial or necessary in all situations. Furthermore, it is unlikely that neighboring tweets possess the optimal much-needed contextual knowledge. To address these limitations, we investigate the extent to which success in detecting false information relies on neighboring context and explore the potential for improving models by introducing optional contextual knowledge from a broader range of sources. We utilize the process of selective attention from visual perception as inspiration and experiment with both locally and globally sourced contextual knowledge. The results indicate that models can occasionally perform better with optional contextual knowledge, and there is a notable gap in performance when using neighboring context alone. Additionally, models can benefit from selective contextual knowledge, and the ability to do so is influenced by the false information detected and the nature of the Twitter users involved. We also introduce a novel model that is designed to handle optional contextual knowledge but does not require it. The analysis of the model's performance reveals that it is on par with the best previously reported results. Notably, the model's ability to benefit from optional contextual knowledge is remarkable, and future research in this area is encouraged. We make the data and models associated with this research available for other scholars to reproduce and replicate the findings.

This entropy-hysteresis diagram, which reveals the interplay between entropy and hysteresis, is expected to be a universal feature applicable to any system exhibiting hysteresis and phase transitions, and whose entropy changes in response to an external force. Furthermore, we identified a critical point where the entropy-hysteresis diagram transitions from showing high entropy and no hysteresis to exhibiting both, mirroring the system's phase transition behavior. The location of this critical point is determined by the mean field theory and a notable correlation with a system's curvature effect is noted. Our analysis is then expanded to consider multiple order parameters, demonstrating how the entropy-hysteresis diagram can be a useful tool for analyzing complex systems with multiple phase transitions. Finally, we applied this framework to study superconductivity in the Ising model on a Cayley tree and found that the model exhibits a phase transition similar to that of the Curie-Weiss model. This indicates that the relationship between entropy and hysteresis can be a universal indicator with implications for the study of complex systems. Additionally, we propose that this framework can be employed to study other phase transitions and hysteresis in complex systems. Moreover, we suggest that the entropy-hysteresis diagram may be a useful analytical tool for understanding superconductivity phase transitions. Lastly, we acknowledge that this study can be expanded to consider dynamic systems by integrating the diagram with flow equilibrium concepts. This paper addresses the challenge of performing Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on data that includes rotational fluctuations, specifically in high-dimensional settings. Our research focuses on a particular approach known as L1-PCA, which aims to select a limited number of principal components by solving an optimization problem. However, the presence of rotational uncertainties hinders the application of traditional methods, thus we develop an alternative two-block formulation for the problem and employ an augmented alternating minimization technique to find the solution. Moreover, we establish the convergence rate of $O(1/k^2)$ for the iterative method in question, essentially wrapping the method in a specific framework that enables the analysis of a broader class of algorithms, thereby demonstrating the desired rate of convergence. Furthermore, our method can be applied to a variety of other problems after a straightforward adaptation. We employ our method on a synthetic dataset that has rotational fluctuations and includes significant Gibbs phenomenon. The results show that our method yields an accurate solution. Additionally, the method is efficient as it converges rapidly and can be an effective tool for the large-scale L1-PCA problems after a straightforward adaptation. Paraphrasing is a technique that allows us to assess the semantic labeling annotations' consistency without a fully-annotated gold standard set. By labeling a paragraph modified from the original text as if it were part of the target domain, we can determine if the annotations are semantically equivalent. Although previous approaches successfully incorporated paraphrasing for this purpose, they were largely restricted to simple tasks due to their reliance on human-generated labels for training. Our research presents a novel self-validation method for paraphrasing-based semantic labeling validation, which utilizes cheaply obtainable annotation data to train models for both paraphrasing and semantic labeling tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by developing a strong model that leverages cheap annotations to deliver accurate validation results on top of that model's predictions. The model's exceptional performance in valid/invalid classification tasks, as evaluated on the SSTD dataset, showcases a notable gap in accuracy compared to models that do not benefit from this training. The model's strong performance is also robust in various validation scenarios that involve different paraphrasing and semantic labeling models. X-ray spectra from the Kedge detector on the Swift satellite have been analyzed for a unique subclass of binary systems known as asynchronous polars. This subseries exhibits high energy levels when its companion star passes close to the focus of the system. Asynchronous polars differ significantly from standard polars in this regard. By studying six asynchronous polars and using the method of spectral mapping to account for their spin periods, researchers discovered that the hot stars at their centers emit similar amounts of energy across all observations except for one. Furthermore, the spectra from the Kedge detector on the Swift satellite reveal that the temperatures of the hot stars increase dramatically during high energy outbursts, supporting previous satellite-based findings. This temperature rise, estimated to be around 0.5-1.0 kiloelectronvolts, suggests that the additional energy is the result of an increase in temperature rather than a rise in the inner accretion disk's brightness. This temperature rise also appears to occur not just in the 2017 exception but also in the exceptional outburst observed in that year, supporting the idea that the extra energy produced during high energy outbursts is a universal phenomenon among asynchronous polars. This research is a continuation of efforts to understand the complex behavior of binary systems that involve compact stars and is based on data from the Swift satellite available from 2005 to 2018. The fluid is computed using a direct method and the solid using a Newmark approach, with the two solved in a feedback loop until the desired precision is reached. This framework is applied to a case study of an elastic tube subjected to fluid flow, demonstrating that the method can produce an accurate solution that meets precision criteria. A combined theory of strain and magnetic ordering in Mn/Fe/Ga(111) heterostructures reveals that the magnetocaloric effect can be independently controlled for spin-up and spin-down electrons. This unique thermal property arises due to the distinct thermal responses generated by in-plane and out-of-plane strain and magnetic ordering, resulting from competing orbital occupancies and nearby exchange interactions. Modifying the heterostructure to include a layer of Ga on top enables opposite thermal responses for spin-up and spin-down electrons, potentially enabling the creation of thermal diodes. These findings also highlight the importance of a proper band structure model in accurately predicting magnetic and thermal properties. Furthermore, experimental observation of these thermal properties is proposed to be feasible through ultrafast thermal reflectometry and scanning thermal conductivity measurements. This study offers a theoretical framework for understanding and manipulating the magnetocaloric effect in transition metal/Spinel transition metal/Semiconductor(111) heterostructures, making them suitable for the development of thermal management technologies that can be controlled by magnetism.

The study of light propagation through semi-conductor heterostructures has long been understood using local methods that only consider the immediate surroundings of the equilibrium positions. Advances in quantum metrology are driving the need for more comprehensive models that capture wider-scale effects. 

In this work, we apply the Effective Gap Width (EGW) approach to photon dispersion relationships, achieving significant improvements over local models and demonstrating the importance of considering non-local phenomena in optical phenomena. The revised model accurately captures the periodicity of the band structure even in regions far removed from the areas immediately surrounding the equilibrium positions. 

The improved model is validated through comparison with experimental data and theoretical models for a graphene layer paired with helium layers, showing excellent agreement. The revised model also facilitates the identification of a crucial in-plane distance that dictates the periodicity of the photon dispersion curve. 

This research demonstrates the EGW approach's utility in photonic applications and suggests the framework may be adapted for other phenomena governed by Boltzmann-Liouville equations. Furthermore, this work offers a promising framework for investigating electron-phonon interactions within optical phenomena. 

In conclusion, this study solidifies the EGW approach's position as a prominent revision of the adiabatic approximation, contributing to a deeper understanding of the adiabatic approximation's limitations and suggesting its potential for exploring more complex situations. This work paves the way for further research into quantum phenomena in large-scale systems.

The calculus of constructions, introduced in 1983 by Guy Cousineau, Thierry Coquand, Christine Paulin-Morris, and Bernd Krieg-Brueckner, has significantly impacted the development of modern programming languages and type theory. Its innovative combination of constructive logic, functional programming, and type reconstruction helped establish the foundation for future innovations such as General Purpose Analog Computing with Memristors and Smoothed complexity in computational geometry. To celebrate the 30th anniversary of the calculus of constructions, this survey re-examines its development and explores its far-reaching influences on contemporary research within programming languages and type theory. The authors' extensive contributions to programming languages research, guided by the principles of the calculus of constructions, have yielded notable outcomes, including Wombat, Coq, and Wombat's modern successor, both of which are critical to their fields. Through this survey, the authors aim to inspire researchers to continue building upon the calculus of constructions and its successes within programming languages and type theory. The authors' own research experiences in developing Wombat and its successor serve as a testament to the enduring value of the calculus of constructions as a research tool and a source of innovative ideas within programming languages and type theory. The authors' vision for future research envisions a future where programming languages research is shaped by the calculus of constructions and its extensions, contributing to the development of reliable and verifiable software that is increasingly critical to addressing global challenges. The authors invite the research community to join this vision by exploring the potential of the calculus of constructions to create programming languages that can be both flexible and mathematically rigorous, and by collaborating on projects that can bring this vision to life. The authors also invite the submission of papers on research projects that have been influenced by the calculus of constructions or have explored its extension in new contexts. The authors look forward to contributing to this ongoing dialogue and sharing their own research experiences in this discussion. Current GPU memory allocators, which prioritize performance over memory safety, often lead to difficult-to-debug issues like memory corruption and system crashes caused by inconsistent GPU memory management. To address this, we present DynaSOAr, a dynamic allocator that uses a separate memory space for bookkeeping to keep the primary memory free from unnecessary data. This approach enables full support for exception handling, allows for easy detection and fixing of memory-related problems, and accelerates memory management through reduced overhead. Evaluations of DynaSOAr reveal a significant reduction in memory allocation and deallocation latency by approximately 2.5-10.5 times and a notable increase in system crash detection rates by around 11-56%. Furthermore, DynaSOAr exhibits superior performance in workloads with high memory allocation frequencies, achieving a notable increase of up to 3.3 in raw performance compared to traditional allocators. Moreover, the intricate nature of GPU memory hierarchy is simplified by DynaSOAr's modular design with minimal performance loss, making it suitable for a wide range of GPU architectures. Additionally, we highlight the challenges and limitations of DynaSOAr, such as its sensitivity to memory configuration and potential for memory fragmentation, and explore potential avenues for further improvement. Through extensive evaluations on diverse GPU architectures and applications, DynaSOAr has demonstrated superior memory safety, reduced latency, increased crash detection rates, and comparable raw performance to traditional allocators. Consequently, we recommend integrating DynaSOAr into production-level GPU applications and believe its dynamic approach can spark interest in safety-centric GPU memory management. As part of this work, we also release open-source code for two production-level GPU applications utilizing DynaSOAr, specifically a deep learning-based sound recognition model and an image recognition model, both of which have been successfully deployed on real-world data sets with DynaSOAr. As part of this work, we also introduce GPUCSafe, a comprehensive testing suite for GPU memory allocators that can handle diverse memory scenarios and is currently available for download alongside DynaSOAr's code. Through GPUCSafe, we report the results of DynaSOAr's performance and memory safety comparisons with two prominent traditional GPU memory allocators, cublasAlloc and cudaMalloc, and one further allocator named SOAR. Ultimately, this research is an initial step towards a comprehensive study of GPU memory allocator safety and efficiency, and as such, it is fully compatible with a range of recent and older NVIDIA GPU architectures. This study investigates the boundedness and continuity of operators on generalized mixed Morrey spaces, which are a diverse array of subspaces that encompass a wide range of well-known spaces, including Morrey, Morrey-Sobolev and Hardy-H\"older spaces. Specifically, we establish the conditions under which operators defined by fractional integral and sublinear maximal operators are bounded or continuous within these spaces. Moreover, our investigation into the continuity of these operators leads us to a significant discovery regarding their boundedness. Moreover, our research is grounded in a novel approach that is free from reliance on interpolation methods. Instead, our key tool is an intriguing inequality that highlights the relationship between the Morrey norm and the Lebesgue norm. This innovative inequality not only facilitates our proof of the continuity of these operators but also sheds light on their boundedness. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Morrey mixed norm operator inequality is a fundamental concept with far-reaching implications, extending even to the realm of boundedness in the context of Calder\'on-Zygmund operators. Additionally, our study paves the way for a broader exploration of the properties of Morrey mixed norm spaces. Lastly, our research is complemented by concrete examples that validate our theoretical findings. These examples not only provide authentic instances of the applicability of our results but also offer a window into the intricate behavior of these operators through concrete data. A new approach is proposed for analyzing cloud morphology using a depth-first search algorithm in combination with texture features. The proposed method adapts the DFST algorithm to account for core and veiled regions within clouds, providing a more accurate assessment of cloud thickness. The algorithm identifies the primary cloud mass ("core") and a surrounding area ("veiled core") by considering pixels with similar optical thickness. The DFST technique recognizes the core as the starting point and traverses neighboring pixels with similar optical thickness until it reaches the veiled core. The algorithm then applies a first-in-last-out policy to determine the cloud boundary, resulting in a more precise measurement of the veiled core's thickness. The proposed method enhances the detection of cloud thickness by considering the veiled core, which is demonstrated through a metric called veiled ratio (VR). The evaluation of the proposed method reveals a significant increase in accuracy (from 0.67 to 0.83) and a notable reduction in error (from 0.33 to 0.17) when assessing cloud thickness with VR. The proposed approach is shown to outperform the current state-of-the-art cloud analysis technique, GAN-based Cloud, based on precision and recall metrics. To comprehend the complex ion distribution in plasmas resulting from interactions with intense, ultra-short laser pulses, particularly those with a negative chirp, researchers utilize computer simulations through particle-in-cell codes. A peculiar phenomenon observed in these simulations, characterized by a thin, low-density secondary layer with significant impact on ion acceleration, has not been thoroughly understood. Further analysis has uncovered that a specific combination of laser-induced phenomena, including void formation, electron depolarization, and a specific electron recirculation pattern, explains the presence and influence of this thin layer. Additionally, it has been found that accelerating ions in this specific ion acceleration regime can be optimized by adjusting the thickness of this thin layer, achieved by modifying the intensity and duration of the laser pulse. Moreover, it has been discovered that a specific relationship exists between the thickness of this layer and the critical amplitude of the chirped laser, as predicted by a simplified theoretical model. We examine the electronic and structural characteristics of TiO2 doped with carbon and nitrogen in both substitutional and interstitial positions utilizing a semi-empirical total-energy technique. When added in substitutional positions at an anion site, these dopants cause a significant shift in their energy levels, making it difficult for them to participate in reactions. In contrast, interstitially-added C and N exhibit delocalized electronic states more similar to those of pure TiO2. To further understand their behavior, we investigate these dopants in combination with each other and with hydrogen, finding that co-doping can facilitate the formation of bondable species despite being unstable in pure form. For example, a C interstitial forms a covalent bond with two O ions when co-doped with two N interstitials. These findings suggest that carefully selecting the type and placement of dopants can effectively utilize the unique properties of TiO2. Additionally, our study indicates that TiO2's reactivity towards C, N, and H can be enhanced by co-doping, offering a promising approach to improving its photocatalytic performance. To validate our results, we performed experiments using XPS, confirming our theoretical predictions regarding the binding energies of these dopants. Experimental observations also demonstrate that these dopants can indeed facilitate the formation of reactive surface species, consistent with our findings. Consequently, our studies suggest that carefully selected dopants and their combinations have great potential to enhance TiO2's photocatalytic activity and modify its electronic properties. Moreover, our results highlight the importance of exploring different dopant positions and combinations to achieve optimal results. Ultimately, our work underscores the value of hybrid theoretical-experimental approaches in material science research. The top quark's flavor-changing neutral current (FCNC) decay and the effective electroweak mixing angle are investigated using semi-elastic processes $p\bar{p}\to W^\ast \bar{b}+X\to j\eta X'$ where $\eta$ represents a neutral boson. This study is based on an integrated luminosity of 9.7 inverse femtobarns of proton-antiproton collision data from the CMS experiment at a 1.96 TeV collision energy. The effective electroweak mixing angle is constrained to be greater than $0.32\gamma$ or greater than $0.31\gamma$ at 95% confidence, depending on whether the neutral boson is a scalar or a vector boson, respectively. Additionally, branching ratio limits are set for the top quark to decay into a neutral boson and bottom quark, with the neutral boson further decaying to a charged lepton and missing energy: the scalar neutral boson's branching ratio is less than $0.40\gamma$ or $0.34\gamma$ depending on the lepton type, the vector neutral boson's branching ratio is less than $0.34\gamma$ for muons but constrained by a single data point for electrons, and the two-gamma decay branching ratio for the neutral boson is less than $0.38\gamma$. These limits are the most stringent to date. The study also constrains the effective electroweak mixing angle to be less than 0.25 for the two-gamma decay of the neutral boson, with certain parameters held constant, leading to the most stringent limit on this parameter to date. The most stringent previous limit was $0.34\gamma$ as set by an LEP experiment. The study's results are insensitive to the neutral boson's spin nature when limits on the effective electroweak mixing angle are applied. The most influential previous constraint on this parameter comes from top quark pair production analyses, with effective electroweak mixing angle limits of $0.26\gamma$ or $0.25\gamma$ depending on the neutral boson's mass, the most stringent limit to date. The study's results, combined with these previous constraints, further narrow the possible range for the effective electroweak mixing angle to be greater than $0.29\gamma$ or greater than $0.28\gamma$ depending on the neutral boson's nature

The goal is to minimize the coloring while adhering to the given criteria. The magnetic properties of stars in extreme states, such as those with intense magnetic fields or powerful magnetic outflows, lie at the heart of several unresolved puzzles in astrophysics. Recent research suggests that stable magnetic fields in these stars must comprise balanced toroidal and poloidal components, consistent with general relativistic stability theories. 

As a result, the strong magnetic fields shared by these stars are likely stabilized by a constant interplay between their toroidal and poloidal components. We're exploring how this 'twin-stabilization' process works in stars with massive winds, specifically looking at how magnetic field loops that lose stability still maintain stable overall magnetic fields. 

By analyzing a series of hypothetical stars with varying magnetic properties, we found that even when unstable magnetic field loops can cause significant changes, the stars' overall magnetic fields remain relatively stable. We're investigating the connection between this stability and the stars' winds, which could potentially observe this 'twin-stabilization' process in action. 

Ultimately, understanding this 'twin-stabilization' process is key to resolving the mysteries surrounding the magnetic properties of stars in extreme states. We propose observing this phenomenon in action with the help of global magnetic mapping techniques and high-cadence photometry and spectropolarimetry instruments available on upcoming fourth-generation telescopes.

Furthermore, studying this phenomenon in pulsars could reveal valuable insights into the nature of these highly stable magnetic fields and possible links to the origin of these cosmic objects.

The formation of massive stars is a complex process that is not yet fully understood and its basis lies in the molecular cores that form and evolve in dense regions of space. Finite Godel algebras are intimately connected with finite forest-like structures, which can be understood through the principles of duality. This connection allows us to translate questions about Godel algebras into more manageable questions about these forest-like structures, which are often easier to analyze. By examining the properties of forest-like structures that are preserved under certain operations, we can determine the associated theories of Godel algebras. For example, the theory associated with forests that contain trees of any height but are otherwise random is none of RKCL. Furthermore, if we restrict the forest to have a maximum tree height of n, we obtain a similar theory to none of RKCL with the additional requirement that the depth of any element is less than n. Additionally, we can use this approach to define theories of Godel algebras with finitely many parameters. Furthermore, this method enables us to capture the behavior of infinite Godel algebras by considering the limits of finite forest-like structures. This technique is particularly useful for demonstrating that some theories of Godel algebras are undecidable. For instance, to show that the theory associated with forests that contain any trees is undecidable, we can take an undecidable set of strings and an undecidable set of strings that are in one-to-one correspondence with the strings in the former set. Then, we can construct a forest that contains all the strings in the first set and demonstrate that the corresponding algebraic theory is undecidable. This undecidability proof relies on a recent advancement in the study of algebraic decision problems. Moreover, we can use this connection between Godel algebras and forest-like structures to reformulate known undecidability results of Godel algebras in a more intuitive understanding of these results. For instance, the undecidability of the theory associated with forests that contain cyclic trees can be seen as the undecidability of determining whether a given forest contains any cyclic trees. Additionally, we can use this connection to a broader class of structures known as forest-like structures. These structures encompass forests as well as more complex entities and can be used to demonstrate the undecidability of a broader range of Godel algebras. Ultimately, this connection between Godel algebras and forest-like structures provides a powerful tool for analyzing the associated theories of Godel algebras. In this study, an examination into the classification capabilities of LiDAR-based 3D point cloud data using deep learning techniques is conducted. Existing research primarily focuses on relying solely on local pattern information for accurate classification results. In contrast, this project aims to investigate the impact of surrounding contextual information on classification performance. A novel method utilizing neighboring point data in a reduced dimensionality feature space is proposed and tested to assess its effectiveness. Experimental evaluations utilizing real-world urban datasets and methodology demonstrate the method's potential for enhancing classification precision and robustness in the presence of modeling variations. Additionally, compared to conventional methods relying solely on local data, the proposed contextual approach achieves comparable accuracy while requiring substantially fewer model parameters. This suggests that future research on LiDAR-based deep learning can explore efficient models leveraging contextual information while minimizing model complexity. Furthermore, the proposed contextual technique's dimensionality-dependent behavior is analyzed to provide insights into its performance and potential applications. In the evaluation, the method's ability to classify trees and buildings is examined, demonstrating promising results and indicating that it can be a valuable approach for addressing other classification challenges. The code used in this project is available at https://github.com/kuangdian/ContextLiDAR.

Classical discrete calculus, as applied to zonal functions on the sphere, has a notable outcome where the h-cotangent and h-secant operators are found to be positive definite. However, this positivity is lost when the operators are applied repeatedly. Investigating this further, our study reveals how both finite difference and integral classical discrete operators affect the positive definiteness of zonal functions. Specifically, we show that the second-order finite difference and integral operators do not yield positive definite results, but do provide an alternative interpretation in the context of the h^2-cotangent and h^2-secant. Moreover, our work also identifies a positive definite outcome with the higher-order finite difference and integral operators, demonstrating that these have a connection to the anisotropic Hermite interpolation. These discoveries were initially presented through informal discussions at NANT 2020, with this paper presenting a more detailed proof and clarification of the underlying concepts.

The connection between ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos, specifically right ascension dependencies, can be investigated using a statistical approach known as multivariate likelihood ratio test. Employing eight neutrino detectors and 12 cosmic ray observatories with accurate right ascension measurements from 2000 to 2019, researchers applied this method to search for common patterns in both data sets. The most significant findings were found by conducting a spatial scan in the sky, and the results revealed a distinctive clustering in the right ascension range of approximately 110 degrees to 180 degrees. Furthermore, detailed analysis indicated that the observed pattern in the neutrino data likely resulted from chance, whereas the finding in cosmic rays was significant at a p-value of 0.046. The discovered dependence in cosmic rays was consistent with a circular symmetry with a radius of about 30 degrees, corresponding to the deflection due to passing through a substantial galaxy cluster along our line of sight. The predicted neutrino cluster, resulting from continuing the cosmic ray pattern into the left ascension range, might be located near right ascension 40 degrees to 80 degrees, potentially overlapping with the alleged Clusters CLASH-1602 and CLASH-0253. The predicted cluster's characteristics are within the detectability range of the upcoming neutrino detectors such as the KM3NeT Gen2 with 10 times its current sensitivity for specific galaxy cluster targets. The findings suggest that future neutrino detectors with sufficient sensitivity might identify ultra-high-energy cosmic ray patterns resulting from the gravitational influence of substantial galaxy clusters, potentially shedding light on the cosmic ray source locations. The long-term stability of liquid foams essentially depends on their surface properties, which determine the occurrence of flow and rupture. To understand and model foam dynamics, the roughness factor, a key surface property, must be accurately measured. Currently, there is no universally accepted method for calculating the roughness factor, particularly in three-dimensional applications. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach based on the analysis of flow and rupture patterns in two-dimensional foams and apply it to three-dimensional foams through geometric analysis of Plateau borders. To support our method, we provide numerical evidence showing that the roughness factor can be effectively obtained using Plateau border characteristics. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the roughless factor and flow and rupture patterns, demonstrating that the proposed approach yields physically meaningful results that can be utilized in models of foam dynamics. To facilitate future studies, we publicly release our calculation code to facilitate discussion and validation of the proposed method through open discussion and validation.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have achieved great success in image classification due to their ability to automatically extract image features and adapt to various datasets. Nonetheless, their accuracy can be hindered by overfitting caused by insufficient training data and misselected hyperparameters. Ensemble-based methods have been proposed to improve model performance by combining multiple models, but they typically train models independently, disregarding the potential synergies between them. This study introduces an ensemble-based deep learning framework known as Cooperative Convolutional Neural Networks (CoCoNNs) that enhances DCNNs' accuracy and robustness for single-image and multi-image classification tasks. CoCoNNs comprises multiple DCNNs that share hidden layers, which learn unique and complementary weight combinations that leverage each model's strengths. This technique not only mitigates overfitting but also facilitates the reduction of model parameters. Experimental evaluations on various datasets reveal that the proposed method surpasses conventional ensemble and deep learning methods in terms of accuracy and outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on certain benchmarks. Moreover, the model's parameter efficiency is enhanced by a factor of 2-5 without compromising performance. The code for the proposed framework is available online at https://github.com/zhengdf42643/CoCoNNs.

A combined experimental and theoretical analysis of a rotating Hele-Shaw cell filled with a non-Newtonian membrane fluid is presented in this study. When the membrane fluid is subjected to a constant surface tension, it is demonstrated through both approaches that increasing tension causes a shift from stable, axisymmetric Taylor-Shelley states to unstable states, and ultimately to stable, helical states. The theoretical model also reveals that the stability of these states is influenced by a dimensionless volume resistance, which is a product of the membrane resistance and the volume of the Taylor-Shelley state. This dimensionless volume resistance serves as an analog to the Bond number in Hele-Shaw systems and determines the state of the system based on rotational velocity and tension. Notably, the predicted relationships between rotational velocity, tension, and state of the system are confirmed by the experiments. Moreover, the theoretical model includes a scaling that helps explain the relationship between the outer and inner ring velocities during the transition from the stable to unstable states. The existence of multiple state stability branches is further illustrated through a plot of the minimum rotational velocity required for each state stability branch as a function of the dimensionless volume resistance. The existence of stable helical states is also confirmed by the experiments, and it is found that the outer ring velocity is proportional to the square of the surface tension divided by the membrane viscosity, demonstrating the same universal scaling as observed in the inner ring velocity. The possibility of rotating Hele-Shaw systems serving as model membranes for lipid bilayers is also discussed. The inter-bubble interactions in Hele-Shaw systems can be adjusted to replicate the properties of lipid membranes, such as the curvature elasticity of lipids or the charge distribution on lipids. By doing so, these systems may provide insights into membrane-mediated phenomena, such as protein-lipid interactions or membrane phase transitions. Additionally, the analysis of the combined effects of surface tension and volume resistance on the stability of these states may have implications for the understanding of stability transitions in other rotating systems of fluids with interfaces. For this scenario, we develop a novel framework that enables the microscopic expression of work, accurately reflecting its internal mechanical performance. Notably, we demonstrate that dissipated work, a critical macroscopic concept, is equivalently represented by the average increase in a system's mean squared motion energy, as well as by internal microwork done by individual microstates. Our team employed the VUV-UV multilayer interferometry method in a flow tube experiment to comprehensively analyze the ultraviolet absorption spectra of two important organic molecules, cyclopentadiene and benzene, when reacting with ozone. This approach allows for a highly resolved spectral analysis, missing in previous studies, and is made possible by using a novel multi-layer interferometry technique in combination with high sensitivity detection. A detailed comparison between calculated and measured spectra revealed that benzene exhibited significantly higher [CCH]/[CN] abundance ratios, with estimated errors of 20-30%, in various benzene dimeric isomers, indicating a higher frequency of carbon-hydrogen bonds in benzene than in cyclopentadiene. Conversely, cyclopentadiene showed higher abundance ratios of [CH]/[CH$_2$] with estimated errors of 20-30%, indicating a higher incidence of bonded CH groups in this molecule rather than in benzene. This was confirmed by subsequent quantum chemical simulations. This study showcases the capability of VUV-UV multilayer interferometry in combination with flow tube experiments to provide detailed molecular structure information through comprehensive ultraviolet absorption analysis, a technique that can be applied to a wide range of complex organic reactions. This approach offers a significant improvement over conventional methods used to identify reaction intermediates and products by comparing calculated and measured ultraviolet spectra. This novel technique can significantly enhance our understanding of complex organic reactions, even in the presence of unstable reaction intermediates that cannot be captured by traditional methods. This approach can also be a valuable tool for validating quantum chemical predictions on reaction pathways and the structures of unstable reaction intermediates by comparing their calculated and measured ultraviolet absorption spectra. We introduce a novel attention mechanism called look-ahead attention in neural machine translation to enhance the performance. By incorporating a future context, look-ahead attention allows the model to consider both current and potential subsequent interactions when generating each word. To effectively exploit future information, we developed a specific scanning pattern for look-ahead attention, and through residual connection and position-wise attention, significantly improved our model's translation quality. Our results show significant gains of +2.8 and +1.4 BLEU scores for large and small vocabulary tests respectively when using the IWSLT'14 subtitling dataset. Furthermore, look-ahead attention allowed a 30% reduction in model size with minimal loss in performance. We also achieved a high score of 33.6 BLEU on the WMT'14 English-to-German dataset using the large vocabulary test. Our code is available online for replication and future reference.

The Gridscape project aims to create a comprehensive framework for developing and utilizing grid computing technologies through a translational approach. This involves transferring successful concepts from scientific research to practical applications and vice versa. The project's website serves as a dynamic knowledge repository that reflects the current state of the project, its technologies, and associated research. The repository is filled with concepts identified through a systematic review of grid computing literature and is openly accessible via OWL web pages. The repository's concepts have been successfully utilized in developing several prominent grid computing projects, including TeraGrid, Globus, and OpenGridServices. The repository has also facilitated the incorporation of semantic technologies into the Gridscape project, specifically in developing the GSN standard for service-level agreements. We start with a fundamental formulation of the Bunch-Davies state for a scalar field in an expanding universe, using the conformal time and computing the two-point correlation function to obtain the mass term's viscosity coefficient. This calculation yields a specific expression that reflects the cosmological mass scale and harmonic number, which in turn influences the decay of relative fluctuations in the field's value. Notably, this effect cannot be described using a simple "viscosity" concept, which is seen to vary dynamically with the cosmological expansion. Instead, it appears as a time-dependent coefficient in a universal diffusion term, which seems to embody the fundamental properties of thermal fluctuations. Consequently, this formulation seems to embody a thermal universe's fundamental characteristics, which underlie both the cosmological perturbation theory and primordial fluctuation magnification, specifically nonlinear, localized gravitational effects that manifest in the universe's late stages. In this context, the cosmic gravitational hierarchy emerges as a manifestation of the thermal universe's self-organization process, where the cosmological mass scale serves as a critical parameter that governs the hierarchy's rate of progression. As a result, this formulation provides a new, thermodynamic perspective on the cosmic gravitational hierarchy, which is supported by the fundamental properties of thermal fluctuations in an expanding universe. Furthermore, this perspective offers a theoretical basis for further exploring the fundamental properties of the thermal universe, its fluctuations, and its gravitational consequences. Ultimately, this could lead to a deeper understanding of the universe's nonlinear gravitational effects and its eventual thermal demise. Recent research in curiosity has focused primarily on an individual's internal motivations and processes. In contrast, our work explores how social factors influence curiosity, building on theories that curiosity serves as a driving force for exploration and discovery. Our study investigates how peers influence curiosity in school settings and found that students' curiosity towards their peers is substantial. Furthermore, our results show that the desire to distinguish oneself from peers and gain their approval can either excite curiosity or lead to its suppression. When the need for distinction or approval is high, individuals may become anxious and less curious due to these competing demands. However, when the desire for distinction or approval is low to moderate, individuals may become curious as they seek to outdo their peers or meet their expectations. These findings highlight the complex interplay between social factors and curiosity and underscore the importance of considering multiple aspects of curiosity, including its causes and consequences, to achieve a comprehensive understanding. Ultimately, our study suggests that curiosity can be seen as a multifaceted driver of exploration and discovery, rather than a mere byproduct. To further this line of inquiry, we propose several theoretical concepts, including the activation of curiosity through distinction and approval, its expansion to consider collective versus individual desires, and its application to analytical and creative domains. Our framework can be applied to various domains, such as education, marketing, and scientific research, and can be utilized to guide the design of experiments and interventions aimed at studying and promoting curiosity. In the context of education, our model suggests that learning goals should be set in a way that allows students to develop their unique interests and that students should be encouraged to explore their individual passions, as well as those of their peers, to foster curiosity. Additionally, our framework implies that curiosity can be triggered through novel experiences that create a sense of distinction, such as novel experiences that create a sense of distinction, and that curiosity can be sustained through engagement with diverse perspectives and ideas. Overall, our study offers a social perspective on curiosity that can be applied across domains and can inform the design of research and interventions aimed at studying and promoting curiosity. Currently, Graph Matérn Gaussian Processes (GMPs) are largely confined to batch learning or can be straightforwardly integrated into Bayesian models using conjugate updates due to their complex marginal likelihood function. In our research, we develop an exact stochastic variational method for batch and non-conjugate learning within GMPs, enabling the seamless incorporation of Graph Matérn Gaussian Processes into modern Bayesian models, particularly those involving inference over graph inputs as side effects like GMP-NNs and Gaussian process Bayesian vector autoregressives. Our solution not only expands the applicability of GMPs but also also allows for influential graph parameters to be learned on a case-by-case basis during posterior updates. We empirically validate the benefits of this approach across synthetic data, GMP-NNs, vector autoregressives, and a real-world application. Our contribution is two-fold: it both broadens the GMPs' usability and enhances their capability to handle complex Bayesian modeling scenarios.

As cities invest heavily in developing smart infrastructure and technologies, the increasing popularity of ridesourcing services such as Uber and Lyft presents an opportunity to enhance sensing capabilities in urban areas. By equipping ridesourcing vehicles with sensors, cities can fill gaps in their sensing coverage, particularly on main roads where these vehicles frequently operate. However, the city's sensing performance is ultimately constrained by the speed of data processing, as only real-time data can be analyzed to optimize traffic management. In this research, we develop a mathematical model to optimize the deployment of sensors in ridesourcing networks to cover critical areas in real-time. Our results show that this "now" coverage can be nearly 100% achievable in some areas, and we analyze the effects of varying key factors such as sensor range, driving speed, and routing protocols. Furthermore, we investigate how to maintain high coverage reliability in the face of moving obstacles and dynamically changing traffic patterns. Our approach involves formulating a sensing problem as an efficient discovery of geometrically optimal spheres and provides a framework for future optimization methods. Additionally, we highlight the potential applications of this research to other mobile sensor networks. To facilitate practical implementation, we develop a prototype system utilizing Uber's API to demonstrate the sensing capabilities of ridesourcing vehicles in an actual city setting. This collaborative approach between cities and ridesourcing companies is crucial to successfully leveraging these resources. We examine a family of variable stepsize Stochastic Gradient Linear Models (SGLMs) for online learning and derive generalization bounds for them in the context of bounded data and smooth loss functions. Our results demonstrate that these models achieve similar generalization performance to traditional fixed stepsize Linear Models when using uniform grid sizes, but can exhibit enhanced performance with nonuniform grid sizes. Furthermore, we investigate a specific algorithm and show that it adheres to a specific total step count constraint, leading to an upper bound on its generalization error. To enhance algorithms, we propose an enhancement that leverages past mean squared errors, resulting in an accelerated algorithm. Computational experiments validate the theoretical findings, revealing that the proposed algorithm accelerates traditional fixed stepsize Linear Models by a factor of $O(\sqrt{T})$, and can also outperform them by a factor of $O(T^{1/3})$ under constrained total step counts. Multi-sensor data analysis can be an complex and intricate problem to solve, often requiring the integration of multiple signal processing techniques to achieve meaningful results. A method known as Minimum-Framework Spatial-Spectral Distance Analysis, or MFSSA, has been previously developed to address this challenge and has demonstrated effectiveness in simulated environments. However, the method's practical applicability in real-world settings remains unclear. To investigate this, we created two analysis scenarios involving temperature curve analysis and remote sensing image analysis. In the first scenario, we aimed to identify the time-dependent temperatures at specific locations within a subject's body by using infrared sensors mounted on the subject in motion. In the second scenario, we sought to locate and characterize artificial objects while analyzing high-resolution satellite images containing subtle color variations and significant background noise. The results from both scenarios showcase MFSSA's capability to yield accurate frameworks and subsequently locate the target features. Furthermore, the method's ability to handle multi-sensor data and robustness to noise were also demonstrated. The code used to analyze the data in both scenarios is openly accessible online. Additionally, the implications of applying MFSSA in real-world scenarios with MFSSA's theoretical framework are explored. To facilitate replication of our methods, the code employed in this research has been made publicly available online.

Determining the fusion rules for non-invertible symmetries within a field theory has long been a challenging problem in theoretical physics. By leveraging the principles of category theory, we develop an overarching framework that seamlessly applies to both lattice regularization and continuum approaches. Our framework intuitively captures the non-invertible symmetries through their action on sector operators and derives the necessary and sufficient conditions for their fusion processes. Most programming pseudocodes adhere to a visual syntax that is easily misunderstood, containing errors common to many programming languages. In contrast, logical pseudocodes are written in a clear, error-free syntax but are often difficult to execute due to their unconventional notation. To address the limitations of both types of pseudocodes, we propose a new specification framework that integrates desirable traits from logical and traditional pseudocodes, ensuring both correctness and safety. This proposed framework serves as a foundation for a pseudocode that can be executed across diverse platforms, including web browsers and mobile apps. To illustrate the effectiveness of this proposed framework, we developed a prototype executor for a pseudocode variant that extends JavaScript syntax. This prototype allows users to execute pseudocodes seamlessly within Node.js applications. To expand the executor's capabilities, we also explored compiling the proposed pseudocodes to native machine code using LLVM. Ultimately, our study aims to stimulate discussions and guide developments towards creating executable pseudocodes that can be freely executed anywhere, promoting clearer and safer programming communication. This proposal and proof-of-concept execution framework are now available online. We look forward to sharing our findings with the programming community through a research paper to be presented at the International Conference on Software Engineering. Our study is openly collaborative, and we invite software engineers to join the ongoing discussion and contribute to this research on GitHub. We believe that this joint effort is crucial to establishing a widely adopted, executable pseudocode standard, which is essential for better programming communication and education.
