The Boolean lattice of order n, denoted as Bn, consists of 2^n elements, arranged in a layered structure where each layer represents a potential binary string of length n. A coloring of a Boolean lattice is considered "rainbow" if every edge connects two nodes of different colors. The purpose of this study is to determine the minimum number (rainbow number) required to color the edges of a Boolean lattice in such a way that every subset of elements in a specific Boolean lattice structure contains a rainbow edge. We are particularly interested in the Boolean lattice with 5 elements, and our findings show that using 27 colors is sufficient to achieve this condition for B5. Additionally, our findings imply that certain smaller rainbow numbers used in previous studies are indeed the smallest possible, which provides a related result. Another key aspect of this study is the identification of a new lower bound for the Boolean rainbow Ramsey number of order 5, set at 27. Notably, this new lower bound is the same as the previously established upper bound, which indicates that 27 is the smallest possible number for this condition. We would like to emphasize that our proof of the 27 lower bound involves a novel approach, in contrast to the existing upper bound proof. Furthermore, our findings highlight an interesting correlation between coloring the edges of a Boolean lattice and the properties of a specific set within that lattice. This correlation can aid researchers in better comprehending the structure of Boolean lattices and their associated rainbow numbers. Lastly, our study paves the way for further exploration into the rainbow numbers of larger Boolean lattices.

Although the $k$-means clustering issue has been extensively researched, the majority of prior coreset applications for this problem required a multi-step process. In contrast, this study presents a novel one-step coreset construction algorithm for $k$-means clustering with an approximately uniform distribution, demonstrating its efficiency and practical value. The proposed method first establishes a coreset with a fixed size $m$ for $k$-means clustering in $O(nkd)$ time, where $n$ represents the number of data points. Furthermore, this algorithm is exceptionally versatile, allowing it to be adapted to various $k$-means variants, such as weighted $k$-means and sparse $k$-means, with comparable efficiency. When the input is nearly ordered, specifically when the $n$th data point is $\Theta(dn^{-\frac{2}{3}})$ away from the $(n-1)$th data point, this method can be refined to create a coreset with an almost uniform distribution in $O(nkd)$ time, significantly surpassing the time complexity of prior coreset construction algorithms for $k$-means clustering. Moreover, this study introduces a new lower bound for the size of coresets required for $k$-means clustering, demonstrating that a coreset of $\Omega(kd\frac{\log k}{\log k})$ points is essential to achieve an approximation ratio of $\Theta(\frac{\log k}{\log k})$. In contrast, this lower bound is outperformed by the proposed one-step coreset construction algorithm, which uses a coreset of $O(kd\frac{\log k}{\log k})$ points to achieve an approximation ratio of $O(\frac{\log k}{\log k})$. The algorithms developed in this study are applicable to any $k$-means variant that can be solved efficiently and may provide a framework for coreset construction in other clustering problems. Additionally, this study introduces a new approach to analyze the quality of clustering, utilizing the expected squared distance between data points and their corresponding cluster centers as a performance metric. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated through experiments on real-world datasets, yielding coresets with superior quality and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code for the algorithms presented in this study is available online.

In large-scale grid worlds, complex scenarios can be simplified by breaking down the map into smaller, independent areas called superstates. Each superstate has its own distinct characteristics, effectively reducing the scope of the search space. This representation enables hierarchical reasoning and allows for efficient computation of policies in partially ordered scenarios. However, scenarios that don't fit this structure require a different approach. In this paper, we focus on hierarchical state space models for pursuit-evasion problems in grid worlds, exploring algorithms that balance computational complexity with optimal solutions. We evaluate and compare multiple methods for computing policies, including linear programming and Monte Carlo planning, considering factors like solution quality, computational time, and scalability. Our findings reveal that Monte Carlo planning is the most reliable and scalable option, even if it's computationally intensive. This study provides a foundation for future work on hierarchical reasoning in pursuit-evasion scenarios, as well as potential applications in various multi-agent systems. Additionally, our research is accompanied by an open-source tool that enables users to generate random pursuit-evasion scenarios and compute optimal policies through Monte Carlo planning. This framework is readily available for download and can be utilized to create custom scenarios or compute policies for up to 5 agents per superstate. As the field continues to evolve, future research should consider more sophisticated hierarchical models and state representations to address more complex pursuit-evasion scenarios. This paper is presented as a chapter for the UM-IU Graduate Student Conference. It has been reviewed by peers from the University of Michigan and the University of Iowa.

In 1991, Graham, Kleitman, and Szemerdi introduced a unique classification for n-tuples that aren't nontransitive in any direction. A class of n elements, represented as pairs (a, b), with a being the outcome of applying a strategy against another, is considered "not [k+1]-transitive" if there's a number k, where applying a different strategy yields a different outcome against the same class, and this new outcome is also different from the original result. It's essential to note that this definition requires the two new outcomes to be from a different relation, such as being k+1 instead of k. For our purposes, we'll use a simplified definition that only needs one outcome to be different. It's also important to note that this definition only works when n is greater than 2. 

In 2016, Antipov and Krasil'nikov established a connection between the nontransitive n-tuples and the polynomials that have n distinct roots. They used a specific transformation to set this connection, and it led to an in-depth analysis of the transitive n-tuples through the use of a specific sum. This analysis included a lower bound for the number of transitive n-tuples, and it also revealed a surprising link between the nontransitive n-tuples and the extremal values of the sum.

In this paper, we're taking the Antipov-Krasil'nikov approach a step further by generalizing the studied sum and identifying new upper and lower bounds for both nontransitive and transitive n-tuples. It's worth noting that these new bounds provide a clearer understanding of the nontransitive n-tuples, and they are more comprehensive than the previous limits established by GKS in 1991. Additionally, our generalized sum and the newly identified bounds can be applied across various relations, including but not limited to k+1 vs. k. 

Our primary objective in this paper is to present these new upper and lower bounds for nontransitive n-tuples, and we're also exploring the possibility of establishing a Supersolvable Antimagic Total Edge k-coloring for certain types of graphs. However, our main focus in this paper is on generalizing the GKS bounds, and we're inviting further discussion on this topic.

This study proposes a new deep learning approach that leverages adaptive instance normalization layers to enhance the cycleGAN framework when applying unsupervised room layout segmentation to RGB images. The proposed adaptive cycleGAN (A-cGAN) architecture improves cycleGAN's performance by integrating AdaIN layers, which facilitates the reversal of complex non-linear transformations and significantly reduces the required numbers of layers. Specifically, the AdaIN layer's ability to apply learned affine transformations to intermediate layer features enables the simple reversal of source and target codes in the cycleGAN architecture. We further analyze how this approach restricts the allowed transformations and demonstrate its efficacy in room layout segmentation applications. The proposed A-cGAN architecture also serves as a starting point for future research on using AdaIN layers in cycleGAN-like architectures. This approach simplifies the comparison between diverse conversational samples by using a common frame of reference, and is easy to train using conversational relevance ranking. The concept of deformed halo structures is explored through the study of lead isotopes. Lead isotopes are exceptional due to the high probability of finding extended distributions of motion typical of halos, combining both rotational and stationary states within a single nucleus. Researchers suggest that the shape of these lead isotopes might transition from halos to deformed shapes as rotational states increase in probability. To investigate this theory, researchers used the FINUDA anti-proton spectrometer at the Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati to study $\beta$-delayed proton spectra for $^{20}$Ne isotopes targeting an antiproton target with a thin $^{15}$N layer. Upon detection, the FINUDA anti-proton spectrometer provided $\beta$-delayed proton spectra for the $^{20}$Ne isotope. By comparing these results with Monte Carlo simulations, researchers were able to determine the antiproton production cross-sections for various final states of the $^{20}$Ne isotope at rest. Furthermore, researchers utilized the FINUDA anti-proton spectrometer to study $\beta$-delayed proton spectra for $^{15}$C, $^{16}$C, $^{17}$C, and $^{18}$C isotopes. The study revealed a notable enhancement in the antiproton production cross-section for the $^{15}$C, $^{16}$C, and $^{18}$C isotopes, attributing it to the breakdown of the Pauli exclusion principle due to highly overlapping wave functions typical of very small nuclei. The research also allowed researchers to compare the antiproton production cross-sections for ground and rotational states in lead isotopes. The analysis indicates that the density distribution of rotating halos is significantly more compact, with a radius around 7% smaller than its stationary counterpart. The discovery of this compactification provides a key insight into the behavior of rotating very extended systems, also relevant to the study of rotating neutron stars. In multi-task reinforcement learning, a single learned dynamics model can lead to suboptimal performance or even failure in other tasks due to its limited coverage and potential bias. This research explores an alternative approach where multiple task models are trained simultaneously to predict future states in a centralized learning framework. We investigate various ways to combine these models, considering their individual performance and a new metric that penalizes models for errors in state predictions that may actually occur. By optimizing this metric, we find a combined model that significantly outperforms individual models and demonstrates robustness in handling complex transition dynamics. Additionally, our results show that centralized learning with multiple models can scale to a large number of tasks. We also examine different architectures for these models and find that a simple structure is sufficient for transition models to achieve good results. Our code is available online for replication of our methods and results. Furthermore, we include an example policy using these models in model-based policy optimization, showing that centralized transition learning can be an effective pretraining strategy for challenging tasks requiring significant exploration, such as navigating an unseen environment after initial state information is withdrawn. Our approach leads to significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods in the simple case and matches or surpasses performance in more challenging scenarios after only a limited additional training. Overall, our work suggests that learning multiple transition models can be an effective way to enhance performance and robustness in model-based reinforcement learning. Our approach also raises interesting questions about the potential benefits of learning these models in an online setting with continuous feedback. We hope our findings motivate further research in this area.

This article examines how the presence of boundaries affects the solution to a differential equation on a noncompact manifold. By establishing an alternative proof of the Fredholm alternative for differential equations with boundary conditions, this research also explores the impact of compact boundaries on the solutions' behavior. Additionally, some numerical examples are provided to illustrate the persistent transients phenomenon observed in differential equations with compact boundaries. This phenomenon involves solutions requiring an extended period to reach a stable, boundary-attracting state. Furthermore, this research also highlights the significance of employing high-order methods to achieve accurate results for periodic solutions occurring in systems with compact boundaries. This is evident from the numerical analysis of an applied mathematical model involving a boundary-driven system of equations. The model in question arises from a limiting process of an original system of equations as a key parameter undergoes a continuous decrease towards a boundary value. The resulting model then comprises a system of equations with compact boundaries, where solutions to this model demonstrate the persistent transients phenomenon. The research also emphasizes the importance of solution smoothness in the presence of compact boundaries, as demonstrated through the application of the Fredholm alternative to a particular differential equation. This involves the use of the Sobolev space $H^2$ in lieu of the smoother space $H^4$. The reason for this preference stems from the increased efficiency and reduced computational requirements of such methods. The research presented in this article is relevant to the ongoing investigation of boundary phenomena in nonlinear differential equations and systems of equations. The associated numerical examples are set within the context of the global asymptotic chemical reaction network model. The goal of the research is to provide an exploration of compact boundary effects on solution behavior through the use of the Fredholm alternative and numerical solution methods. The study is also intended to serve as a call to action for furthering the understanding of persistent transients in nonlinear differential equations and systems of equations. The research is complemented by an accompanying technical report, which includes an alternative proof of the Fredholm alternative for differential equations with boundary conditions, as well as a discussion on the convergence of approximate solutions. We challenged the long-held assumption in camera calibration that a combination of image features and object points is necessary, instead advocating for direct regression of camera parameters from images alone. Our approach, novel in the context of self-calibration and minimalistic, eliminates the need for prior object detection or segmentation, significantly simplifying the calibration process. We demonstrate the efficacy of direct regression by surpassing traditional methods on multiple benchmarks, while our experiments in a more practical setting suggest our approach holds promise. To facilitate future research, we introduce a simple yet effective method for estimating camera distortion from a single image, and our code and models are readily available for use.

This paper examines the concept of invariance in fractional order systems and develops a theoretical framework for linear subspaces that remain unchanged under the action of fractional order dynamics. To facilitate this exploration, the paper reinterprets the fractional integration operator in the context of linear operators. Building upon this framework, we derive the conditions under which a linear subspace will be invariant to the fractional order dynamics. Specifically, we establish the relationship between these conditions and the compatibility matrix of the system. Finally, we apply this framework to examine the properties of subspaces in both the Caputo and Riemann-Liouville approaches to fractional order systems. Through this analysis, we highlight the distinct characteristics of the subspaces that remain invariant in these systems. To further illustrate this, we present examples of the invariance properties of specific subspaces in both Caputo and Riemann-Liouville systems. As terahertz frequencies gain prominence for high-throughput wireless communications, research into the feasibility of multi-hop terahertz links is increasing. These links offer a reliable path for sustainable data transmission and can provide connectivity to distant endpoints. However, terahertz signals are prone to significant attenuation and require sophisticated beam training techniques to compensate. We introduce an efficient method for beam training in multi-hop terahertz links that leverages joint training across all hops for improved performance. By optimizing the training process for a subset of hops, we can beam train an entire multi-hop system with reduced complexity. Our results show that this method achieves comparable accuracy to traditional methods while significantly enhancing efficiency. Furthermore, we find that terahertz beam training can be modeled as an interference problem and develop an iterative optimization algorithm to minimize training complexity. Additionally, we investigate various efficiency enhancement strategies and find that a quasi-deterministic approach can substantially reduce complexity. To validate our findings, we employ a large-scale simulation with up to 64 antennas per hop. Finally, we explore the practical implications of our research for future multi-hop terahertz communications networks.

During these observations, taken in 2019 and 2020, we detected scintillations from the pulsar and located 32 individual scattering screens, with distances ranging uniformly from approximately 1.6 to 3.2 kiloparsecs, providing a precise measurement of the distance to this system. Annotating large sets of text documents for machine learning applications is often hindered by the time and expense associated with manual labeling. While existing tools offer some automation for specific tasks, there remains a significant need for advanced technology to enhance annotator efficiency. In response to this challenge, we've developed ActiveDocument, a system designed to let human annotators work in an interactive loop with the support of machine learning models. By leveraging a limited number of model-driven suggestions per document, we've seen a notable increase - around 40% - in annotation speed with no decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our system allows for diverse annotation styles to be easily incorporated, demonstrating its potential as a platform for creating a wide range of annotated datasets. Additionally, we found that simply providing model-driven suggestions to annotators isn't enough, and that a more strategic approach is required to maximize benefits. To support the development of similar systems, we're releasing around 150,000 annotated sentence pairs in three different style transfer tasks, along with the models used to suggest annotations, as part of the CoQA Suggests dataset. These resources showcase the effectiveness of our system and its potential to contribute to significant advances in text generation tasks. Highway maintenance agencies face significant challenges identifying and prioritizing sections for rehabilitation or repair.  An effective solution involves utilizing mobile sensors and annotation tools to streamline the process, but a robust annotation platform is crucial for successful inspection workflows.  To address this need, we present RoadAtlas, a web-based application designed to streamline the road inspection process by providing a 3D visualization environment and enabling users to annotate and prioritize mobile sensor data.  Built using a web-based 3D rendering framework, RoadAtlas enables users to load and prioritize mobile sensor data in 3D, as well as annotate defects in a hierarchical manner and assign confidence levels to their identifications.  Furthermore, we evaluate RoadAtlas by conducting user experience evaluations and comparing its data quality to a conventional, in-situ annotation approach.  Results show that RoadAtlas leads to a significant reduction in inspection costs and yields data quality comparable to the in-situ approach, we also found that users find the application easy to use and prefer it over the conventional approach.  Overall, RoadAtlas contributes to more efficient and cost-effective road inspection processes by minimizing the need for in-situ annotations and providing a robust annotation environment that is easy to use.  By streamlining the inspection workflow, we believe that RoadAtlas has the potential to play a key role in making highway maintenance data more accurate, comprehensive, and timely.  To facilitate replication and advancement of this work, we make the RoadAtlas application available online at https://roadatlas.cs.washington.edu.  Future developers and researchers can build upon this application by using the open-source code hosted on https://github.com/wazowski/RoadAtlas.  We also provide the anonymized replication packages for the evaluations conducted in this paper at https://zenodo.org/record/4880452.  We plan to enhance RoadAtlas by incorporating real-time mobile sensor data visualization, improving its annotation capabilities, and expanding its support for additional sensor modalities.  We invite the research community to join us in further developing and refining RoadAtlas to address similar challenges in other domains and applications.  We have initial results indicating that the approach used in RoadAtlas can be applied to annotate and prioritize data in tunnels, but we require additional research to fully explore its feasibility in this context. However, the reliability of these models heavily depends on the accuracy of the underlying hyperbolic space assignment. In order to address this limitation, we propose a new type of graph convolutional network called the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN). This innovative model treats the graph structure as a flexible manifold that can be both Euclidean and non-Euclidean, allowing for accurate node feature representation through a fixed parametric transformation without needing explicit assignment of the underlying manifold. Furthermore, we devise an accurate and efficient method for computing closed-form ancestors in the context of Lorentzian graphs. Moreover, we develop a distinctive abstraction technique for graph normalization, making it applicable to varied graph manifolds. Lastly, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed LGCN by showcasing substantial performance improvements over existing HGCNs on numerous datasets across both node classification and link prediction tasks. Additionally, we showcase the versatility of our method by successfully applying it to Euclidean graphs, achieving notable gains over baseline models. The variability of a linearized gravity theory, specifically general relativity, is analyzed in this research to understand how adding a mass term to the perturbation affects the number of degrees of freedom. The inclusion of a mass term is examined in the context of both pure gravity and Brans-Dicke gravity theories. The study reveals that the number of propagating modes in linearized gravity can differ based on the specific metric used to analyze the variables, highlighting a long-standing issue in the field. The research proposes a clear resolution to this controversy and provides a novel explanation for the discrepancies. The reasons for the varying results in previous studies are identified and distinguished from the valid solutions by a key distinction: they fail to satisfy the necessary criteria for physical degrees of freedom established by Bouchendira et al. In contrast, the proposed analysis meets these requirements. The study specifically examines the variable metric approach used in the research and argues that it provides the most accurate and consistent results. The inclusion of a mass term in the Einstein gravity theory is found to increase the number of degrees of freedom from one to two in some analyses; however, it is shown that these results are contingent upon the specific gauge chosen and may not hold across all conditions. The theory is further analyzed under the conformal metric approach, and the results are consistent with the established criteria for physical degrees of freedom. The study also examines the Brans-Dicke gravity theory and finds that adding a mass term does not increase the number of degrees of freedom in either the variable or conformal metric approaches. Unfortunately, many existing methods primarily focus on data reduction, neglecting the development of user-friendly visualization tools. The framework is freely accessible online, offering an interactive demo alongside comprehensive documentation, complemented by an accompanying tutorial for users to create their own ViDaExpert instances. As the field of high-dimensional data analysis continually evolves, we anticipate ViDaExpert to be a useful tool for the community, contributing to the visualization of complex data across diverse applications. The Monomial Based Approximation project has previously demonstrated the benefits of utilizing higher-order 2D and 3D approximations to represent functions and operators within a bounded domain. This project extends those benefits to unbounded domains by applying a change of variables to transform the domain into a bounded one. The novel approach involves using a 2D or 3D monomial approximation to capture the non-periodic aspects of a function across the domain. The project also explores the potential of a one-dimensional approximation to identify the dominant directions in a function's periodicity. The potential of these methods is evaluated through the approximation of the Laplacian operator and a linear PDE solution using an FFT-based solver as a comparison. The results indicate that higher-order monomial approximations can provide accurate function and operator representations, while the most informative one-dimensional approximation can significantly reduce the number of monomials required. The effects of the monomial degree and the most informative dimension on the approximation error are also examined, highlighting the potential of these methods to significantly improve the efficiency of high-order finite element methods. The proposed methods are openly available under an permissive license at <https://github.com/ghanizadeh/MBA>. The source code used to produce the results presented in this paper can be found at <https://github.com/ghanizadeh/MBA-Solvers>. The results obtained from this project suggest that high-order monomial approximations have the potential to significantly enhance the performance of iterative solvers, and the project's open-source implementation of solvers and its source code are provided to facilitate further research in this area.
